PFE is *not* the same as current exposure or an average; it is an estimate of future increase and is typically larger. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The concepts of current vs potential exposure are part of the Basel CCR framework and apply universally.

title: Exposure Metrics (EE, EPE, Peak)
one_screen: Banks summarize CCR over time using metrics like Expected Exposure (EE), Expected Positive Exposure (EPE), and peak exposure. These metrics aggregate exposure profiles into single numbers for capital and limit setting. EPE is essentially the time-weighted average of expected exposures (only when positive) over the first year; peak exposure is the high percentile of exposures.
bodyText: Expected Exposure (EE) is the average potential exposure at a specific future date. It includes only positive exposures (zero is the floor). Expected Positive Exposure (EPE) is the average of EE over multiple future dates, usually up to one year. The Basel CCR guidelines define EPE as the weighted average of expected exposures over time. “Effective EPE” is a slight variant used in IMM that applies the max of EPE or certain floors. Banks may cap EPE at the maximum expected exposure to reflect worst-case scenarios. Peak exposure (or “Peak EEPE”) is the (say) 95th or 99th percentile of all future exposure values, representing a stress point. This is used for limit-setting to ensure capital covers extreme outcomes. Typically, banks’ exposure profiles start low (time-zero exposure is often zero if no up-front payment) and rise as time passes, then fall near maturity for some products. The shape depends on the type of derivative. For example, a vanilla interest rate swap might have exposures that rise and then fall. ### Permanent rule Regulatory capital for CCR often uses EPE (a weighted average exposure) and peak exposures, not just point-in-time values. ### Permanent trap Using one date’s exposure as representative, or confusing average (EPE) with worst-case (peak). EPE is an average, not a worst-case measure. ### Never confuse **Expected Positive Exposure (EPE)** — The time-weighted average of expected exposures (only positive) over a horizon. --- **Peak Exposure** — A high percentile (e.g. 95%) of exposure across time. Peak exposure is *not* the same as EPE (average); it typically exceeds EPE. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Basel CCR metrics like EPE and peak are used globally; all jurisdictions adopting SA-CCR follow this.

title: Wrong-Way Risk
one_screen: Wrong-way risk arises when market movements that increase exposure to a counterparty coincide with an increase in that counterparty’s default probability. In general WWR, the counterparty’s credit quality worsens with adverse market factors. In specific WWR, a direct link exists (e.g. the counterparty has credit exposure to the underlying).
bodyText: Wrong-way risk (WWR) means exposure and credit risk are positively correlated. If exposure to a bank is higher exactly when that bank is more likely to default, losses can be severe. Specific WWR examples include: a bank sells credit protection on itself, or an airline enters a fuel swap where fuel price spikes hurt the airline’s credit. General WWR examples include: a corporate bond dealer holds interest rate swaps with companies; if interest rates rise, swap exposure grows while those companies’ creditworthiness may fall. Banks must identify both general and specific WWR. Specific WWR often comes from linked transactions or collateral (e.g. dealer pledges defaultable collateral). General WWR emerges from broad market shifts (e.g. recession). Basel rules and supervisory guidance require monitoring of WWR through stress tests. According to Fed guidance: “Wrong-way risk occurs when the exposure to a counterparty is positively correlated with the probability of default of the counterparty itself. Specific WWR arises from the nature of the transactions; general WWR arises from market factors”. ### Permanent rule Banks must identify WWR and avoid taking on transactions where exposure and counterparty strength move together. WWR should be quantified in stress scenarios. ### Permanent trap Ignoring correlations between market moves and credit risk. For example, assuming collateral fully protects without considering if collateral value is itself at risk in the same scenario. ### Never confuse **General Wrong-Way Risk** — Exposure correlated with broad market factors affecting credit (macro-driven). --- **Specific Wrong-Way Risk** — Exposure directly linked to counterparty’s default risk (contract-specific link). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** WWR concepts are universal in Basel/ICS framework.

title: Close-Out Netting
one_screen: Close-out netting is a legal mechanism allowing a bank to terminate all transactions with a defaulted counterparty and net them into a single amount owed by one party to the other. If enforceable, netting greatly reduces exposure, since only the netted positive value is at risk rather than each trade’s full value.
bodyText: Netting is documented in master agreements (like an ISDA Master). Upon default, all trades in a netting set are “closed out” at current market values and netted. The surviving bank then has a single net claim or obligation. Enforceability of netting depends on jurisdiction and legal opinions. If netting fails (e.g. in bankruptcy some local law does not recognize it), the bank faces each trade’s exposure separately. Netting reduces CCR by off-setting gains and losses. For example, if bank A owes $5 on one swap but is owed $3 on another with the same counterparty, netting lets A owe only $2 instead of risking $8. Banks rely on netting to lower capital and collateral needs. Supervisors require proof that netting agreements are legally valid. A broken netting could double-count exposure and increase losses. ### Permanent rule Only legally enforceable netting agreements count toward reducing exposure. Without enforceability, netting benefits cannot be recognized. ### Permanent trap Assuming netting always works. If a jurisdiction or failure scenario prohibits close-out netting, exposures cannot be netted. Each contract’s exposure must then be held separately. ### Never confuse **Bilateral Netting (Master netting)** — Offsetting trades between two parties under one agreement, where obligations are legally netted. --- **Portfolio Compression** — A multilateral process of reducing notional without involving close-out netting. It does not affect legal netting sets. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Netting rules vary by law, but the concept of enforceability is universal. Banks obtain legal opinions country by country.

title: Collateral and Margin
one_screen: Collateral is a key mitigation tool for CCR. Variation margin (VM) and initial margin (IM) are two collateral types. VM is exchanged to cover current mark-to-market exposure daily, protecting against immediate losses. IM is posted upfront or periodically to cover potential future exposure over a margin period of risk.
bodyText: Under a margin agreement (CSA), counterparties exchange VM whenever the contract’s market value changes. VM ensures that current exposures are collateralized. Initial margin (sometimes called independent amount) is additional collateral that covers the risk during the margin period of risk (the time to close out trades after default). Thus IM protects against volatile moves that occur between margin calls. Collateral agreements may include **thresholds** (amounts below which no VM is exchanged) and **minimum transfer amounts** (small amounts exempt). These can leave small exposures uncollateralized. IM is typically applied symmetrically (both parties must post if in scope). Once posted, collateral is often rehypothecated (re-used) by the receiver, which can introduce risk if that receiver fails. Margin requirements for non-cleared trades (BCBS-IOSCO rules) phased in from 2016–2022; by 2022 most large participants must exchange both VM and IM on bilateral trades. These global rules standardize collateral for non-centrally-cleared derivatives. Variation margin is typically transferred daily, while initial margin amounts depend on regulatory formulae or models. ### Permanent rule Collateral must be valued daily, and variation margin called frequently (often daily). Collateral credit quality should be high (e.g. cash, sovereign debt) to avoid further risk. ### Permanent trap Treating posted collateral as risk-free. If collateral is rehypothecated or volatile, it may not fully protect against loss. Also, assuming thresholds or IM exempt all risk. ### Never confuse **Variation Margin (VM)** — Collateral exchanged to cover current exposure (daily mark-to-market). --- **Initial Margin (IM)** — Up-front collateral to cover potential future exposure over a margin period. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** BCBS-IOSCO margining standards apply globally for regulated participants. Some jurisdictions (e.g. India) are still using older models with updated add-on factors.

title: Margin Period of Risk & Related Terms
one_screen: The margin period of risk (MPR) is the time assumed between a counterparty’s default and the liquidation or hedging of the position. It determines how much additional future price movement risk the initial margin must cover. Regulators often assume 10 days or more for the MPR.
bodyText: When a counterparty defaults, trades do not immediately settle; the surviving party needs time to revalue or replace trades. The MPR covers this lag. For example, if a bank assumes a 10-day MPR, it calculates potential exposure assuming markets move during those 10 days. IM posted is meant to cover losses that could arise in that period. A longer MPR means greater PFE (since more days of potential move), so higher IM. Other collateral terms: **Threshold** is the uncollateralized exposure allowed (e.g. $0 for major banks), **Minimum Transfer Amount (MTA)** is a floor below which no margin is transferred, and **Independent Amount (IA)** is an extra fixed IM buffer. These terms are specified in the CSA. A bank must model the MPR correctly; underestimating it can leave exposure when collateral is stale. ### Permanent rule When computing PFE (in SA-CCR or IMM), include an appropriate margin period of risk. Regulators mandate conservative MPR assumptions (often 10–20 days for non-cleared). ### Permanent trap Forgetting that collateral calls aren’t instantaneous. A default may occur during periods when collateral isn’t updated (e.g. weekend or holiday), so exposure can grow. ### Never confuse **Margin Period of Risk (MPR)** — The assumed time to close out positions after default, used in PFE calculation. --- **Maturity (T)** — The time until a trade’s normal expiration. These get mixed up but MPR is usually much shorter than T. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Basel SA-CCR and IMM define MPR parameters; implementations are consistent across major regulators.

title: Rehypothecation
one_screen: Rehypothecation is the practice where the collateral receiver re-uses (re-pledges) the client’s collateral to fund its own activities. This can create risk: if the receiver defaults, the original pledgor might not get full collateral back.
bodyText: Many counterparties allow rehypothecation of collateral (especially cash), effectively giving the collateral-receiver a lien on it. This can improve liquidity for dealers but introduces systemic risk. If the client counterparty defaults but its posted collateral is rehypothecated and then lost or seized, the client cannot reclaim it. As a result, regulators have restricted rehypothecation in some cases (e.g. segregated accounts), and banking regulations may require some client collateral be held in special segregated accounts. Rehypothecation issues arose in past crises (e.g. 2008 Bear Stearns). Current guidelines encourage limiting rehypothecation or requiring full disclosure to clients. In CCR terms, rehypothecated collateral may not provide full protection: banks should consider the availability of collateral in stress (if collateral is encumbered elsewhere). ### Permanent rule Do not double-count rehypothecated collateral. Once collateral is rehypothecated, the receiving party’s obligation to return it remains, but the collateral may not be free to use for own risk. ### Permanent trap Assuming posted collateral is safe and available even if rehypothecated. In reality, if the receiving bank is insolvent, the collateral may be tied up. ### Never confuse **Pledged Collateral** — Collateral a counterparty provides as security. --- **Rehypothecation** — The reuse of pledged collateral by the receiver. These are not the same; rehypothecated collateral may be co-mingled with others’ assets. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Rules on rehypothecation may vary legally, but concept is global. Many jurisdictions allow limited rehypothecation under CSAs.

title: Uncleared Margin Rules
one_screen: The global “Uncleared Margin Rules” (UMR) require banks and other dealers to post both variation and initial margin on non-centrally-cleared OTC derivatives. Phased implementation began in 2016, with the last group of counterparties complying by 2022. UMR ensure broad use of VM/IM even for bilateral trades.
bodyText: UMR (BCBS-IOSCO) mandated that each phase, based on aggregate notional, requires IM for entities above a threshold. The key goal is to mitigate tail risk by ensuring collateral is posted on nearly all large OTC trades. Before UMR, many bilateral trades had no margin except VM for regulated dealers; now even unregistered entities might need to post VM/IM when counterparties are in scope. Under UMR, variation margin was required from 2016 for the largest dealers, and initial margin was phased in by 2022 for basically all participants with US$50bn+ notional. By 2022, most major dealers globally must exchange VM (daily) and IM (initial margin) for new and legacy trades. This rule is enforceable via regulations in each jurisdiction (e.g. US final rule, EU regulation, etc.). ### Permanent rule Global margining standards under UMR must be incorporated. Failing to post required margin can lead to capital add-ons or regulatory penalties. ### Permanent trap Overlooking smaller counterparties. Even many hedge funds, asset managers, and corporates are now subject to initial margin requirements once thresholds were reduced in phase 6. ### Never confuse **Uncleared Margin Rules (UMR)** — Global regulatory requirements for posting IM/VM on non-cleared derivatives. --- **Clearinghouse Margin** — Collateral required by a CCP for cleared trades. UMR applies to bilateral trades only. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** UMR are a global BCBS-IOSCO standard; all G20 jurisdictions have rules implementing the schedule.

title: Central Clearing and CCPs
one_screen: Central counterparties (CCPs) mitigate bilateral CCR by interposing themselves between participants. When two parties clear through a CCP, each party’s counterparty becomes the CCP. The CCP nets trades among all members and manages default risk via margins and a waterfall. CCP clearing removes bilateral credit exposure but introduces new exposures to the CCP itself.
bodyText: A CCP provides multilateral netting: all trades in a given product with the CCP are netted across parties daily. This significantly lowers gross exposures. CCPs require initial and variation margin from members, and maintain a default fund contributed by members (and sometimes the CCP’s own capital). If a member defaults, its margin is used first; then its default fund contribution; then the CCP’s “skin in the game”; then possibly a mutualized fund of other members. Thus, CCP risk is mutualized. However, CCPs do not eliminate all risk. Members now face the CCP’s credit and liquidity risk. A CCP could face simultaneous defaults (e.g. extreme market moves), in which case default fund and possibly additional loss-sharing can be used. Clients clearing through a member have either “house” or “client” accounts; in some models, client positions are segregated, reducing risk of using client funds to cover a dealer’s losses. Central clearing is usually mandated or incentivized for standardized derivatives (e.g. interest rate swaps). Studies show CCPs greatly reduce systemic exposure but can concentrate risk in the CCP, so regulators treat CCP exposures carefully. ### Permanent rule When a trade is centrally cleared, CCR is replaced by the CCP’s counterparty risk. A bank must hold capital for its exposure to the CCP under special rules. ### Permanent trap Assuming central clearing removes all CCR. Even with a CCP, residual risk (e.g. gap risk, liquidity, CCP default) remains. ### Never confuse **Clearing Member** — A firm that is a direct member of a CCP. --- **Client** — An end-user or customer whose trades are cleared by a member. Clients have indirect exposure to the CCP through the member. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Basel and major regulators recognize CCP clearing similarly. Entities are categorized (e.g. QCCP) under capital rules.

title: Default Waterfall
one_screen: A CCP’s default waterfall is its ordered pool of resources to cover a member’s losses. Typically, waterfall layers are: the defaulting member’s initial margin → the member’s default fund contribution → the CCP’s own capital (“skin in the game”) → the mutualized default fund of surviving members. If losses exceed all, additional measures (like assessments or equity auction) are used.
bodyText: For example, if Member X defaults on a large loss, the CCP applies X’s margin first. If that is insufficient, it takes X’s share of the default fund. If still short, the CCP’s own capital absorbs the remainder (to align incentives). Finally, non-defaulting members’ default fund contributions cover any further shortfall. This ensures that members have “skin” in the outcome of defaults. Waterfalls vary by CCP, but all include these layers. An incentivized contribution (skin in game) is usually 5–10% of required default fund. Capital regulations may allow partial offset for default fund contributions. The structure ensures losses are contained and predictable. Client clearing often has special default procedures: for example, a clearing member’s default may lead to porting client positions to other members or liquidating client trades separately, depending on segregation arrangements. ### Permanent rule Only pledged margin and default fund contributions are at risk first. The order of the waterfall must be respected. Clearing members must cover their contributions on demand to ensure the waterfall is fully funded. ### Permanent trap Assuming mutualized funds are available immediately. In a crisis, liquidity to cover losses may not be instant, and clawback provisions may differ. ### Never confuse **Initial Margin** vs **Default Fund Contribution**. Initial margin is collateral posted for each member. Default fund contributions are shared resources by all members. They serve different roles in the waterfall. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Global CCP frameworks (CPMI-IOSCO Principles) require similar default waterfalls. Details (e.g. mandatory skin-in-game) are converging internationally.

title: Client Clearing Structures
one_screen: When clients clear through a clearing member, there are typically two models: omnibus and segregated. In omnibus clearing, all client positions are pooled under the member’s account; the member’s risk to the CCP is net of all its clients. In segregated clearing, each client’s positions are separately collateralized, isolating them in case the member defaults.
bodyText: In the omnibus model, a client’s margin might be held with other clients’, so if a client defaults or the member goes under, there can be confusion over entitlements (to be unwound by legal agreement). Segregated models (e.g. client-specific accounts) protect clients’ collateral from each other. Regulators often require at least partial segregation. If a clearing member defaults, segregated client positions can be ported or liquidated without affecting other clients; omnibus positions require more coordination. Clearing members must report client exposures to regulators and meet margin calls including client trades. The client still faces the clearing member credit risk unless the clearing is fully segregated (in which the client’s only counterparty is the CCP, effectively). Capital rules often treat client-cleared positions differently from house positions (e.g. risk weights, recognition of client collateral). ### Permanent rule A clearing member must disclose and segregate client funds and trades as per CCP rules. Clients must be informed how their positions are held (omnibus vs segregated). ### Permanent trap Assuming client collateral fully covers client losses even if pooled with others. In omnibus accounts, one client’s losses can erode others’ assets. ### Never confuse **House Account** — The clearing member’s own trading account with the CCP. --- **Client Account** — The account (omnibus or segregated) holding client trades. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Most regulators require client fund protection but allow either omnibus or segregated models, with slight preference for segregation (e.g. Dodd-Frank requires segregation for many customer positions).

title: CCP Exposures and Capital Treatment
one_screen: Even with clearing, banks must hold capital for exposures to CCPs. Under Basel rules, a clearing member’s trade exposure to a qualifying CCP generally gets a low risk weight (often 2%) reflecting the CCP’s risk-absorbing structure. Client exposures to a CCP (via a member) also have regulatory treatment recognizing default fund offsets.
bodyText: Basel III (Chapter 5) provides special capital formulas for CCPs. For example, a clearing member may assign a 2% risk weight to its trade exposure (after netting) to a well-regulated CCP (QCCP). For contributions to a CCP’s default fund, banks may use a haircut approach or even deduction if not performing obligations. The goal is to encourage central clearing by lowering capital. However, non-clearing member (client) exposures can be higher risk – often treated like a bank loan to the member, adjusted for collateral. Thus, CCP exposures are not risk-free: banks cannot fully ignore them. Nonetheless, the capital charges are far lower than for bilateral OTC. This incentivizes central clearing of standard products. ### Permanent rule Identify CCPs that qualify as “QCCPs” (per supervisory list) to apply favorable capital treatment. Always ensure margin and default fund contributions are included in exposure measures. ### Permanent trap Overlooking CCP contributions. For example, thinking collateral to the CCP doesn’t affect capital – regulators usually require including posted margin and default fund contributions in exposure calculations (albeit with reductions). ### Never confuse **Trade Exposure to CCP** — The current and future exposure to the clearing house (subject to 2% RW). --- **Default Fund Exposure** — The risk from loss mutualization. Banks must separately calculate capital for this (often higher). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Global Basel standards treat CCP exposures similarly. National regulators (e.g. SEC/CFTC or PRA/EBA) list recognized CCPs (QCCPs) for capital rules.

title: SA-CCR (Standardized Approach to CCR)
one_screen: SA-CCR is the Basel III capital approach for measuring CCR exposure. It computes Exposure at Default (EAD) as **EAD = α × (Replacement Cost + Potential Future Exposure)**, with α=1.4. Replacement Cost (RC) is the positive current value net of haircut collateral. Potential Future Exposure (PFE) is derived from standardized add-on factors by asset class, aggregated by hedging sets and offset by correlation, then net of initial margin (subject to a small 5% floor). This approach accounts for margining, netting, asset classes, and uses a higher multiplier for safety.
bodyText: SA-CCR’s formula: **EAD = 1.4 × (RC + PFE)**. For example, RC = max(MTM, 0) – collateral. PFE add-ons use supervisory notional * factors (similar to old CEM add-ons but more refined). Trades are grouped by asset class and hedging sets to allow some offset. Initial margin reduces PFE but only up to 95% (the multiplier means at least 5% of IM benefit is ignored, ensuring some capital). SA-CCR replaced the older CEM and SM and was calibrated to be risk-sensitive (accounting for netting, hedges, margin). It avoids banks’ using bespoke models (except IMM). SA-CCR became effective 2017 globally (though actual regulatory implementation varied by jurisdiction). ### Permanent rule EAD under SA-CCR always uses α=1.4 as a conservatism buffer. Replacement Cost cannot be negative (floor at zero). ### Permanent trap Ignoring netting sets or collateral: SA-CCR explicitly nets trades and collaterals first. Also, forgetting to use correct supervisory factors for add-ons by product type and maturity. ### Never confuse **Replacement Cost (RC)** — Current exposure (MTM) minus collateral. --- **Potential Future Exposure (PFE)** — The supervisory-derived add-on component for future risk. RC is “today’s” risk, PFE is “future” risk. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Basel SA-CCR formula is standard. Jurisdictions implement it verbatim (e.g. EU CRR, UK PRA rules, Fed final rule).

title: Internal Model Method (IMM)
one_screen: The Internal Model Method (IMM) allows a bank to use its own approved models to compute CCR exposures (particularly PFE) for capital, subject to strict regulatory criteria. It is most often used for calculating CVA capital under Basel. For exposure, IMM required sophisticated simulation of netting sets and collateral to estimate expected and unexpected exposures. Basel has largely phased out the IMM shortcut (except for CVA) in favor of SA-CCR, but some large banks use IMM for advanced CCR metrics.
bodyText: Under IMM, banks simulate future exposures (e.g. via Monte Carlo) to compute EPE or CVA capital directly. IMM can capture portfolio-specific correlations and netting more precisely than SA-CCR. However, only very large institutions with approved models may use it, and they must back-test their results. The “IMM shortcut method” of Basel (an alternative simplistic approach) was eliminated once SA-CCR took effect. Now “Internal Model Method” usually refers to CVA exposure models or bilateral EAD models used for regulatory capital, with extensive validation and restrictions on collateral. ### Permanent rule IMM requires supervisory approval and continuous validation. Models must be conservative and cover wrong-way risk and stress. ### Permanent trap Assuming one can freely choose IMM. Regulators often discourage new IMM approval because SA-CCR exists; IMM is complex, costly, and under scrutiny after the crisis. ### Never confuse **Internal Model Method (IMM)** — A regulatory capital method using advanced models for CCR exposures. --- **Initial Margin (IM)** — Collateral posted to cover future exposure (not a modeling method). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** IMM rules (for CVA and CCR) are largely superseded by Basel SA-CCR except as grandfathered. Regulators generally stick to SA-CCR except for CVA VaR models.

title: CEM and SM Retirement
one_screen: The old methods for CCR, the Current Exposure Method (CEM) and the Standardized Method (SM), have been replaced by SA-CCR. CEM (used since Basel II) computed CCR as RC + add-on factors on notional by asset class and maturity. SM was a simpler approach for certain transactions. Both were considered insufficiently risk-sensitive. Basel finalized SA-CCR to replace these from 2017 onward.
bodyText: Under CEM, each trade’s PFE was a percentage of notional (e.g. 1% per year on interest rate swaps, up to caps). CEM did not recognize hedging across asset classes or margin. The Standardized Method applied broad risk weights or a CEM variant. Neither captured netting or actual collateral effects well. Basel Committee’s 2014 standard explicitly “replaced both the Current Exposure Method and the Standardized Method” with SA-CCR. Thus, for capital calculations, banks must use SA-CCR (or IMM if allowed). CEM and SM are now obsolete except as possible fallbacks for small institutions until SA-CCR is implemented. ### Permanent rule After SA-CCR’s effective date, do not use CEM or SM for capital purposes. Any regulatory references to CEM/SM are historical or transitional. ### Permanent trap Mistakenly applying CEM factors or SM calculations. For example, calculating add-ons on notional as under CEM will understate capital if SA-CCR is mandated. ### Never confuse **Current Exposure Method (CEM)** — Old CCR method: RC + fixed add-ons on notional. --- **Standardized Method (SM)** — An older Basel approach for CCR (e.g. index-based factors). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** All Basel members have moved to SA-CCR for regulated banks. Any national capital rules referencing CEM/SM should be updated.

title: Default vs CVA Capital
one_screen: Basel requires two separate capital charges for counterparty risk: a **default risk charge** (credit risk capital) and a **CVA risk charge**. The default charge covers expected loss if the counterparty outright defaults; CVA capital covers volatility in mark-to-market credit spreads (the risk of the counterparty’s changing credit quality).
bodyText: Default capital is calculated like any credit exposure: EAD × PD × LGD (for IRB banks) or risk-weighted under standardized. CVA capital (also called “Market risk” for CVA) is designed to capture losses from sudden widening of credit spreads on derivatives. Basel frameworks include a standardized CVA charge (and previously an advanced CVA VaR approach) to ensure banks hold capital against this risk. Notably, hedges (like single-name CDS) can reduce CVA capital if recognized. Thus banks need both: default capital (part of credit risk RWA) and CVA capital (part of market risk RWA in trading or CVA desks). These are distinct: a low-default-probability counterparty could still incur large CVA losses if its credit spreads move. ### Permanent rule Always compute capital for CCR exposure under credit risk rules *and* for CVA risk. Don’t double-count (deduct CVA exposures when already in default RWA). ### Permanent trap Thinking credit risk capital is enough for CCR. CVA capital is separate for mark-to-market movements. Some banks once tried to net CVA and default exposures – Basel forbids netting them for capital. ### Never confuse **Default Risk Capital** — Capital against expected loss from default (PD × LGD). --- **CVA Capital** — Capital for mark-to-market credit spread risk on counterparty exposures. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The need for two charges is a global standard. The methods (basic vs standardized CVA) vary slightly: final Basel rules now use standardized CVA capital for all banks.

title: Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA)
one_screen: CVA is the adjustment to the fair value of a derivative portfolio reflecting the counterparty’s credit risk. It is effectively the market value of expected loss from counterparty default, similar to “credit spread” on the portfolio. Banks include CVA in pricing and may hold hedges for it.
bodyText: Mathematically, CVA = ∑ (Discounted Expected Exposure × LGD × PD). It is the amount by which a portfolio’s value is marked down to price in default risk. Basel requires capital for CVA risk changes, and accounting rules require recognition of CVA in mark-to-market (e.g. IFRS 13). CVA exists because bilateral contracts would not otherwise price in default risk. CVA is widely hedged using credit derivatives. Managing CVA involves modeling exposure profiles (EPE) and counterparty credit spreads. Market CVA desks track and capitalise CVA. After the financial crisis, regulators required explicit CVA capital requirements since CVA swings caused bank losses. ### Permanent rule Value derivatives portfolios including CVA to reflect counterparty risk, and hold capital for CVA volatility. CVA must be revalued as the counterparty’s credit quality changes. ### Permanent trap Ignoring CVA in pricing or hedging. A bank that marks trades without CVA or hedging CVA can underprice risk and build uncapitalized positions. ### Never confuse **CVA (Credit Valuation Adjustment)** — Adjustment reflecting the counterparty’s credit risk in valuation. --- **DVA (Debit Valuation Adjustment)** — Similar adjustment reflecting the bank’s own credit. CVA (debit to bank) and DVA (credit to bank) often confuse people (see next atom). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Basel and accounting standards (IFRS 13/ASC 820) recognize CVA. Some specific rules exist for which trades count in CVA (e.g. some sovereigns are exempt in standardized CVA formula).

title: Debit Valuation Adjustment (DVA) and Funding Costs
one_screen: DVA is the opposite of CVA: it is the value adjustment reflecting the bank’s own credit risk on its liabilities. In practice, DVA means the bank would mark a gain if its own credit spread widens (bad for stakeholders but accounting shows a profit). DVA is controversial because it ties reported earnings to the bank’s health.
bodyText: When a bank owes a counterparty, its deteriorating credit actually reduces the expected payment, hence an accounting gain (DVA). However, regulators typically do not allow banks to rely on DVA gains to reduce capital or to distribute to shareholders. DVA mainly matters for pricing certain trades. Some regulators net CVA and DVA differently for capital. Funding Valuation Adjustment (FVA) is another concept: it accounts for the cost of funding collateral. If a bank must borrow to post collateral, that funding cost reduces trade value (FVA). FVA debates arose around whether to include it in fair value; many banks include FVA/MVA (margin valuation adjustment) in their pricing for completeness. ### Permanent rule Include DVA in valuations if following mid-market accounting, but regulatory capital ignores DVA (no capital relief). FVA should be considered in pricing, but typical regulatory capital frameworks do not have a specific FVA charge (it is considered in IRRBB, not CCR capital). ### Permanent trap Double-counting or incorrect offset of CVA by DVA. While both arise from same framework, regulations treat them asymmetrically (CVA is capitalized, DVA is not). ### Never confuse **CVA** (benefit from widening credit spreads of the counterparty) vs **DVA** (benefit from widening credit spreads of yourself). They cancel in a risk-neutral value if both are allowed, but only CVA is capital-adjusted. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These valuation adjustments are accounting concepts; regulatory treatment is broadly similar: CVA capital is required, DVA yields no capital benefit.

title: FVA, MVA, KVA and the XVA Family
one_screen: Beyond CVA and DVA, a suite of valuation adjustments (XVAs) addresses other costs. The key ones are: Funding Valuation Adjustment (FVA), Margin Valuation Adjustment (MVA), and Capital Valuation Adjustment (KVA). FVA is the cost of funding collateral flows. MVA is specifically the cost of funding initial margin. KVA is a charge reflecting the cost of holding regulatory capital. These are mainly used in internal pricing rather than capital rules.
bodyText: In practice, banks often compute FVA and MVA when pricing uncollateralized or margined trades, particularly since replacement to central clearing became common. KVA is a newer concept: it estimates the present value of future capital costs from holding exposures. Collectively, these adjustments ensure a derivative’s price covers not only market risk, but also funding, liquidity and capital costs. Importantly, regulators do not yet require capital for FVA/MVA/KVA. These are internal or accounting adjustments. They are included here for completeness of CCR context. CVA (and DVA) are the primary regulator-view adjustments. FVA/MVA are aligned to CVA in cost-of-carry models; KVA is still largely theoretical. ### Permanent rule Banks should clearly separate risk capital from valuation adjustments. XVAs beyond CVA are modeling/ALM issues, not additional capital requirements. ### Permanent trap Confusing FVA with regulatory charges. Banks sometimes thought FVA could be offset by CVA profits; regulators clarified that XVA hedges only apply to CVA capital. ### Never confuse **FVA** — Cost of funding derivative exposures. --- **Capital Charge** — A regulatory cost (separate from FVA). KVA is an internal pricing layer for this charge. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** XVA concepts are primarily driven by internal risk management and accounting. No jurisdiction requires KVA hold.

title: CVA Capital Charge
one_screen: Capital rules specify methodologies for CVA capital. Basel 3.1 (Basel IV) replaced the Advanced CVA approach with two standardized approaches: a “standardized approach for CVA” (SA-CVA) using risk weights on counterparty exposures and CDS spreads, and a “basic approach” (BA-CVA) using broad factors. Under SA-CVA, a bank computes a regulatory CVA VaR or formula-based capital based on net exposures, counterparty risk weights, and allows limited hedge recognition. The details are complex and specified in regulatory texts. In all approaches, recognized CVA hedges (single-name CDS or index) can reduce capital, up to 50% by Basel rules.
bodyText: The **Basic Approach** is a simpler formula (often a flat rate on net expected exposures). The **Standardized Approach** is more risk-sensitive, effectively charging against CVA volatility at the 99% quantile. Eligible hedges (credit derivatives) get offsets. Only standardized methodology is allowed for large internationally active banks now. Small banks or some portfolios may use the BA. Key point: under Basel’s finalized CVA framework, banks must hold capital for CVA risk using these global formulas. EU/UK transposed these in CRR3/UK Basel 3.1 (effective ~2025) and the US is updating its rule. Hedging rules (what qualifies and to what extent) follow Basel’s main text. ### Permanent rule When calculating CCR capital, CVA risk is a separate add-on: follow the prescribed CVA framework (basic or standardized) based on bank size and model usage. CVA hedges can reduce CVA RWA only as explicitly permitted. ### Permanent trap Mixing CVA and default exposures incorrectly. For example, one should not double-count risk reduction. Also, misidentifying which hedges are recognized (only certain counterparty CVA hedges). ### Never confuse **Basic CVA Approach (BA-CVA)** — Simple standardized calculation (like fixed factor * EAD). --- **Standardized CVA Approach (SA-CVA)** — Basel’s detailed formula or CVA VaR-based method. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s draft CCR circular focuses on CEM add-ons; India has not yet mandated a separate CVA capital charge for banks. (NBFCs under Ind AS would follow global norms, but banks follow RBI norms). **UK** — Basel 3.1 includes the revised CVA framework (implemented by mid-2025, final CRR3 expected Jan 2025). **EU** — CRR3 (approved by end-2023) implements Basel’s new CVA rules from Jan 2025. **US** — Agencies have proposed changes (Nov 2022) to align with Basel 3.1 CVA rules, but finalization is pending.

title: Settlement vs Pre-Settlement Risk
one_screen: Pre-settlement risk is the counterparty credit risk during the life of a trade (as described above). Settlement risk (often called Herstatt risk in FX) is the risk that one party pays while the other does not at settlement time, usually due to timing differences. For instance, in an FX trade across time zones, a bank may deliver EUR but not yet receive USD if the counterparty fails.
bodyText: Herstatt risk famously arose when a German bank failed mid-day, causing FX payments to be one-sided. To mitigate settlement risk in FX, most participants now use payment-versus-payment (PvP) systems like CLS, which ensure the final transfer of one currency occurs only if the other currency’s payment is finalized. PvP is mandated or recommended for major FX pairs. Settlement risk can also occur in securities (delivery vs payment), but standard solutions exist (DVP settlement at exchanges or clearinghouses). In short, pre-settlement (counterparty) risk is before trade completion; settlement risk is the risk of final exchange of value. Both affect CCR practice, but capital for CCR typically concerns pre-settlement exposures. ### Permanent rule Implement PvP (e.g. through CLS) for FX trades to eliminate Herstatt risk when possible. Use delivery-versus-payment (DVP) for securities. ### Permanent trap Equating CCR capital with settlement risk. Regulators require CCR capital for trades that are bilateral; settlement risk is operational/liquidity risk, not included in CCR capital. ### Never confuse **Pre-settlement risk (CCR)** — Counterparty default risk before and up to settlement of cash flows. --- **Settlement risk (Herstatt)** — Risk of loss due to one party failing to make payment at settlement time (e.g. FX PvP risk). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Settlement risk management is driven by market infrastructure (CLS, clearinghouses). Basel mandates PvP where available. Regulatory capital for settlement risk is not separate; it is managed via operational standards.

title: Basel Framework (Global Standard)
one_screen: The Basel Committee’s published standards (Basel III, Basel 3.1, etc.) are the definitive source for CCR methodologies and capital. Key texts include BCBS 279 (SA-CCR standard) and the Basel III Revised Framework for market risk/CVA. These set the universal baseline for capital and definitions in all jurisdictions.
bodyText: For example, BCBS 279 (2014) finalized SA-CCR. Basel 3.1 (2023) updated CCR/CVA for capital (implemented by 2025 in many countries). Regulators in each jurisdiction (Fed, PRA, EBA, RBI) transposed these rules but cannot deviate from core calculations. Thus, for universal CCR concepts (like SA-CCR formula, CVA definitions, netting rules), citing the Basel text is authoritative. ### Permanent rule Always refer to the latest Basel Framework text for definitions and formulas of CCR metrics. National rules follow this text. ### Permanent trap Using outdated or local circulars instead of Basel standards for universal concepts. ### Never confuse **Basel III Standards** — Internationally agreed rules by BCBS. --- **Local Regulations** — Jurisdictional laws implementing Basel (may lag or add conservatism). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Basel standards themselves do not vary by country. Differences arise only in national adoption timetables or stricter add-ons, not in the core mathematics.

title: UK/EU Implementation
one_screen: The UK and EU have adopted Basel CCR and CVA rules through their capital regulations. The EU’s CRR3 (part of Basel 3.1 package) was agreed in late 2023 and takes effect Jan 1, 2025. It includes SA-CCR for calculating exposures and the new standardized CVA capital approach. The UK’s PRA released draft standards (PS17/23) on CCR/CVA, finalizing them for implementation by July 2025.
bodyText: In detail, EU CRR2 already implemented SA-CCR (from Jan 2023) and amended CVA rules. CRR3 (Basel 3.1) further updates CVA capital (transition Jan 2025) and keeps SA-CCR as is. The UK follows the same schedule: the PRA’s policy says Basel 3.1 reforms (CVA and margining) will be in force by mid-2025. Both jurisdictions require qualifying CCP (QCCP) treatment for exposures (EU and UK lists). They also follow the same definitions of EE/EPE, WWR, etc, as Basel. ### Permanent rule Use CRR or UK Prudential Regulation Authority rules for final figures in these jurisdictions. Generally, EU/UK text mirrors Basel with local choices (e.g. sovereign CVA exemptions in EU). ### Permanent trap Forgetting conversion factors or treatment differences. For instance, EU CVA rules used to exempt certain sovereigns; UK may diverge post-Brexit. ### Never confuse **CRR2/3 (EU)** — European regulations implementing Basel (CRR3 is latest, full Basel 3.1). --- **UK PRA rules** — UK’s onshore regs (PRA policy statements for Basel 3.1). ### Jurisdiction variants **UK** — PRA announced Basel 3.1 implementation by July 2025, including CCR and CVA changes (reducing SA-CCR alpha to 1.0 for non-financials, transitional treatment). **EU** — CRR3 (Basel 3.1) adopted with application date Jan 1, 2025; CRR2 already moved banks to SA-CCR in 2023 and updated CVA.

title: India’s CCR Regulation
one_screen: The RBI currently uses Basel III’s CCR guidance but has not fully adopted SA-CCR yet. In India, the Basel III Capital Regulations (Master Circular) still prescribe the Current Exposure Method (CEM) with updated add-on factors. In August 2025 RBI invited comments on revisions to CEM add-ons in its Basel III circular. It has indicated a phased move towards SA-CCR after FY26–27 (2026–27), subject to market readiness (industry sources).
bodyText: Thus, while Basel global rules exist, Indian banks (scheduled commercial banks) have not implemented SA-CCR for now. They continue to compute PFE using CEM add-ons (recently revised to align with BCBS). RBI’s master circular (April 2025) discusses the future potential of SA-CCR in context of investment funds, but general bank norms will likely shift later. CCIL (Clearing Corp of India) provides CCP services for interest rate and FX derivatives, facilitating clearing, but netting benefits and new global standards are gradually being incorporated. ### Permanent rule For Indian banks, follow RBI’s Basel III master directions. As of now, CCR capital uses CEM (not SA-CCR) for banks. Check RBI circulars for updates on implementation timelines. ### Permanent trap Assuming India already uses SA-CCR for banks. It does *not*. RBI is aligning CEM parameters and planning SA-CCR in the future, but until then use CEM as per RBI’s instructions. ### Never confuse **RBI Master Directions (Basel III)** — Indian regulations (CEM-based CCR for banks). --- **Ind AS 109 (IFRS)** — Indian accounting standard on impairment, not applicable to banks’ prudential CCR. (Banks have separate RBI norms.) ### Jurisdiction variants **IN** — RBI’s draft capital rules (Apr 2025) keep CEM with revised add-ons. SA-CCR adoption is indicated for the future, not yet mandatory. CCIL is India’s main CCP for IRS/FRA (see CCIL FAQs).

title: US CCR Regulation
one_screen: The US banking regulators have implemented SA-CCR for U.S. banks. A final rule (Nov 2019) required bank holding companies and large banks to use SA-CCR for derivatives exposures (effective April 2020, with mandatory compliance by Jan 2022). This rule also updated hedging recognition and collateral treatment. For CVA, the U.S. agencies in late 2022 released proposals to revise the CVA capital charge in line with Basel, but no final rule is in force yet.
bodyText: Specifically, U.S. rules now use SA-CCR in place of the previous Current Exposure Method. The FFIEC and Basel rules define the calculation. U.S. guidance also harmonizes with global standards for netting and margin. For CVA capital, banks currently use the standardized CVA approach (Basel-aligned) as per existing regulations, but agencies have sought comment on further changes. ### Permanent rule Large U.S. banks must compute CCR RWA under SA-CCR. For capital, counterparty exposures use SA-CCR EAD, and CVA risk uses the standardized CVA approach. ### Permanent trap Misapplying older Basel I/II rules. Also, small U.S. banks had the option to use the simpler exposure method but even those are encouraged to adopt SA-CCR. ### Never confuse **Fed/OCC rules** — U.S. regulations implementing Basel (SA-CCR, CVA). --- **FRB’s Exchange Act rules** — Another set of U.S. rules (generally consistent). ### Jurisdiction variants **US** — SA-CCR has been mandatory since Jan 2022. U.S. regulators are aligning CVA standards with Basel 3.1 (proposed in 2022). No separate CVA regime in India; UK/EU have updated theirs as noted above.

title: Obligor, borrower and counterparty
one_screen: Credit risk attaches to a person that owes performance, not to a customer label. **Obligor** identifies the legal or natural person responsible for the credit obligation; **borrower** and **counterparty** describe roles that may coincide with the obligor but need not.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What it means | Why credit risk cares | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Obligor | Person contractually responsible for an obligation | Default status and wholesale borrower risk normally attach here | | Borrower | Person receiving or using borrowed funds | Often the obligor in loans; not a safe synonym in every structure | | Counterparty | Other contractual party to a transaction | Central for derivatives, securities financing and settlement exposures | | Commercial customer | Relationship-management label | May contain several legal obligors and therefore several credit risks | One corporate group can contain several obligors. One obligor can have many facilities. A derivative counterparty can create a credit exposure whose amount changes with market value even though no conventional loan exists. ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Front office / onboarding establishes legal identity and contractual roles | | Approves | Credit / legal functions confirm the risk-bearing entity and structure | | Consumes | Underwriting, limits, modelling, collections, capital and reporting | | Challenges | Independent risk, legal, compliance and audit test entity mapping and aggregation | ### Permanent rule Credit risk must be mapped to the legal or natural person responsible for the obligation before ratings, defaults, limits or exposures are aggregated. ### Never confuse [Obligor] and [Counterparty] **Obligor** — the person responsible for a credit obligation. --- **Counterparty** — the other party to a transaction; the term describes the transactional relationship and may or may not coincide with a loan borrower. ### Permanent trap Using “customer”, “borrower”, “obligor” and “counterparty” as database synonyms can propagate one entity’s rating, default or limit status to legally separate persons. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Legal definitions and regulatory wording vary, but identifying the person responsible for an obligation is universal.

title: Product, facility and account
one_screen: A product is a reusable lending design, a facility is a specific contractual grant of credit, and an account is an operational record used to book and service activity. Credit risk measures become ambiguous unless they declare which level they attach to.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Level | Owns | Typical examples of fields | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Product | Reusable commercial design | Product type, standard terms, target segment | | Facility | Actual contractual credit availability | Limit, currency, maturity, repayment schedule, covenants, security | | Account | Operational booking and servicing | Balance, postings, due dates, arrears, interest, fees | | Obligor | Person responsible for obligations | Rating, default state, aggregate limits | A simple term loan may be one facility with one account. A revolving facility can have several operational accounts. One obligor can hold facilities with different collateral, seniority and drawdown behaviour even when a common obligor PD is used. ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Every risk measure must state its level: product, facility, account, obligor or a defined aggregate. ### Never confuse [Facility] and [Account] **Facility** — the contractual grant or commitment of credit, including its limit and terms. --- **Account** — the operational record through which balances, payments and arrears are booked; one facility need not equal one account. ### Permanent trap Treating an account-level delinquency flag as automatically equivalent to an obligor-level credit state can misclassify other facilities when the governing default framework applies a different propagation rule. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Regulatory rules differ on when account or facility events propagate to an obligor, but the object hierarchy itself is universal.

title: Exposure and aggregation levels
one_screen: Exposure is the amount or value subject to credit loss for a stated purpose; it is not automatically today’s drawn balance. The same relationship can produce different valid exposure numbers at account, facility, obligor, connected-group and portfolio levels.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Level | Question answered | What may be included | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Account | What is booked here now? | Outstanding principal, accrued items | | Facility | What credit position belongs to this contract? | Drawn amount plus relevant undrawn or contingent exposure | | Obligor | How much depends on this legal person? | Relevant facilities to the same obligor | | Connected group | How much depends on one linked economic risk? | Exposures to connected counterparties | | Portfolio | How much exposure exists across the book? | All included obligors/groups under the chosen perimeter | Funded and non-funded positions can both create credit exposure. A commitment or guarantee may have little or no current loan balance while still creating future or contingent loss potential. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Every exposure number requires both a **measurement basis** and an **aggregation level**. ### Never confuse [Outstanding balance] and [Exposure] **Outstanding balance** — the amount currently booked as drawn or owed. --- **Exposure** — the amount relevant to a stated credit-risk question; it can include future drawings, contingent claims or aggregation above account level. ### Permanent trap Setting exposure equal to current drawn balance for revolving or committed facilities can omit the amount that may be drawn or become due before default. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) The RBI Commercial Banks IRACP Directions define exposure to include funded and non-funded exposures, including underwriting and similar commitments. #### UK (PRA) Detailed regulatory exposure values depend on the applicable prudential approach; the conceptual distinction between booked balance and risk exposure does not change. #### EU CRR exposure-value rules vary by exposure type and credit-risk approach; the aggregation principle is unchanged. #### US US regulatory capital rules define exposure measures by asset and approach; current balance is not a universal substitute for exposure at default.

title: Connected counterparties and economic groups
one_screen: Legal separation does not guarantee independent credit risk. Connected-counterparty analysis aggregates persons when control or economic interdependence creates a common failure channel, so one concentrated risk cannot be disguised as several names.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Connection test | Core question | Credit consequence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Control | Does one person directly or indirectly control another, or are several under common control? | Treat connected exposures as one concentration where the rule requires | | Economic interdependence | Would financial difficulty at one likely cause funding or repayment difficulty at another? | Aggregate because apparent legal diversification is not economic diversification | | Mere commercial relationship | Are entities simply customers/suppliers without material dependency? | Investigate; do not aggregate automatically | Connection for concentration purposes is not the same as default propagation. Two companies can be aggregated for a large-exposure limit yet retain separate ratings and default statuses if the applicable default rules assess them separately. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Relationship teams and credit analysis identify ownership and dependency evidence | | Approves | Credit risk / designated governance confirms connected-group treatment | | Consumes | Limits, portfolio risk, regulatory reporting and capital assessment | | Challenges | Independent risk, compliance and audit test completeness and consistency | ### Permanent rule Count common failure mechanisms, not merely legal names. ### Never confuse [Connected counterparties] and [Single obligor] **Connected counterparties** — separate persons aggregated because their risks are linked by control or economic dependency. --- **Single obligor** — one legal or natural person responsible for obligations. ### Permanent trap “Same corporate group” does not automatically mean “same defaulted obligor”, and separate incorporation does not automatically mean independent concentration risk. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI’s Large Exposures Framework applies Indian prudential aggregation and limits to single counterparties and groups of connected counterparties; use the RBI framework in force for the reporting date. #### UK (PRA) PRA SS3/25 sets expectations for groups of connected clients using control and economic dependency concepts. #### EU The CRR large-exposures framework uses groups of connected clients and tests based on control and economic interconnection. #### US US legal lending-limit and aggregation rules use US-specific control/common-enterprise tests; they should not be assumed identical to the Basel connected-counterparty test.

title: Underwriting and the credit decision
one_screen: Underwriting converts information about the obligor, facility and environment into a governed decision to approve, decline or reshape credit. The decision starts with a sustainable **primary source of repayment**; collateral and guarantees can reduce loss if repayment fails, but they do not repair weak repayment capacity.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Decision layer | Question | Output | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Credit policy | What business and risk will the institution accept? | Target markets, criteria, limits, prohibited/exception cases | | Repayment capacity | From what recurring cash flow or resources will contractual payments be made? | Base-case debt service assessment | | Downside resilience | What happens if revenue, rates, costs or asset values move adversely? | Stressed repayment capacity and weaknesses | | Structure | Can tenor, amortisation, covenants, limit or pricing make the risk acceptable? | Proposed terms and controls | | Mitigants | What secondary recovery exists if primary repayment fails? | Collateral / guarantee assessment | | Approval authority | Who may accept this size, risk and exception profile? | Approve / decline / approve with conditions / escalate | A sound decision is not “good borrower versus bad borrower”. It is **borrower + purpose + amount + structure + repayment source + downside + mitigants + price**, all within policy and delegated authority. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Front office / credit analyst assembles facts, cash-flow analysis and recommendation | | Approves | Delegated credit officer, committee, senior management or board according to authority | | Consumes | Documentation, operations, monitoring, portfolio management and finance | | Challenges | Independent credit risk, second-line policy governance and internal audit | ### Permanent rule Approve credit primarily on sustainable repayment capacity. Treat collateral and guarantees as secondary protection unless the product is explicitly designed to repay from asset sale or liquidation. ### Never confuse [Credit policy] and [Approval authority] **Credit policy** — sets what risks may be taken and under what criteria. --- **Approval authority** — determines who may accept a particular exposure, size, risk or exception. ### Permanent trap A high collateral value can make an uneconomic loan look safe. If the borrower cannot service the debt, the bank has underwritten a workout, not a performing credit. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the core rule.** Local consumer-protection, responsible-lending, related-party and governance requirements vary, but sound underwriting universally requires defined criteria, repayment-capacity analysis and controlled approval authority.

title: Collateral, security and guarantees
one_screen: Collateral, security interests and guarantees are credit-risk mitigants only to the extent that the bank can legally rely on them and realise value when needed. Their underwriting job is to provide a credible **secondary way out**; their later LGD role is separate and depends on realised recovery cash flows.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Mitigant | What must be true | Main failure mode | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Collateral asset | Identifiable, valued, controllable and realisable | Value falls, asset disappears, sale is delayed | | Security interest | Validly created and perfected under applicable law | Priority or enforceability fails | | Guarantee | Legally effective claim on a capable guarantor | Guarantor lacks capacity or defaults with borrower | | Covenant / structural protection | Trigger and remedy are clear and monitorable | Breach occurs too late or remedy is weak | **Eligible value is not appraisal value.** A lending or risk value normally considers valuation uncertainty, volatility, liquidation time, prior claims, currency mismatch, concentration and policy/regulatory haircuts. ### Formula ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Credit, legal, valuation and collateral-management teams establish evidence | | Approves | Credit authority accepts the mitigant within policy | | Consumes | Operations, monitoring, workout, capital and LGD estimation | | Challenges | Legal, independent risk, valuation review and audit test perfection and values | ### Permanent rule A mitigant is worth only what can be legally enforced and economically realised when the borrower is under stress. ### Never confuse [Collateral value] and [Repayment capacity] **Collateral value** — secondary recovery value available if repayment fails. --- **Repayment capacity** — the borrower’s ability to meet contractual payments from the primary repayment source. ### Never confuse [Guarantee] and [Collateral] **Guarantee** — a contractual promise by another person to perform or pay if the obligor does not. --- **Collateral** — an asset or property interest available to secure recovery. ### Permanent trap Counting a guarantee at face value without testing legal effectiveness, coverage and guarantor credit quality merely moves the credit risk to an unmeasured second obligor. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the economics.** Perfection, priority, insolvency treatment, valuation standards and regulatory recognition are jurisdiction-specific; production treatment must follow local law and the applicable prudential framework.

title: Default: defining the event
one_screen: Default is a governed credit state, not a synonym for arrears, loss, bankruptcy or write-off. Every PD, default rate, cure rate and LGD inherits the unit and events used in the default definition, so the event must be fixed before the metric.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Component | Question that must be answered | | :--- | :--- | | Unit | Does default apply to an obligor, facility, account or retail pool? | | Event | Which qualitative and quantitative conditions trigger default? | | Materiality | Which past-due amounts are material enough to count? | | Propagation | Does one facility’s default affect other facilities? | | Exit | What permits return to non-default? | | History | Which date and state are preserved for modelling and recovery? | Basel’s IRB reference definition uses two routes for an obligor: **unlikeliness to pay in full without recourse to actions such as realising security**, or **more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation**. The routes are alternatives; later atoms own their mechanics. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Define default before measuring default risk, then preserve that definition across development, calibration, validation and reporting. ### Never confuse [Default] and [Loss] **Default** — entry into a defined credit-risk state. --- **Loss** — the economic or accounting shortfall arising from outcomes around or after default; default can still produce substantial recovery. ### Permanent trap Combining historical “bad” flags that mean 90 DPD, charge-off, bankruptcy or NPA creates a target variable with no stable economic meaning. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI commercial-bank asset classification is built around prudential **NPA** rules, not a word-for-word Basel IRB default definition. The IRACP Directions also cross-reference “default” in RBI’s stressed-asset resolution framework; mappings must state which definition is used. From **1 April 2027**, RBI’s 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions mandate an expected-credit-loss provisioning framework for commercial banks; that future provisioning regime does not make the Basel IRB default definition and RBI prudential classifications interchangeable. #### UK (PRA) The current UK framework remains CRR-derived. The January 2026 PRA SS3/24 version is **future policy effective 1 January 2027**, not the framework in force on 29 August 2026. #### EU CRR Article 178 uses UTP and past-due criteria. EBA’s May 2026 amended Guidelines have an **application date of 19 October 2026** and are future-effective on 29 August 2026. #### US Advanced Approaches rules distinguish wholesale and retail default definitions; specified retail categories use different mechanical thresholds.

title: Arrears, days past due and delinquency states
one_screen: Arrears measure unpaid contractual amounts; days past due measure how long payment has remained unpaid; delinquency buckets convert that clock into operational states. These are payment facts, not loss estimates or the complete definition of default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Measure | What it answers | Typical mistake | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Arrears | How much required payment is unpaid? | Treating amount as duration | | DPD | How long has the relevant payment been overdue? | Starting the clock from statement or month-end instead of due date | | Delinquency bucket | Which monitoring state does the DPD fall into? | Treating a bucket boundary as a universal default rule | | Out-of-order test | Is a revolving/OD/CC facility persistently irregular under its rule? | Applying instalment logic to revolving credit | DPD describes payment behaviour; the default definition determines when that behaviour, or separate qualitative evidence, becomes a governed credit state. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Calculate delinquency from the contractual obligation and the specified counting convention; do not infer default merely from an informal bucket label. ### Never confuse [Arrears] and [Days past due] **Arrears** — the unpaid amount. --- **Days past due** — elapsed time associated with an unpaid contractual obligation. ### Permanent trap Changing due-date logic, allocation of payments or day-end convention can create apparent credit deterioration or improvement without any change in borrower behaviour. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI requires overdue, SMA and NPA status to be determined through the day-end process for the relevant date. Its illustration moves a continuously overdue account to SMA-1 after 30 days, SMA-2 after 60 days and NPA after the applicable 90-day progression; OD/CC products use the defined “out of order” test. #### UK (PRA) Past-due status and materiality are inputs to the current regulatory default framework; arrears buckets used operationally are not themselves the complete definition of default. #### EU CRR/EBA rules distinguish days-past-due mechanics, materiality and unlikeliness-to-pay indicators; reporting past-due bands do not replace Article 178 default. #### US Different regulatory purposes and retail categories use different delinquency/default thresholds; there is no safe universal “90 DPD for everything” rule.

title: Unlikeliness to pay
one_screen: Unlikeliness to pay identifies default from the substance of credit deterioration before a delinquency clock necessarily reaches its backstop. It asks whether full payment remains likely without extraordinary recovery action; it is governed judgement, not a discretionary weakness label.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Evidence | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Repayment capacity deterioration | Can expected cash flow still service the obligation in full? | | Distressed restructuring | Would the borrower fail or suffer material difficulty without a concession? | | Credit-related write-down / sale loss | Does the bank’s own action evidence material deterioration? | | Insolvency / bankruptcy event | Does legal distress indicate repayment will be avoided or delayed? | | Security dependence | Is repayment only credible through enforcement or realisation of collateral? | A watch-list flag, downgrade or adverse news item is an **input**, not automatically default. Documented triggers and evidence standards prevent UTP from drifting across teams or cycles. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Relationship/credit monitoring identifies deterioration and evidence | | Approves | Credit risk or delegated default governance determines UTP status | | Consumes | Collections, restructuring, modelling, finance and regulatory reporting | | Challenges | Independent risk, model validation and audit test consistency | ### Permanent rule Assess UTP on the ability and likelihood to pay the credit obligation in full, not on how much the bank expects to recover after failure. ### Never confuse [Unlikely to pay] and [High LGD] **Unlikely to pay** — a default-likelihood conclusion about full contractual payment. --- **High LGD** — a severity conclusion about the size of loss conditional on default. ### Permanent trap Calling a fully secured exposure “not defaulted” because collateral should cover the debt confuses borrower repayment with recovery from security. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI commercial-bank NPA classification is its own prudential framework. Do not import a Basel IRB UTP label into RBI NPA reporting without an explicit mapping to the RBI rules in force. #### UK (PRA) The current UK framework includes unlikeliness-to-pay indicators. PRA SS3/24 provides the future Basel 3.1 expectations from 1 January 2027. #### EU UTP is an independent limb of CRR Article 178. The May 2026 EBA amendments apply from 19 October 2026 and should be treated as future-effective until then. #### US Advanced Approaches wholesale default expressly includes a determination that the obligor is unlikely to pay in full without recourse to actions such as realising collateral.

title: Past-due backstops and the 90-day rule
one_screen: A past-due backstop is an outer mechanical trigger, not permission to wait for the clock when earlier evidence already establishes default. In the Basel wholesale reference definition, UTP and more-than-90-days-past-due are joined by **OR**, not by a sequence requiring both.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism UTP trigger met first → Default now Past-due clock reaches applicable material backstop first → Default now Neither met → Continue non-default monitoring The backstop constrains optimism. It preserves an objective point beyond which prolonged material non-payment cannot remain outside default merely because judgement has not acted. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule The backstop is the latest mechanical trigger under its rule, not a grace period that overrides earlier qualitative default evidence. ### Never confuse [Backstop] and [Definition of default] **Backstop** — an outer mechanical trigger based on elapsed delinquency under a specified rule. --- **Definition of default** — the full set of qualitative and quantitative conditions governing entry to default. ### Permanent trap Writing “default = 90 DPD” into data dictionaries suppresses early defaults, mixes products with different rules and trains models on a delayed target. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) For commercial banks, a term loan is classified NPA when interest and/or principal remains overdue for **more than 90 days**. RBI also prescribes distinct tests for OD/CC, working-capital irregularity, bills, agricultural exposures and other categories; asset classification is borrower-wise subject to specified exceptions. #### UK (PRA) The current UK CRR-derived default framework uses past-due and materiality rules alongside UTP. The updated PRA Basel 3.1 package, including the January 2026 SS3/24 version, takes effect on 1 January 2027. #### EU CRR Article 178 uses a past-due limb alongside UTP, supported by materiality rules. The EBA’s May 2026 amended Guidelines become applicable on 19 October 2026. #### US Advanced Approaches wholesale default includes more than 90 days past due on a material obligation, while specified retail categories use different mechanical thresholds; “90 days everywhere” is therefore wrong.

title: Restructuring, forbearance and distressed concessions
one_screen: Restructuring changes contractual terms; forbearance is a concession associated with the debtor’s financial difficulty. A modification can preserve value, but cannot erase the deterioration that made the original terms unsustainable.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Situation | Credit interpretation | | :--- | :--- | | Healthy commercial amendment | Terms change for ordinary business reasons; distress not implied | | Concession because of financial difficulty | Forbearance / distressed modification analysis required | | Material forgiveness or postponement | Test whether diminished financial obligation indicates UTP/default | | New contract after old arrears are capitalised | Preserve pre-modification history; do not reset the borrower to “new” | | Repeated restructuring | Escalating evidence that apparent cure may be unstable | The key question is **why terms changed and what risk the concession reveals**. Extending maturity may restore short-term affordability; capitalising arrears can clean DPD without improving cash generation; principal forgiveness changes expected recovery. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Workout / relationship team documents distress, proposal and economics | | Approves | Restructuring authority / credit committee approves within policy | | Consumes | Operations, finance, default management, modelling and reporting | | Challenges | Independent credit risk and audit test classification and economic substance | ### Permanent rule A new contractual schedule must not erase the borrower’s prior distress, default date or economic concession. ### Never confuse [Restructuring] and [Forbearance] **Restructuring** — a modification of contractual credit terms. --- **Forbearance** — a concession linked to the debtor’s financial difficulty; not every restructuring is forbearance. ### Permanent trap Evergreening converts unpaid amounts into a formally current contract while leaving repayment capacity unchanged; operational current status is not proof of economic cure. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Commercial banks apply the IRACP Directions together with the RBI *Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025* where relevant; restructuring classification and provisioning must follow those rules rather than a generic Basel label. #### UK (PRA) Distressed restructuring can be an UTP indicator under the definition-of-default framework; forbearance and regulatory default remain distinct classifications. #### EU CRR/EBA rules distinguish forbearance, non-performing exposure and default. The May 2026 EBA amendment retains the 1% NPV-loss threshold in the relevant distressed-restructuring guidance and becomes applicable on 19 October 2026. #### US Accounting modification, troubled-credit treatment and regulatory default are separate determinations; Advanced Approaches default remains governed by 12 CFR Part 217.

title: Cure, probation and re-default
one_screen: Cure is the governed transition from default back to non-default after the default conditions have ceased and renewed performance is credible. Re-default is a later return to default; a temporary payment or zero-DPD snapshot is not enough to prove a durable cure.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Default ↓ Original trigger ceases ↓ Required arrears / viability conditions met ↓ Probation or observation requirement, where applicable ↓ Cured / non-default ↓ New qualifying trigger? ↓ Re-default A sound data model keeps the entire state history: first default date, cause, restructuring events, cure date, probation, re-default and recovery. Deleting default history after cure produces survivorship bias and makes weak restructurings look successful. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Cure removes the current default state; it does not remove the historical fact that default occurred. ### Never confuse [Cure] and [Arrears clearance] **Cure** — return to non-default under the complete exit criteria. --- **Arrears clearance** — payment of overdue amounts; UTP or other default conditions may still remain. ### Permanent trap Resetting a cured customer to “never defaulted” inflates apparent portfolio quality and corrupts PD, transition and restructuring-performance analysis. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) Under the current commercial-bank IRACP Directions, an NPA may be upgraded to standard only when the **entire arrears of interest and principal are paid**; where the borrower has more than one facility with the bank, arrears across all those credit facilities must be repaid, subject to additional restructuring rules where relevant. #### UK (PRA) Return-to-non-default is governed under the current definition-of-default framework. The updated PRA SS3/24 sets the future Basel 3.1 expectations from 1 January 2027. #### EU EBA Guidelines govern return-to-non-default and probation concepts. The May 2026 amended version has an application date of 19 October 2026, so the applicable version must be identified by observation date. #### US Advanced Approaches rules provide return-from-default standards for wholesale obligors and retail exposures under the US framework; the relevant unit must be preserved.

title: Write-off, recovery and economic loss
one_screen: Write-off changes the carrying amount or prudential treatment of an exposure; recovery records value collected after credit failure; economic loss measures what was ultimately lost after recoveries, costs and timing. None of these events should erase the default lifecycle that produced them.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Lifecycle item | What it means | What must stay in history | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Default | Governed credit state begins | Default date, trigger, EAD | | Provision / allowance | Loss is recognised or reserved under the applicable framework | Amount, basis, date | | Write-off / charge-off | Carrying amount is reduced or removed under relevant rules | Written-off amount and date | | Recovery | Cash or value is collected after default/write-off | Gross proceeds, source and timing | | Workout cost | Legal, collection, maintenance and disposal costs | Cash outflow and timing | | Economic loss | Net shortfall measured on a consistent basis | Final discounted loss calculation | Post-write-off recoveries are economically real.
