A technical write-off can coexist with continuing collection activity and legal liability; the database therefore needs both accounting status and recovery status. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Never delete default, write-off or post-default recovery history merely because the balance sheet carrying amount has changed. ### Never confuse [Write-off] and [Debt forgiveness] **Write-off** — accounting or prudential reduction/removal of carrying amount under the applicable framework. --- **Debt forgiveness** — release of the debtor’s legal obligation; write-off does not necessarily produce forgiveness. ### Permanent trap Using the write-off amount as “LGD” automatically ignores later recoveries, workout costs, timing and the exposure actually outstanding at default. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) The commercial-bank IRACP Directions recognise write-offs, technical write-offs and subsequent recoveries. A partial or technical write-off does not permit the remaining exposure to be shown as standard merely because part has been written off. The current IRACP provisioning regime is replaced for covered commercial banks from **1 April 2027** by RBI’s 2026 expected-credit-loss-based Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions. #### UK (PRA) For IFRS reporters, IFRS 9 write-off requirements operate separately from prudential regulatory default. The two statuses must be mapped, not conflated. #### EU IFRS-reporting entities apply IFRS 9 write-off principles while CRR regulatory default remains a separate prudential state. #### US CECL allowance and charge-off practice is separate from regulatory default and nonaccrual classifications; modelling must preserve those distinctions.

title: Probability of default
one_screen: Probability of default is the probability that a defined obligor, facility or pool enters a defined default state over a specified future horizon, conditional on information available at an observation date. A number labelled “PD” is incomplete until its **unit, event, horizon and conditioning information** are known.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Component | Required statement | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Unit | Obligor, facility or homogeneous pool | Changes what can default | | Event | Regulatory default, internal default or other defined target | Changes the outcome being predicted | | Horizon | One year, 12 months, lifetime or another period | Changes probability mechanically | | Observation date | Information available at prediction time | Prevents hindsight and leakage | | Calibration basis | Mapping from score/grade to probability | Turns ranking into a probability estimate | PD is not a declaration that a named borrower “will default”. It is a probability assigned before the outcome is known. Across repeated comparable populations, realised default frequencies should be consistent with well-calibrated probabilities within sampling and cyclical variation. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule No PD is interpretable without its unit, default definition, horizon and observation date. ### Never confuse [PD] and [Credit score] **PD** — a calibrated probability of a specified future default event. --- **Credit score** — a ranking or predictive output that need not itself be a probability. ### Permanent trap Multiplying a raw score by LGD and EAD because the score “looks like a probability” creates a loss number with no valid probabilistic interpretation. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in probability mathematics.** Regulatory frameworks can prescribe different default definitions, parameter floors, horizons and calibration standards; those rules change the parameter specification, not what probability means.

title: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle PD
one_screen: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle describe how strongly a rating or PD responds to current versus cyclical conditions. They are conditioning philosophies on a spectrum, not synonyms for short-horizon and long-horizon probability.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | Point-in-time tendency | Through-the-cycle tendency | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Current borrower information | High sensitivity | Greater emphasis on persistent characteristics | | Current macro conditions | More direct response | Temporary cyclical effects damped | | Rating migration | Typically more frequent through the cycle | Typically more stable through ordinary cycles | | Near-term risk monitoring | Naturally responsive | Can lag rapid cyclical change if used alone | | Long-run calibration | May still require long-run anchoring depending on use | Does not automatically satisfy any regulatory calibration rule | A one-year PD can be PIT, TTC-like or somewhere between. Likewise, a lifetime forecast can use changing point-in-time macroeconomic paths. **Horizon and cyclical conditioning are separate axes.** ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule PIT/TTC describes sensitivity to current and cyclical conditions; it does not by itself specify the PD horizon. ### Never confuse [Point-in-time] and [Short horizon] **Point-in-time** — strong conditioning on information and conditions at the observation date. --- **Short horizon** — a forecast interval; it says nothing by itself about how cyclical information enters the model. ### Never confuse [Through-the-cycle] and [Long-run average PD] **Through-the-cycle** — a rating philosophy designed to damp temporary cyclical movements. --- **Long-run average PD** — a calibration concept; averaging observed defaults is not by itself a TTC rating system. ### Permanent trap Calling a multi-year average default rate “TTC” without examining rating assignment, macro sensitivity and calibration confuses statistical smoothing with rating philosophy. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Supervisors and accounting standards may require particular calibration or forward-looking treatment for specific uses, but PIT/TTC remains the same conceptual distinction.

title: Loss given default and recovery rate
one_screen: Loss given default is loss severity **conditional on default**. Collateral and guarantees influence LGD only through legally available, economically realised recovery value; an appraisal at origination is therefore an input to recovery expectations, not the LGD itself.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | LGD driver | Effect on net recovery | | :--- | :--- | | Borrower post-default payments | Increase recovery | | Collateral sale proceeds | Increase recovery after priority and costs | | Guarantee proceeds | Increase recovery if guarantee is enforceable and guarantor performs | | Legal / collection / maintenance costs | Reduce recovery | | Delay to recovery | Reduces present value | | Seniority and prior claims | Determine how recovery value is shared | | Downturn conditions | Can reduce collateral prices and recovery capacity together | A simple `1 − recovery rate` relationship is valid only when recovery rate and LGD use the same exposure base, cash-flow perimeter, costs and discounting convention. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Measure LGD from the default event using a consistent exposure base and economically complete recovery cash flows. ### Never confuse [Collateral value] and [LGD] **Collateral value** — one potential source of recovery, subject to legal rights, priority, sale value, time and costs. --- **LGD** — total economic loss severity conditional on default across all recovery sources and costs. ### Permanent trap `LGD = 1 − collateral value / current balance` ignores pre-default drawings, borrower payments, guarantor proceeds, senior claims, costs, timing and collateral-value stress. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the economic mechanism.** Prudential frameworks differ in recognised collateral, supervisory or internal LGDs, downturn treatment, floors and discounting rules.

title: Exposure at default and credit conversion factors
one_screen: Exposure at default estimates or prescribes how much is exposed when default occurs, not how much is drawn today. Credit conversion factors translate undrawn or contingent amounts into exposure, making pre-default utilisation behaviour part of credit risk.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Facility component | Credit question | | :--- | :--- | | Current drawn amount | What is already exposed? | | Undrawn commitment | How much can still be drawn before default? | | Contingent item | What amount can crystallise into a claim? | | Accrued interest/fees | What additional amount may be outstanding at default under the chosen basis? | | Limit cancellation / draw-stop behaviour | How much future drawdown is actually possible? | For a fully drawn amortising loan, EAD can be close to expected balance at default. For cards, overdrafts and revolving commitments, distressed borrowers may draw further before failure, so current utilisation can materially understate EAD. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule EAD is anchored to the default event. Current balance is an input, not the definition. ### Never confuse [EAD] and [Current utilisation] **EAD** — exposure expected or prescribed at default. --- **Current utilisation** — amount drawn now, often expressed relative to the facility limit. ### Permanent trap Estimating revolving-credit loss on today’s balance while LGD is measured against default-date exposure creates a denominator mismatch and usually understates drawdown risk. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the mechanism.** Regulatory conversion factors, modelling permissions and off-balance-sheet exposure rules differ by jurisdiction and prudential approach.

title: Expected loss: PD × LGD × EAD
one_screen: `EL = PD × LGD × EAD` is a compact one-period loss decomposition only when the three inputs describe compatible default events, horizons, populations and economic conditions. The arithmetic is trivial; parameter alignment is the real mechanism.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Parameter | Role in loss | Alignment test | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | PD | Chance default occurs | Same default event and horizon as the loss measurement | | LGD | Severity if default occurs | Conditional on that same default definition and exposure basis | | EAD | Amount exposed at default | Measured for the same default event and population | For a low-PD loan, the most likely realised loss may be zero while expected loss is positive. EL is an average across possible outcomes, not a prediction that every individual exposure will lose a fractional amount. Dependence can hide inside the inputs. Revolving utilisation and recovery severity can both worsen around default or in recessions. Multiplying three independently estimated averages without considering their conditional meaning can therefore misstate the true expectation. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Reconcile event, horizon, population, observation point and valuation basis before multiplying PD, LGD and EAD. ### Never confuse [Expected loss] and [Most likely loss] **Expected loss** — probability-weighted average loss over the defined horizon. --- **Most likely loss** — the modal outcome; for many low-PD exposures it is zero. ### Permanent trap Combining a regulatory one-year PD, a lifetime accounting LGD and today’s balance creates a numeric answer whose components do not describe one coherent loss experiment. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) For covered commercial banks, RBI’s 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions mandate an expected-credit-loss provisioning framework from **1 April 2027**. **No delta in the probability decomposition.** Regulatory capital, accounting ECL and internal economics prescribe different parameter horizons, conditions and treatments; the same formula label does not make those calculations interchangeable.

title: Retail versus wholesale credit modelling
one_screen: Retail credit is usually managed through large pools of comparatively homogeneous exposures, making repeated statistical patterns powerful evidence. Wholesale credit is usually more obligor-centred because exposures are larger, populations are smaller and borrower-specific financial, structural and legal information matters more.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | Retail tendency | Wholesale tendency | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Number of exposures | Large | Smaller | | Individual exposure size | Comparatively small | Often material | | Homogeneity | Higher within designed segments | Lower | | Primary modelling unit | Pool / segment / facility behaviour | Obligor rating plus facility analysis | | Data evidence | Repeated behavioural observations | Financial statements, sector, management, structure, expert judgement | | Default application | Can permit facility/pool treatment under applicable rules | Generally obligor-centred in Basel-style wholesale frameworks | “Retail = model” and “wholesale = judgement” is too crude. Retail systems still need policy, overrides and fraud controls; wholesale ratings can use powerful quantitative models. The difference is how much **repeatable population evidence** versus **case-specific information** can support the decision. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Choose the modelling unit and method to match the economic homogeneity, data density and materiality of the exposures. ### Never confuse [Retail modelling] and [Automated lending] **Retail modelling** — pool-oriented estimation using repeated observations with similar risk characteristics. --- **Automated lending** — an operational decision process; retail credit can include manual review, and wholesale credit can use automation. ### Permanent trap Applying a mass-retail scorecard to a small, heterogeneous set of large corporates creates apparent statistical precision without a genuinely comparable population. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the economic logic.** Regulatory definitions determine which exposures qualify for retail or wholesale treatment and can impose size, pooling or management criteria.

title: Application, behavioural and bureau credit data
one_screen: Application models use information available at or before origination; behavioural models use information generated after the relationship exists; bureau or credit-information data add externally reported indebtedness and repayment history. Their common discipline is **time**: only information genuinely available at the decision or observation date may enter the prediction.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Information source | Observation point | Typical content | Limitation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Application | Origination | Declared/verified income, financials, demographics permitted by law, requested facility | No future account behaviour exists yet | | Internal behaviour | Post-origination | Payments, utilisation, arrears, balance trends, excesses | Requires account seasoning and clean observation windows | | Bureau / credit information | External reported history available at observation date | Other obligations, balances, enquiries, repayment history | Coverage, reporting lag, errors and thin files | | Policy / affordability | Decision-time rules | Eligibility, repayment capacity, limits | Not itself a statistical score | A bureau score or internal score is not automatically a PD. It must have a defined target, population and calibration. A “clean” thin file is also weaker evidence than a long clean history: absence of observed problems can mean absence of observation. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule A model may use only information that was available at the point in time at which the prediction is supposed to be made. ### Never confuse [Application score] and [Behavioural score] **Application score** — risk ranking from information available around origination. --- **Behavioural score** — risk ranking from subsequent account-performance information. ### Never confuse [Clean bureau] and [Strong repayment capacity] **Clean bureau** — no adverse event observed in the covered reported history. --- **Strong repayment capacity** — sustainable ability to meet future obligations from cash flow or resources; bureau history is only one input. ### Permanent trap Allowing later delinquency, post-decision bureau updates or other future information into an origination model creates target leakage and makes model performance look unrealistically strong. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the modelling logic.** Data availability, permissible variables, consumer rights, credit-reporting frequency and automated-decision requirements vary materially by law and jurisdiction.

title: Rating grades, master scales and migration
one_screen: A rating grade is a discrete class of borrower credit quality; a master scale defines the ordered meaning of all grades; migration records movement through that scale over time. A grade is not meaningful because it is called “4” or “BBB-like”—its meaning comes from assignment criteria, ordering, default boundary and calibrated risk.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Element | Owns | Test of quality | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Rating criteria | How an obligor is assigned | Consistent use of relevant risk drivers | | Master scale | Ordered risk states | Clear monotonic deterioration from strong to weak | | Grade PD | Probability attached to grade/pool | Calibration consistent with observed/default definition | | Override | Governed expert departure | Reason, authority and performance tracked | | Migration | Movement between grades | Stable state definitions through time | | Default grade | Terminal/default state for the relevant system | Aligned with governed default definition | A transition matrix counts or estimates movement from each starting grade to each ending grade over a fixed interval, including default. Migration separates a static stock of weak borrowers from a portfolio actively deteriorating toward those grades. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Rating model/process assigns and documents the grade | | Approves | Credit authority or rating governance confirms assignment/override where required | | Consumes | Underwriting, portfolio monitoring, pricing, capital and reporting | | Challenges | Independent credit risk, model validation and audit test scale performance | ### Permanent rule A grade must retain a stable, documented meaning if historical default and migration statistics are to remain comparable. ### Never confuse [Rating migration] and [PD recalibration] **Rating migration** — the obligor moves from one risk grade to another. --- **PD recalibration** — the probability mapped to a grade or score changes; the grade label can remain unchanged. ### Permanent trap Changing grade criteria and then analysing the old and new labels as one continuous transition history produces false migration statistics. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the concept.** Regulatory frameworks differ in rating-system granularity, approval, floors, use tests and validation requirements.

title: Vintage analysis and roll rates
one_screen: Vintage analysis follows exposures originated at similar times as they season; roll-rate analysis follows movement between delinquency or credit states. Both restore the time dimension that a portfolio snapshot destroys.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Method | Groups by | Compares | Best at revealing | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Vintage | Origination period | Performance at the same months-on-book | Underwriting/channel/cohort changes | | Roll rate | Current credit state | Next-period movement to worse, same or better state | Direction and speed of delinquency | | Snapshot | Observation date | Stock in each state today | Current composition only | A six-month-old cohort and a three-year-old cohort have had different time to season. Comparing their cumulative defaults on the same calendar date confounds credit quality with age. Vintage curves instead align performance at month 1, month 2, month 3 and so on. Roll rates answer a different question: of accounts now at 30–59 DPD, how many cure, stay, move to 60–89 DPD or default next period? Identical current delinquency stocks can therefore hide opposite future directions. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Compare like with like in time: equal seasoning for vintages, and fixed start/end states and intervals for roll rates. ### Never confuse [Vintage analysis] and [Roll-rate analysis] **Vintage analysis** — follows origination cohorts through account age. --- **Roll-rate analysis** — follows transitions between credit or delinquency states through time. ### Permanent trap A fast-growing young book can look safer than a mature book simply because many accounts have not existed long enough to reach default. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These are analytical methods; local definitions determine the delinquency and default states being tracked.

title: Concentration and diversification
one_screen: Concentration risk arises when too much exposure depends on the same name, connected group, sector, geography, collateral type or underlying economic driver. Diversification comes from genuinely different sources of loss, not from the number of rows, facilities or legal entities in a dataset.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Concentration form | Common failure source | Example diagnostic | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Single name | One obligor | Exposure / capital or portfolio share | | Connected group | Control or economic dependency | Aggregated group exposure | | Sector | Common industry conditions | Sector share and stressed sector loss | | Geography | Local economy / law / property market | Regional exposure share | | Product / collateral | Common underwriting or recovery mechanism | Product or collateral-type share | | Hidden factor | Shared commodity, customer, currency or funding driver | Factor mapping / scenario analysis | Ten equal exposures to genuinely independent obligors diversify idiosyncratic failure better than one exposure of the same total size. One thousand borrowers can still be concentrated if most depend on the same property market or commodity price. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Risk data and portfolio teams aggregate exposures and common drivers | | Approves | Board/senior risk governance sets appetite and concentration limits | | Consumes | Underwriting, limits, strategy, stress testing and capital planning | | Challenges | Independent risk and audit test aggregation, taxonomy and limit exceptions | ### Permanent rule Diversification must be judged by independence of loss drivers, not by nominal borrower count. ### Never confuse [Concentration] and [Large exposure] **Concentration** — dependence on a common source of loss, which may be name, sector, geography, collateral or another factor. --- **Large exposure** — an exposure or connected-group exposure meeting a defined regulatory or internal size threshold; concentration is broader. ### Permanent trap Splitting one economic group across subsidiaries or one common sector across narrow industry codes can improve a report while leaving the underlying loss concentration unchanged. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) RBI’s Large Exposures Framework governs prudential single-counterparty and connected-counterparty aggregation and limits. Internal concentration management must still capture sector and common-factor risks outside the legal large-exposure perimeter. #### UK (PRA) PRA large-exposure rules and SS3/25 govern connected-client identification; concentration risk also feeds broader supervisory and Pillar 2 assessment. #### EU CRR large-exposure rules constrain single clients and groups of connected clients; broader concentration risk remains a risk-management and supervisory concern. #### US US legal lending limits use US-specific aggregation rules. Internal sector and factor concentration management is broader than statutory single-borrower limits.

title: Correlation and systematic credit risk
one_screen: Credit correlation means default and loss outcomes are not independent because common economic forces move many borrowers together. Idiosyncratic risk can be diversified across sufficiently independent exposures; systematic risk cannot be removed by adding more borrowers exposed to the same underlying conditions.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Risk source | Example | Diversification effect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Idiosyncratic | Fraud, plant failure, loss of one customer | Falls as many independent names are added | | Sector systematic | Commodity-price collapse, industry disruption | Persists across borrowers in the same sector | | Macro systematic | Recession, unemployment, rate shock | Can affect many sectors and borrowers together | | Recovery dependence | Property prices fall during mortgage defaults | Defaults and LGDs can worsen together | | Utilisation dependence | Revolvers draw in stress | Defaults and EAD can worsen together | Correlation does not require equal PDs. A 1% PD firm and a 5% PD firm can still become riskier at the same time because both respond to recession, rates or a common customer base. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Adding exposures diversifies risk only to the extent that their failure drivers are not the same. ### Never confuse [Correlation] and [Concentration] **Correlation** — dependence between credit outcomes. --- **Concentration** — disproportionate exposure to names or common drivers; concentration magnifies the consequence of dependence but is not the same concept. ### Permanent trap Assuming legal independence implies default independence systematically understates loss clustering during common economic stress. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Correlation and systematic risk are economic and statistical properties; prudential frameworks differ in how dependence is parameterised, stressed or capitalised.

title: Unexpected loss and capital
one_screen: Expected loss is the average credit cost under a defined measurement; unexpected loss is adverse variation around that average. Capital protects solvency against sufficiently severe outcomes above ordinary expected-loss capacity, so portfolio dispersion and dependence matter even when exposure-level EL is unchanged.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Question | Main drivers | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Expected loss | What loss is anticipated on average? | PD, LGD, EAD and their aligned conditioning | | Loss volatility | How much can realised loss vary? | Granularity, parameter variation, migration | | Tail / unexpected loss | How severe can adverse loss become above the mean? | Concentration, correlation, systematic stress | | Capital | What loss-absorbing resources protect solvency? | Prudential/economic confidence standard and capital rules | Two portfolios can have identical EL but very different tail risk. One may contain thousands of diversified exposures; another may depend on a few correlated names. Their average loss can match while their severe-loss quantiles do not. ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Formula ### Permanent rule Expected loss and capital answer different questions: average credit cost versus protection against adverse loss beyond that average. ### Never confuse [Expected loss] and [Capital] **Expected loss** — probability-weighted average credit loss for the defined measurement. --- **Capital** — loss-absorbing resources held under a regulatory or internal solvency framework; it is not simply `PD × LGD × EAD`. ### Permanent trap Calling exposure-level EL “capital” ignores diversification, correlation, concentration and the shape of the portfolio loss distribution. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta in the conceptual split.** Regulatory capital formulas, buffers, Pillar 2 practices and accounting/provision regimes vary materially across jurisdictions.

title: The credit-loss architecture
one_screen: Credit risk is one continuous system: identify the person and exposure, decide whether repayment is sustainable, recognise default consistently, measure probability, severity and exposure, then aggregate common loss drivers into portfolio tail risk. The architecture fails when adjacent layers are collapsed—for example, collateral into repayment capacity, DPD into default, score into PD, or expected loss into capital.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Owns the question | Core objects | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Credit object | Who owes what? | Obligor · Facility · Account · Exposure · Connected group | | Credit decision | Should this risk be taken and on what terms? | Policy · Repayment capacity · Approval · Mitigants | | Credit state | Has contractual credit performance failed under the governed rule? | DPD · UTP · Default · Restructuring · Cure · Write-off | | Risk parameters | How likely, how severe, how much exposed? | PD · LGD · EAD | | Expected loss | What is the average loss cost? | PD × LGD × EAD under aligned definitions | | Risk measurement system | How is risk ranked and observed through time? | Retail pools · Scores · Bureau data · Ratings · Migration · Vintages | | Portfolio tail | What can fail together? | Concentration · Correlation · Systematic risk | | Solvency protection | What absorbs severe loss above the mean? | Unexpected loss · Capital | ### Flow ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Keep each layer’s question separate, then connect the outputs deliberately. A precise answer at the wrong layer is still the wrong risk measure. ### Never confuse [Expected loss capacity] and [Capital] **Expected loss capacity** — pricing, provisions/allowances or other mechanisms that recognise and absorb anticipated credit cost under the applicable framework. --- **Capital** — resources protecting solvency against adverse outcomes beyond ordinary expected loss, under the applicable capital regime. ### Permanent trap A credit pack becomes incoherent when the same label is used for several layers—for example “risk” meaning score, PD, EL, provision and capital depending on the page. Always name the object, state and measure. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The architecture is universal. Jurisdictions differ in prudential definitions, accounting treatment, regulatory formulas, thresholds and legal enforceability, but those variants sit inside the same object → state → parameter → portfolio-loss chain.

title: Risk Data as a Discipline
one_screen: In the 2007–2009 financial crisis, banks could not aggregate their risk exposures quickly or accurately. This failure impaired timely decision-making, prompting regulators to formalize risk data management as a discipline (e.g. Basel BCBS 239) to ensure banks maintain accurate, timely, end-to-end risk data aggregation and reporting.
bodyText: Banks historically maintained data in silos and spreadsheets, impeding a holistic risk view. When Lehman Brothers collapsed in 2008, many institutions realized their systems could not tell the board or regulators the full picture of their exposures. The Basel Committee responded with BCBS 239 (2013) to “strengthen banks’ risk data aggregation capabilities and internal risk reporting practices”. Globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs) had to comply by 2016; supervisors applied similar standards to domestic SIBs. In practice, risk data discipline means implementing corporate-wide data governance, architecture and controls so that any material risk metric can be produced “fully, quickly and accurately.” This underpins effective risk management and regulatory compliance. Key outcomes of this discipline include board-level data governance, documented processes, and accountability for data quality. It also requires banks to invest in integrated data architectures and automation, since manual consolidation is deemed unacceptable. The discipline encompasses ongoing improvement: recent Basel progress reports note that, years on, many banks still need work to fully meet BCBS 239. ### Permanent rule Timely, accurate risk data is essential for sound decision-making and regulatory compliance. ### Permanent trap Relying on last-minute, manual spreadsheet aggregations (especially during stress) can give a false sense of security. ### Never confuse **Risk data** — Information on potential losses or exposures (e.g. credit, market risk metrics). It is forward-looking and used for risk management. --- **Accounting (financial) data** — Realized financial transactions (P&L, balance sheets) as recorded in accounts. Risk data and accounting data serve different purposes and must be reconciled, not conflated. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The need for robust risk data aggregation and reporting is a universal lesson from the financial crisis.

title: Risk Data Aggregation vs Risk Reporting
one_screen: Risk data aggregation is the internal process of collecting and consolidating all relevant risk data across the bank. Risk reporting is the output of that process, conveying the aggregated data in reports. BCBS 239 treats them as separate obligations: the former ensures data is accurate and complete; the latter ensures reports are clear and delivered on time.
bodyText: Risk data aggregation focuses on gathering data points (e.g. exposures, positions) from all business lines, legal entities and regions into a single view. It requires data warehousing, reconciliation with accounting systems, and automated controls to meet BCBS 239’s principles on accuracy, completeness, timeliness and adaptability. By contrast, risk reporting is about designing and distributing the reports themselves. It covers how aggregated data is formatted, explained and delivered to decision-makers and regulators. Reporting practices include ensuring reports are “accurate, comprehensive, and written for their intended audience” with appropriate frequency and escalation paths. In effect, aggregation is about the data pipelines (the “back office” work) and reporting is about the presentation. For example, Principle 4 (completeness) demands data from *all* material sources be captured, whereas Principle 9 (clarity) demands that reports be understandable to non-technical users. A bank may have strong data pipelines but still produce poor reports if it fails the latter principle. BCBS 239 Group II (Principles 3–6) governs aggregation; Group III (Principles 7–11) governs reporting. Both must be in place: good aggregation without clear reporting fails to inform stakeholders, and good reports without sound data defeat regulators’ objectives. ### Permanent rule Aggregation and reporting are distinct steps: you must first consolidate all required data, then use it in reports designed for the audience. ### Permanent trap Fixating on report templates or dashboards without ensuring the underlying data is comprehensive and reconciled leads to misleading outputs. ### Never confuse **Risk data aggregation** — Internal consolidation of all risk data (the “what” and “how” data is collected). --- **Risk reporting** — The communication of aggregated risk metrics (the “presentation” of that data to management/regulators). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** All jurisdictions distinguish between banks’ data-processing capabilities and the reports they deliver to supervisors.

title: BCBS 239 Principles Overview
one_screen: BCBS 239 comprises 14 principles organized in four groups: (I) Governance & Infrastructure (board accountability, data architecture), (II) Risk Data Aggregation Capabilities (accuracy, completeness, timeliness, adaptability), (III) Risk Reporting Practices (comprehensiveness, clarity, frequency, distribution), and (IV) Supervisory Review (how regulators assess banks). Together they form a principles-based framework requiring banks to implement robust data policies and systems.
bodyText: BCBS 239’s purpose is to ensure banks can identify their risk exposures at any time. It mandates that the board of directors oversee data quality, and that the Chief Risk Officer is accountable day-to-day. Principle 1 demands “strong governance” consistent with other Basel standards, and Principle 2 requires a data architecture that supports aggregation in normal and stress conditions (avoiding last-minute spreadsheets). The second group (Principles 3–6) then focuses on aggregation: data must reconcile with accounting, cover all material sources (at least ~95%), be updated rapidly (daily or intraday for critical metrics), and support ad hoc queries under stress. The third group (Principles 7–11) covers reporting: risk reports must be “accurate, comprehensive, and written for their intended audience,” delivered at appropriate frequency, and distributed along the approved chain of command. Finally, Principles 12–14 describe supervisory review: they guide how regulators should evaluate compliance, require remediation plans for deficiencies, and address home/host coordination for global banks. BCBS 239 is principles-based: it does not prescribe specific IT architectures but sets outcomes. National supervisors (e.g. PRA in the UK, Fed in the US, RBI in India) expect banks to meet these outcomes, potentially imposing Pillar 2 add-ons for serious shortcomings. The standard has no formal legal force by itself; compliance is enforced through local regulation and supervision. ### Permanent rule The board of directors must ultimately own the risk data framework, not just delegate it to IT – strong governance is mandatory. ### Permanent trap Treating BCBS 239 as optional guidance; in practice, major regulators treat it as mandatory for significant banks. ### Never confuse **BCBS 239** — Basel Committee principles for risk data aggregation and reporting. Its focus is data and reporting quality. --- **Basel III/CRR** — Regulatory framework for capital and liquidity. While related to risk, Basel III addresses capital adequacy, not data architecture. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The 14 principles and their objectives are identical globally; they were adopted for G-SIBs with the same intent by all major regulators.

title: Risk Data Aggregation Capabilities (Accuracy, Completeness, Timeliness, Adaptability)
one_screen: BCBS 239 mandates that a bank’s risk data aggregation be **accurate, complete, timely, and adaptable**. In practice, this means automated data pipelines, extensive reconciliations, and flexible reporting capabilities. Banks must reconcile risk data with accounting records, cover ~95% of exposures across all entities, refresh data fast (daily or intraday for critical metrics), and be able to run ad-hoc reports on demand.
bodyText: The principle of **Accuracy and Integrity** (Principle 3) requires that risk data reconcile with the general ledger and management reports, and that automated checks minimize manual errors. Any manual adjustments must have documented rationale and approval. **Completeness** (Principle 4) means capturing data across all material business lines, legal entities and geographies. Supervisors typically expect banks to cover at least 95% of risk sources; any gaps trigger examination findings. **Timeliness** (Principle 5) demands that consolidated risk metrics be available fast enough for decision-making in stress; for example, daily VaR and credit portfolio reports as a baseline, potentially intraday for key measures. Finally, **Adaptability** (Principle 6) requires systems to produce new, ad-hoc reports quickly – for instance, answering a one-off supervisory query without months of coding. Banking institutions implement these requirements by building data warehouses or data lakes that collect source-system data nightly (or more frequently) and standardizing it. They set quality rules so that any discrepancy (e.g. mismatched values) is flagged. Importantly, the infrastructure must operate in crisis scenarios as well (e.g. with market freezes or system outages) to ensure data is still deliverable. The perpetual struggle is that legacy siloed systems and manual processes often fall short of these standards, which is why many banks have ongoing data improvement programs. Nonetheless, under BCBS 239, the **permanent requirement** is clear: all material risk data must be consolidated accurately and on time. ```text ### Permanent rule Risk aggregation must cover all material data and reconcile to accounting — incomplete or unverified data is unacceptable. ### Permanent trap Assuming that old processes (e.g. monthly spreadsheet closes) are sufficient; BCBS 239 expects daily or intraday capabilities and automation. ### Never confuse **Completeness** — capturing *all* relevant risk data (nearly 100% coverage). --- **Consistency (or validity)** — ensuring data adheres to business rules. While related, completeness means no gaps, consistency means matching definitions. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Data aggregation requirements (accuracy, completeness, etc.) are consistent under BCBS 239 across jurisdictions, as these are quantitative targets not subject to local modification.

title: Risk Reporting Practices
one_screen: BCBS 239 requires risk reports to be **accurate, comprehensive, clear, frequent, and properly distributed**. Reports must be tailored to their audience (e.g. board vs risk manager) and sufficiently granular. This ensures stakeholders get the right information at the right time.
bodyText: A bank’s risk reports should paint a complete picture: covering all major risk types (credit, market, liquidity, etc.) and including both totals and trend analysis. They must be error-free and understandable; jargon must be explained for non-experts. BCBS 239 (Principle 7–11) says reports should be of high quality (“comprehensive, timely, clear”) and delivered at the mandated frequency. For instance, daily and weekly dashboards for market risk, and periodic reports for portfolios, with exceptions escalated as needed. The reports must include documented definitions (so recipients know what each metric means) and must follow a regular schedule. Distribution (Principle 11) demands reports go to the right people (board, risk committee, regulators) and that escalation paths exist if limits are breached. In summary, risk reporting is about governance of the report content and process: it involves standard templates, sign-off procedures, and validation checks (ensuring the report matches the aggregated data). A common failure (trap) is producing reports without reconciling them back to source data (so-called “data drift”). Another mistake is listing raw data without analysis. Regulators have noted banks sometimes produce stat sheets but not insightful narrative or exception lists. Under BCBS 239, the **permanent expectation** is that reports translate data into actionable intelligence, validated end-to-end. ### Permanent rule Each risk report must be accompanied by context and definition, and approved by the appropriate officer; raw numbers alone are insufficient. ### Permanent trap Dumping large tables of figures in a report with no explanatory content or without ensuring they match the underlying data. ### Never confuse **Frequency** vs **Response Time**: Frequency — how often reports are published (e.g. daily, monthly). Response Time (Timeliness) — how quickly updated data is produced during stress. Reporting frequency must align with decision needs but is not the same as intraday data availability. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These qualitative reporting expectations are set at the global level by BCBS 239; national supervisors typically echo them.

title: Supervisory Review and Compliance Record
one_screen: The final BCBS 239 principles cover supervisory review (Principles 12–14) and require banks to act on regulators’ findings. By 2023, global reports show banks remain at “different stages” of compliance and need significant work to meet the standard.
bodyText: Principles 12–14 instruct how supervisors should review the data framework and require remediation if the bank’s practices are deficient. They encourage cross-border coordination for global groups, and detail potential supervisory measures (e.g. requiring capital add-ons for data weaknesses). In effect, they push banks to treat risk data as a first-class issue. Recent Basel progress reports note that almost a decade after BCBS 239’s publication, no major bank is fully compliant. The press release observes “banks are at different stages of alignment” and “additional work is required at all banks to attain or sustain full compliance”. Supervisors worldwide (Fed, ECB, PRA, RBI, etc.) have been pressing banks via Stress Test frameworks and Pillar 2 dialogues to close gaps. A critical point: BCBS 239 itself has no formal legal force (it relies on member commitments). In the UK, the PRA explicitly incorporates its expectations into SREP for major banks. The ECB can impose Pillar 2 guidance for data issues, and the Fed expects high-quality data for its FR Y-14 stress tests. Thus, compliance is enforced locally. Globally, the common narrative is that risk data deficiencies have been a repeat finding in audits and reviews. The **permanent expectation** is that any material data issue must be escalated and fixed, and supervisors will hold senior management accountable. ### Permanent rule BCBS 239 principles must be embedded institution-wide and are enforced by national regulators. Formal remediation plans are expected when issues are found. ### Permanent trap Treating audit comments on data as mere “to-dos” rather than core risk-control failures. Senior management must lead remediation. ### Never confuse **BCBS 239** — A supervisory standard, not a law. --- **Accounting standard** — (e.g. IFRS) Rules for financial statements. BCBS 239 is about data systems, not accounting treatment. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** All major jurisdictions (UK PRA, ECB, Fed, RBI etc.) regard BCBS 239 outcomes as required for SIBs, though enforcement mechanisms vary.

title: Golden Source of Data
one_screen: A golden source is the single authoritative source of truth for a given data element across the organization. It contains the most accurate and up-to-date version of that data, and all systems reference this “one source” to avoid discrepancies.
bodyText: For example, a bank might designate one system or database as the golden source for the exchange rate used in all risk reports, or the official customer master record. All downstream processes then draw from that gold record. This prevents situations where different departments have conflicting values for the same metric. Building a golden source requires strong data governance: clear ownership of the data field, defined quality rules, and processes to update the source whenever new information arrives. The golden source concept is vital under BCBS 239 Principle 2 (Data Architecture): it supports reconciliation and ensures “a single, authoritative source” for each risk metric. Without it, banks often hit the trap of “multiple authorities” – e.g. one system reporting Value-at-Risk one way, another giving a different number. A common rule is that only the golden source can feed regulators; any other calculation must reconcile back to it. Golden source is sometimes synonymous with “source of truth” or “master dataset.” It is not static: it is updated continuously to reflect the latest true data. Achieving a golden source typically involves integrating data pipelines and may use technologies like master data management (MDM) tools. The permanent expectation is that *every key data field* has one golden source designated, so that accuracy and consistency are maintained. ### Permanent rule For each key data element, the bank must designate one authoritative source and use it consistently. ### Permanent trap Allowing multiple “masters” for the same data field (e.g. one report using Core banking data, another using Risk system) causes conflicts and undermines trust. ### Never confuse **Golden source** — The official, authoritative dataset for a piece of information. --- **Data lake** — A repository of raw data. A data lake is not by itself an authoritative source unless governance ensures it contains only validated data. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The concept of a single authoritative source is best practice worldwide; regulators expect banks to avoid conflicting data sources.

title: Critical Data Elements (CDEs)
one_screen: Critical Data Elements (CDEs) are the data points an organization deems essential to its core operations, decision-making, and compliance. In banking, CDEs include fields like customer ID, credit exposure amounts, collateral valuations, etc. They require special governance attention since errors in CDEs can have significant impact.
bodyText: Organizations identify CDEs based on risk and business significance. For example, any data field that feeds risk-weight calculations or capital models would be a CDE. Under BCBS 239, regulators effectively treat all material risk data as CDEs. Good data governance frameworks inventory CDEs and assign them owners and stewards. The owner (often a senior business manager) is responsible for the definition and quality of each CDE; stewards implement controls and fixes. Marking data as “critical” means prioritizing quality rules, monitoring, and issue management for those fields. The idea is to avoid the opposite of the CDE philosophy: that all data gets equal, impractical scrutiny. By focusing on CDEs, banks can allocate resources to where mistakes matter most. Identifying CDEs is not a one-time task; it must be revisited as regulations and products change. ### Permanent rule Banks must explicitly identify and govern their critical data elements (CDEs) to ensure governance efforts focus on high-impact fields. ### Permanent trap Treating all data elements alike; without highlighting CDEs, governance becomes spread too thin. ### Never confuse **CDE** — A specific field deemed critical (e.g. a risk exposure amount). --- **Data catalog** — A comprehensive inventory of all data assets (it may list CDEs but also all other fields). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The notion of identifying and governing CDEs is best practice internationally (no one sets different rules on which fields count as “critical”).

title: Data Lineage (Business vs Technical)
one_screen: Data lineage tracks the journey of data from its origin to its final use. *Business lineage* is a high-level, user-friendly map of what data comes from where for reporting purposes; *technical lineage* is the detailed breakdown of data flows through systems and code. Both are essential for understanding and troubleshooting data issues.
bodyText: Business lineage answers “what data needed to produce a report and why.” It’s often documented in a business requirements document (BRD): e.g. a line item in a report is defined as “sum of loan commitments by country.” Technical lineage, by contrast, traces exactly how that sum is calculated: which tables in the core banking system, what transformations (aggregations, currency conversion) were applied, and how it moved into the data warehouse. Regulators and auditors require lineage evidence to trust reports. For instance, if a regulator sees a credit risk report, they may ask the bank to show the chain of systems and transformations leading to each number. Clear lineage helps identify root causes of data discrepancies. If a report number is wrong, technical lineage lets data engineers pinpoint where the anomaly occurred in the pipeline. Business lineage helps managers understand the impact (e.g. which products are affected). Both together provide a “complete picture.” Under BCBS 239, documenting lineage is part of demonstrating data governance; many banks include lineage diagrams in their data management plans. ### Permanent rule Always document both business and technical lineage when creating data flows or reports. This double perspective ensures clarity for both business and IT stakeholders. ### Permanent trap Providing only high-level lineage (“loans come from system X”) without the technical detail needed for audit. ### Never confuse **Business lineage** — A high-level mapping (for example, “Loan system ⇒ (sum) ⇒ monthly risk report”), understandable by non-IT stakeholders. --- **Technical lineage** — A precise record of ETL steps, database tables and transformations that produce the data. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Both forms of lineage are part of global data governance expectations (e.g. BCBS 239 Principle 2’s call for documented architecture).

title: Metadata and Business Glossary
one_screen: Metadata is “data about data” – information that defines and describes data elements. A business glossary is a centralized catalog of business terms and their definitions. Together, they ensure everyone has a common understanding of data definitions.
bodyText: For example, a report might include a column “Non-Performing Asset Ratio.” Metadata would record that this is calculated as “Total NPA amount / Total advances” and has business unit “Retail Loans.” The business glossary would define “Non-Performing Asset” (e.g. a loan overdue >90 days). Good metadata systems also track data source, format, and constraints for each field. Under RBI guidance, banks are urged to use common taxonomies and sync metadata across systems. This means aligning internal definitions with external ones (e.g. RBI’s definition of NPA). A single business glossary prevents mismatches where one department uses one term differently from another. Both metadata and glossary entries should have clear ownership, and be updated when policies change. This is a cornerstone of data governance: without metadata, reports can’t be properly interpreted and controls on data validity are weak. ### Permanent rule All regulatory and risk data fields must have definitions and metadata documented, linked to the official business glossary. ### Permanent trap Assuming everyone understands a term; failing to codify definitions causes inconsistent reporting and confusion. ### Never confuse **Metadata** — Details about data fields (type, format, source, lineage). --- **Business glossary** — A dictionary of business terms with plain-language definitions (bridges business and technical meaning). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Standardizing metadata and glossaries is universally recommended (e.g. BIS mentions using international codes and definitions for RBI reporting).

title: Data Dictionary and Data Model
one_screen: A data dictionary is a detailed catalog of all fields (data elements), describing each one’s attributes (name, type, description, format, valid values, etc.). A data model (conceptual or logical) is a diagram showing entities and relationships between them. Together they help design systems and prevent misinterpretation.
bodyText: For instance, in a bank’s credit risk data model, entities might include `Customer`, `Loan`, `Collateral`. The data dictionary would list that `Loan.Amount` is a numeric field in rupees, defined as “principal outstanding.” The dictionary is a repository of these definitions for technical staff, while the model visualizes how `Loan` relates to `Customer` and `Collateral`. Having a data model ensures database tables and fields align with business concepts (avoids missing fields). The dictionary ensures anyone writing queries or reports knows exactly what each field means. Both should be version-controlled. When regulations introduce new report items, the dictionary/model must be updated. Without them, even a simple mapping exercise is error-prone, and data integration between systems becomes guesswork. ### Permanent rule Every data field in any regulatory report or risk system must be defined in the data dictionary and accounted for in the data model. ### Permanent trap Skipping the dictionary for “obvious” fields; even basic terms like “balance” need precise definition in a banking context. ### Never confuse **Data dictionary** — A detailed list of fields and technical specs for developers and analysts. --- **Data catalog** — A broader inventory (often tool-based) that may include the data dictionary and also lineage, quality metrics, etc. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The use of data dictionaries and models is a technical practice not dictated by law; best practices are common globally.

title: Reference Data vs Master Data
one_screen: Master data consists of core business entities (e.g. customers, accounts, products) that are critical to operations, while reference data consists of standardized code sets or classifications (e.g. country codes, currency codes, security identifiers). Master data changes as business grows; reference data is relatively stable and often global (ISO codes, etc.).
bodyText: For example, a customer record (with name, KYC info) is master data; the country code “IN” used in an address is reference data. Master data is usually owned by business functions (e.g. front office), whereas reference data can be managed centrally (often by risk or finance teams). Both must be maintained carefully: a glitch in master data can misstate exposure for an entity; a stale reference code (like an outdated ISIN) can disrupt reporting. Regulatory data reporting relies on reference data standards (e.g. RBI may mandate ISO country codes in returns). Master data alignment ensures all systems recognize the same legal entity (which ties into entity resolution and LEIs). In practice, data governance tracks both types. Tools like MDM systems often manage master data, while governance tools or data catalogs manage reference codes. But conceptually, **never confusing** them is key. Reference data supports interpretation of master data. ### Permanent rule Maintain a single master record for each core entity and use standard reference data sets (e.g. ISO codes) across the bank. ### Permanent trap Letting departments define their own “local” reference lists (e.g. local sector codes instead of international standards), leading to integration headaches. ### Never confuse **Master data** — Business-critical records (customers, accounts) that the bank transacts with. --- **Reference data** — Shared classification codes and lists (currency codes, country codes, industry codes) used for categorizing data. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Distinction between master vs reference data is a general data management concept, not subject to regulatory variation.

title: Data Quality Dimensions
one_screen: Data quality is multi-dimensional. Key dimensions include **accuracy** (data correctly reflects reality), **completeness** (no missing values), **consistency** (data aligns across sources), **timeliness** (data is up-to-date and available when needed), **validity** (data follows defined formats and rules), and **uniqueness** (no duplicates).
bodyText: For regulatory reporting, all dimensions matter. For example, an asset balance must be accurate (matches the general ledger), complete (every balance is reported), valid (currency format, non-negative), and timely (as of the report date). Consistency ensures that if two reports reference the same exposure, they use the same amount. Defining these dimensions allows setting measurable targets: e.g. 99% of accounts must be filled (completeness threshold), or 100% of country codes must match ISO lists (validity). Banks implement data quality frameworks that automate checks against these dimensions. Scorecards might flag any loans with null values (completeness) or duplicate customer IDs (uniqueness). Working these dimensions into BCBS 239 compliance means building controls for each: reconciliation for accuracy, data completeness reports, etc. ### Permanent rule All regulatory data must meet the necessary quality dimensions for its use. Missing or outdated key data invalidates a report. ### Permanent trap Focusing on only one dimension (e.g. only completeness) while ignoring others (like not verifying that “complete” data is accurate). ### Never confuse **Accuracy** — Data matches the true value or source system. --- **Consistency** — Data is uniform across systems (e.g. same value for Customer ID in trading vs risk systems). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Data quality dimensions are agreed best practice in all jurisdictions; regulators expect rigorous checks regardless of country.

title: Data Quality Rules, Thresholds, and Exception Management
one_screen: Data quality rules are specific checks or constraints (e.g. “loan amount ≥ 0”, “interest date must not precede loan date”). Thresholds set acceptable levels for quality metrics (e.g. “95% of records must be complete”). When data fails a rule or threshold, it is flagged as an exception to be investigated and resolved.
bodyText: For example, a completeness rule might state that 99% of trade records must have an associated counterparty ID. If only 97% do, that misses the threshold and triggers an exception report. Exception management then enters: the issue is logged with severity, root causes are analyzed (e.g. missing entries in a source feed), and corrective action is taken (perhaps a process fix or data backfill). Exception tracking tools or ticket systems typically record these issues. Banks document quality rules in their governance frameworks, often aligning with BCBS 239’s accuracy/integrity principle. At each reporting cycle, automated validators run the rules. Validations can be cross-checks (e.g. sum of sub-portfolios equals total) or plausibility checks (e.g. a ratio must lie in [0,100]). When thresholds are narrowly missed, some banks issue warnings; larger gaps may halt report submission until fixed. The **permanent expectation** is that no data anomaly goes unchecked. Adopting robust exception management means assigning issues to data stewards or owners, tracking SLA for fixes, and reporting status to management. Regulators have become wary of banks “papering over” persistent exceptions. Best practice is to classify and resolve high-impact exceptions immediately, while monitoring low-impact ones until clearance. ### Permanent rule Every failed quality check must be logged and owned; unresolved exceptions compromise report integrity. ### Permanent trap Archiving known data issues without resolution, assuming they are “small” or won’t recur. ### Never confuse **Data quality rule** — A specific constraint (e.g. a value range). --- **Threshold** — The allowable error rate (e.g. 1% missing data). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These practices are part of robust data governance everywhere; regulators everywhere expect strict validation and issue tracking.

title: Reconciliation (Front-to-Back and Risk-to-Finance)
one_screen: Reconciliation is the process of comparing data between systems to detect and resolve differences. *Front-to-back* reconciliation ensures that transactions recorded in front-office systems (trading, loans booking) match entries in the back-office accounting system. *Risk-to-finance* reconciliation ensures that risk metrics (e.g. aggregated exposures) reconcile to financial accounts (e.g. total assets or regulatory capital). Both are critical controls for data integrity.
bodyText: Front-to-back reconciliation typically involves comparing trade tickets or loan disbursements against the general ledger entries. Any mismatch (e.g. a trade missing from the ledger) is investigated. For example, the Risk data might sum all counterparty exposures and compare to the Finance system’s total asset value. Discrepancies often arise from timing differences or mapping errors. A common permanent rule is to run these reconciliations daily or at least monthly; material breaks must be cleared before period-end. Risk-to-finance reconciliation is especially vital under BCBS 239. If a bank reports a credit exposure of ₹100 bn to risk management, the finance team’s asset ledger should also reflect ₹100 bn (allowing for minor classification differences). Regulators expect banks to explain any gaps. A perennial trap is to ignore small mismatches that then grow unnoticed. Instead, banks should categorize breaks (e.g. expected timing lag vs error) and resolve root causes. Reconciliation tasks often uncover underlying data issues (bad mappings, missing code standards) that feed back into data quality improvement. ### Permanent rule Perform both front-to-back and risk-to-finance reconciliations regularly; document and fix all significant breaks. ### Permanent trap Only reconciling at quarter-end or audit time. Instead, reconciliation must be integrated into daily processes. ### Never confuse **Front-to-back reconciliation** — Comparing transactional data (front office) to accounting ledgers (back office). --- **Risk-to-finance reconciliation** — Comparing risk aggregate data (used in risk reports) to financial statements or accounting reports. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These reconciliations are standard controls in all banks worldwide.

title: Data Ownership vs Stewardship
one_screen: **Data owners** are senior business managers who are accountable for data assets; **data stewards** are specialists who manage data quality day-to-day. The owner defines data policies and sets quality standards, while the steward implements these standards and handles operational issues.
bodyText: For each CDE or data domain, an owner is formally assigned (often at executive or business-unit level). The owner’s responsibilities include approving definitions and prioritizing data initiatives. A data steward (usually in risk or finance department) is then responsible for monitoring data quality, investigating issues, and coordinating fixes with IT and business teams. The Reserve Bank recommends clarifying these roles: assigning ownership of key data elements and requiring data stewards to update the data governance committee. In practice, confusion between these roles is a trap. If nobody is accountable, issues languish; if too many claim ownership, governance muddles. Clear role definitions – documented in a data governance policy – are essential. For example, the data owner might be the Head of Credit Risk for loan data, while the data steward is a risk analyst reporting to them. Together they ensure questions like “Who decides loan classification rules?” have an answer. ### Permanent rule Every critical data element must have a single business owner assigned (with ultimate accountability) and one or more stewards (with operational responsibilities). ### Permanent trap Assigning ownership to IT or multiple owners by default. Ownership should reside in the business line that “owns” the risk. ### Never confuse **Data owner** — Business executive responsible for a domain or data set (e.g. loans, market data). Accountable for policies. --- **Data steward** — Practitioner who enforces data standards and quality, reports to the owner. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Defining data ownership and stewardship is a standard governance practice across banks globally.

title: Data Governance Models
one_screen: Data governance models define how oversight is structured. Common models are *centralized* (a single data governance committee sets policies for all) and *federated* (each business unit has its own governance under corporate guidelines). RBI notes typical models based on process, subject area, or geography, but emphasizes business-function-based ownership.
bodyText: In a centralized model, a bank-wide data council or steering committee makes decisions on data standards and conflicts. This ensures consistency but can be slow to react. In a federated model, each line of business governs its own data (loans, payments, etc.) with a chief data steward, under high-level corporate policy. This is more agile but risks inconsistent rules. Many banks use a hybrid: enterprise-wide standards set by a central group, with subcommittees or local owners refining for their area. Choosing a model depends on bank size and culture. Large global banks often need a strong central committee (reporting to the board) to coordinate regional offices. A smaller bank might use a subject-based structure (e.g. separate governance for retail vs corporate banking data). RBI’s guidance suggests ownership should follow business functions, with an executive data governance committee and clear roles. Regardless of model, a permanent rule is that the structure and responsibilities must be documented. A trap is letting data governance stay informal or ad hoc. Best practice: publish an operating model (committees, roles, processes), and review it periodically. The goal is a sustainable model where policies are enforced, quality is measured (e.g. via KPIs), and issue remediation is managed end-to-end. ### Permanent rule Define and publish your data governance structure (committees, roles, processes) and measure its effectiveness. ### Permanent trap Believing “one size fits all” – e.g. centralizing without business input can lead to resistance. Balance central oversight with local expertise. ### Never confuse **Centralized governance** — A single corporate body governs all data decisions. --- **Federated governance** — Each division/business unit has autonomy (within overall guidelines). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These are organizational choices; regulators expect some governance model, but don’t mandate a specific structure.

title: Issue Management and Remediation
one_screen: Data issues must be formally managed: identified, tracked, and remediated through a controlled process. This typically involves logging issues in an issue-tracking system, prioritizing by severity, performing root-cause analysis, and implementing fixes under governance oversight.
bodyText: In practice, once a data validation or reconciliation uncovers an error (for example, a daily report mismatch), an issue ticket is created. The ticket includes description, severity (e.g. Critical if it affects a report submission), and owner (often a data steward). Root cause might be a system defect, a mapping error, or missing data. The solution plan is documented – e.g. code correction or process change – with milestones. Senior management tracks progress via dashboards or committee reports. BCBS 239 requires that material data/reporting issues be escalated “to the highest appropriate level” and that timely action be taken. A bank’s “issue management” process is a key part of its data governance framework. A trap is failing to monitor slow fixes; regulators expect permanent resolution, not temporary workarounds. A permanent rule is that any critical data quality issue (especially those impacting regulatory reports) should be escalated through the risk committee or even board if needed. Remediation may involve multiple steps: short-term manual fixes (to enable report filing) and long-term system changes. Banks often set a standard (e.g. 30 days to fix a critical break). Progress is reported to risk committees, often via heatmaps of outstanding issues. Ultimately, management sign-off on the fix closes the loop. ### Permanent rule Every significant data discrepancy or report error must be tracked until fully resolved, with evidence of the fix. ### Permanent trap Treating issue tickets as “done” when a report is patched, rather than fixing the underlying data problem. ### Never confuse **Remediation** — The corrective actions taken to fix a data defect (code fixes, process changes). --- **Workaround** — A temporary solution to allow reporting to proceed (e.g. manual data entry) before full remediation. Both need controls and tracking. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** All regulators expect banks to have formal issue remediation processes (though naming may vary).

title: Regulatory Returns and Production Cycle
one_screen: A *regulatory return* is a standardized report or form that banks must submit to supervisors (e.g. capital, liquidity, or risk data). The production cycle involves: extracting data from source systems, transforming and mapping it to the return’s schema, aggregating as needed, validating the report against business rules, then submitting and attesting.
bodyText: Concretely, a bank’s risk data team gathers the necessary raw data (from trading, lending, finance systems) and runs it through a predefined mapping specification. This mapping (often in code or ETL tools) converts internal field names and units into the regulatory template fields. Aggregation steps consolidate records (e.g. summing exposures by counterparty type). Once the draft return is built, a series of validation checks ensures the filing is consistent (e.g. column sums match subsidiary filings, no negative values). Issue items from validations are resolved by adjusting mappings or cleaning data. Finally, the return is submitted electronically (often in XBRL or other formats) and signed off. Attestation and sign-off are usually required: typically a senior executive or compliance officer must certify the return is true and correct. Restatements occur when errors post-submission require a corrected filing; these must be communicated to the regulator. In data projects, understanding this full cycle is crucial: changes in business definitions or systems can break mappings, so any reporting change project must consider end-to-end impact. A sample production flow: ### Permanent rule Every field in a regulatory return must be traceable back to source data via the mapping logic. ### Permanent trap Neglecting to re-validate mappings after source system changes; a code update might redirect a column without testers noticing. ### Never confuse **Regulatory return** — A formal submission to a supervisor with pre-defined data items. --- **Regulatory report (internal)** — An internal risk report (like VaR reports) which is not directly submitted to regulators. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** All regulators require banks to follow this general extract-transform-validate-submit cycle for returns. (The details of formats differ.)

title: Attestation, Restatements, and Reporting Change Programs
one_screen: **Attestation and sign-off:** Senior management (often the board, CEO or Chief Risk Officer) must formally attest that each regulatory report is accurate and complete. This is both a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and an internal control. **Restatements:** If a material error is discovered after submission, the bank must correct (“restatement”) the return. Restatements can impact capital calculations or regulatory standings, so timely correction and explanation are critical. **Reporting change programs:** When regulations change or new reports are added, a change program is launched. This involves requirement analysis, mapping updates, system development, testing, and parallel runs.
bodyText: In practice, attestation is typically documented via a cover letter or checkbox in the submission portal. It holds senior officers legally responsible if the data is faulty. Restatements usually follow a defined protocol: e.g. notify the regulator, submit a corrected report, and explain the cause. Each restatement is logged to avoid repeat mistakes. Reporting changes (like new BCBS rules or formats) require project management. For instance, moving from manual to XBRL filing or adding a new COREP schedule. Such projects demand coordination between IT, data teams, and regulators. They produce new mapping specs and update test packs. A common trap is underestimating the regression testing needed across old reports. Compliance requires that all related reports still match after change. ### Permanent rule No report is final until attested. All corrections must be documented: one should never “forget” a restatement or leave an unexplained discrepancy. ### Permanent trap Thinking of reporting change as just a format switch; in reality it often involves changing data definitions, so deep validation is needed. ### Never confuse **Attestation** — Management’s certification of a report’s accuracy. --- **Audit** — Independent verification by internal or external auditors. Attestation is self-certification; audit is independent checking. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Attestation/sign-off processes and requirements for restatements are universal (though e.g. Indian banks may align with Companies Act and RBI letters).

title: Delivery Layer: Requirements, Mapping, and Testing
one_screen: The delivery layer in a data program consists of business requirements, mapping specifications, and testing. A Business Requirements Document (BRD) defines *what* reports/data are needed (with business context). A Data Mapping Specification details *how* each target field is derived from source fields with transformation logic. Testing involves pre-defined result sets and user acceptance testing (UAT) to validate that the implemented mappings produce the expected outputs.
bodyText: **BRD:** In regulatory/risk contexts, the BRD describes needed data points, calculation methods, timing, and exceptions. It often cites regulatory definitions. The BRD ensures developers and analysts understand the objectives. **Data Mapping Spec:** This is the core deliverable. It is typically a spreadsheet or document listing: Source Field → Transformation Rule → Target Field. For example: “LoanBook.EndDate → Calendar Quarter End for report.” Each mapping should include any conversion (currency, units) and business rules applied. It serves as the blueprint for ETL developers. **Testing:** Test packs with known inputs and results are prepared. For example, a small dataset with calculated expected totals. During UAT, business users verify that outputs match these expectations. Automated regression tests and reconciliation reports are also built to compare results against legacy systems or previous runs. UAT covers functional correctness and edge cases. A strong delivery approach uses examples: e.g. test that negative balances or unusual security types still produce correct report lines. Downstream extracts (e.g. FINREP extracts sent to ECB) should also be checked – that is, one might run a script on the final data extract to verify totals against source systems. The process is iterative: any discrepancies found in UAT or extracts feed back into the mapping (looping through the cycle again until clean). ### Permanent rule Every data transformation must be traceable (via the mapping spec) and tested with expected results before production use. ### Permanent trap Skipping UAT or not involving actual report users. Testing by IT alone often misses business logic errors. ### Never confuse **Business Requirements Document (BRD)** — Describes the *what* and *why* (business needs, regulatory requirements). --- **Mapping Specification** — Details the *how* (the exact field mappings and calculations). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** These delivery practices apply to any data/reporting project, regardless of jurisdiction.

title: Jurisdiction-Specific Reporting Frameworks
one_screen: Regulatory reporting frameworks differ by jurisdiction. BCBS 239 itself is a global set of principles with **no direct legal force**. In practice:
bodyText: **IN** — India’s RBI has instituted the *Automated Data Flow (ADF)* system. Since 2010, banks build a Centralised Data Repository (CDR) to consolidate required data elements, and submit many returns in XBRL format. RBI’s standards (e.g. on coding, unique IDs) govern data in this system. **UK** — The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) expects UK banks (especially “significant institutions”) to apply BCBS 239 outcomes.
