If the chance of default is small (p ≪ 1) and number of loans large, Binomial(n,p) ≈ Poisson(λ=np). For portfolios with many small exposures and low default rate, default counts ≈ Poisson. Poisson also arises for counting loan prepayments or rare credit events. It has one parameter λ (mean=variance). Using the correct distribution is crucial for risk metrics: e.g. mis-specifying default count as normal (when events are rare) underestimates tail risk. Each distribution’s parameters should be estimated from data or expert priors, and used consistently in simulations or VaR calculations. ### Permanent rule Each distribution’s assumptions must match the credit context (e.g. non-negative, skewed, independent events). Using a normal model for highly skewed or discrete data leads to wrong estimates. ### Permanent trap Treating an inherently skewed quantity (like loan loss amounts) as normally distributed can underestimate extreme losses. For example, assuming symmetric losses when actual losses (e.g. severe defaults) follow a long-tailed lognormal can understate required provisions. ### Never confuse **Binomial distribution** — count of successes (e.g. defaults) in a fixed number of trials (loans) with success probability *p*. --- **Poisson distribution** — count of independent events (e.g. defaults) over fixed exposure/time when events are rare. Poisson can approximate binomial for large *n* and small *p* (np=λ). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Probability distributions and their shapes are mathematical truths. Specific regulatory models (e.g. Basel IRB) may use these distributions (e.g. Vasicek’s normal-based model), but the underlying math is universal.

title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and Credit Risk
one_screen: The CLT states that the sum (or average) of many independent, identically distributed random variables approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the original distribution. In credit, it justifies using normal approximations for aggregated risks (like portfolio losses) when individual variations are small.
bodyText: If a bank has a large, diversified loan portfolio, each loan’s default or loss contributes a little to total risk. By the CLT, the distribution of total loss approximates normal, even if individual loan losses are skewed. For example, if many similar small loans each have random loss, their average or sum will be near normal. This helps in risk capital models (e.g. using normal quantiles to set capital). However, the CLT has conditions: loans should be *independent* (or only weakly correlated) and none *too large* (“fine-grained” portfolio). Credit portfolios often violate CLT ideal assumptions. Defaults can be correlated through economic cycles (violating independence), and large exposures (“lumpiness”) also break the identical small-size assumption. Basel’s IRB capital formula assumes infinite, independent loans (the “asymptotically fine-grained” condition). In reality, correlated defaults (systematic risk) mean aggregate losses can have fat tails. Thus, CLT only licenses normal approximations under strong diversification. **In practice:** one uses CLT as a guide but tests its validity. Risk managers might apply normal approximations to portfolio VaR only after verifying no extreme concentration. If not, alternative distributions (e.g. Vasicek distribution for correlated losses) are used. The *permanent rule*: use CLT for large, well-diversified groups, but check for correlation or large-exposure breaks. ### Permanent rule Large, independent loan portfolios produce approximately normal aggregate losses, but only if no single loan dominates and correlations are low. If not, explicitly model tail risk instead of relying on CLT. ### Permanent trap Assuming CLT holds when loans are correlated or a few loans are huge. E.g. a bank with a $1B loan and many $1k loans is not “fine-grained” – CLT fails. Basel notes that violating these assumptions (lumpiness or multiple risk factors) “would result in an incorrect assessment of portfolio risk”. ### Never confuse **Normal approximation (CLT)** — valid when summing many i.i.d. variables (small loans, independent). --- **Exact distribution** — e.g. Vasicek’s model or empirical simulation; needed if defaults correlate or portfolio is not fine-grained. CLT’s normal result is a special-case approximation, not always applicable. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** CLT is a mathematical theorem. Regulatory models like Basel’s IRB build on CLT assumptions, but if portfolio deviates, banks must adjust (e.g. use RWA add-ons).

title: Hypothesis Testing and p-values
one_screen: Hypothesis testing assesses if observed data significantly differ from a specified model (null hypothesis). A *p-value* measures the probability of observing data as extreme as ours if the null hypothesis were true. It is **not** the probability the hypothesis is true.
bodyText: In credit analysis, one might test if a new scorecard has a higher default rate than historical average. The null hypothesis (H₀) could be "new model’s default rate = old rate." After collecting data, compute a test statistic (e.g. difference of proportions) and derive a p-value: the probability of seeing such a difference (or more extreme) by chance if H₀ holds. If p is below a chosen significance level (e.g. 5%), H₀ is rejected, suggesting a real difference. **Common misinterpretation:** p < 0.05 does *not* mean there’s only 5% chance H₀ is true. Instead, it means that if H₀ were true, only 5% of repeated experiments would yield data at least this extreme. StatPearls clarifies: “The p-value is not the probability of the null hypothesis itself. It is the probability that, if the study were repeated infinitely, one would get results at least as extreme as observed.” Thus, p informs us about data extreme-ness under H₀, not the truth of H₀. For example, testing “portfolio default rate > 2%” with sample data: suppose sample default was 2.5%, p = 0.03. This means there’s a 3% chance of seeing ≥2.5% defaults if true rate =2%. We might then conclude rate >2%. But if sample size is small, p can be misleading; also p=0.03 doesn’t prove a big effect, just that result is unlikely by chance. Practically, credit risk model validators use hypothesis tests (often z-tests or chi-square) for things like comparing PDs across time or segments. The permanent rule: set significance (alpha) before testing; treat p-value < alpha as evidence against H₀, but don’t over-interpret it. Statistical significance ≠ business significance: a tiny difference may be statistically significant with large data but irrelevant. Always interpret in context. ### Permanent rule Use p-values as a measure of data incompatibility with the null, not as proof of hypothesis truth. Treat p<α as grounds to examine assumptions, but also check effect size and practical importance. ### Permanent trap Believing p=0.03 means “there’s 97% chance this model is superior.” Actually, p=0.03 means “if there were no real difference, only 3% of experiments yield this result”. Don’t confuse p-value with certainty about hypotheses. ### Never confuse **p-value** — probability of observing data (or more extreme) under the null hypothesis. --- **Confidence level** — (1–α), e.g. 95% CI means 5% significance; but CI is about parameter range (QNT-05), not the probability that H₀ is false. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The logic of hypothesis testing and p-values is the same universally (frequentist inference). Regulatory models may stress statistical rigor (e.g. IRB model validations), but the math doesn’t change by locale. 0.05?" a="No. Failing to reject H₀ (p>0.05) is not proof that the null is true; it just means insufficient evidence against H₀ given sample size." />

title: Confidence Intervals
one_screen: A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of values for an unknown parameter (e.g. portfolio PD) such that, in repeated sampling, a specified percentage (e.g. 95%) of such intervals will contain the true parameter. It quantifies sampling uncertainty around an estimate.
bodyText: After estimating a parameter, say the default rate of a loan grade, we compute a CI. A 95% CI from 1.8% to 2.4% means if we repeated the borrower selection many times, about 95% of those intervals would include the true default rate. Importantly, it doesn’t mean “95% chance the true rate lies in this specific interval.” The true rate is fixed (unknown); the CI’s endpoints are random from sample variance. In credit risk, CIs are crucial. For example, IRB models often use confidence bounds on PDs or LGDs to ensure conservatism. When validating a new PD model, a regulator might require that observed default rates fall within the model’s forecast CI. If 2% forecast with ±0.2% margin, and observed is 2.3%, the interval check helps assess if deviation is within sampling noise or indicates miscalibration. **Calculation:** For large samples, a CI can be approximate normal: estimate ± z*SE, where SE is the standard error of the estimate. For proportion PD, SE = sqrt(p*(1-p)/n). For small samples or rare events, use exact (binomial) or bootstrap CIs. Also, always report confidence level (e.g. 95%) and sample size context. In summary, CI expresses estimation uncertainty: wider if data are sparse or variable, narrower with more/larger data. The permanent rule: always pair point estimates (like PD) with a CI to show reliability. Regulators often look at these intervals when backtesting models. ### Permanent rule Report estimates with their confidence intervals. The interval indicates how much estimation error might exist due to finite data. ### Permanent trap Misinterpreting CI as probability of parameter. E.g. “We’re 95% sure true PD is between 1.8–2.4%” is wrong. Actually, if we repeated data collection, 95% of such intervals would contain the true PD. ### Never confuse **95% confidence interval** — range capturing the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. --- **Credible interval (Bayesian)** — range where the parameter has 95% probability given the data (Bayesian concept). CI’s guarantee is about the method, not the single interval’s probability. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Statistical confidence intervals are universal. Financial regulations (e.g. RBI or ECB validation) may stipulate certain confidence levels, but methodology is the same.

title: Correlation vs Causation; Confounding
one_screen: Correlation means two variables move together; causation means one variable directly influences another. A *confounder* is a hidden common cause that creates a spurious correlation. In credit data, misidentifying causation can lead to wrong risk decisions.
bodyText: For example, a bank might observe that customers with many cellphone lines have higher default rates. This is a correlation. But is having multiple lines causing defaults? Likely not. A confounder like income or employment stability might cause both more phone lines and more default. If we ignorantly treat the phone lines variable as causal, we could erroneously deny credit to people with many phones, which is a mistake. Statistics: we often measure correlation by Pearson’s r (for continuous), or contingency tables for categorical. But high correlation doesn’t prove one causes the other. Another example: when credit scores rose during a boom, did positive sentiment cause better credit history, or did third factors (like unemployment falling) cause both? Without random experimentation, we cannot be sure. **Confounding** is common in observational credit data. Suppose a score model finds married customers default less. Marriage isn’t causing lower defaults per se; perhaps married people are older with steadier jobs (confounders). To claim causation, one needs to control for confounders or use techniques like propensity scoring. Practically, risk analysts should: ask if a predictive factor makes economic sense as a cause, and check if unobserved factors could be driving both. If unsure, treat correlated predictors with caution. For example, IGNORED: days-with-current-employer might correlate with income; controlling for both avoids blaming employer tenure incorrectly. ### Permanent rule Always question causality claims in credit models. Use domain knowledge and control for confounders to avoid spurious attributions. No matter how strong a correlation, it may be caused by hidden variables. ### Permanent trap Automatically assuming that a correlated predictor is causal. E.g., “Since region correlates with default, region causes default.” In reality, region may proxy economic conditions (the real cause). Mis-specifying this can lead to misdirected interventions. ### Never confuse **Correlation** — statistical association between two variables’ values (e.g. high debt ratio and defaults). --- **Causation** — one variable directly influences the other. They are not the same: correlation is necessary but not sufficient for causation. Always consider other variables that might explain the link. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The principle that correlation is not causation is fundamental to statistics. However, regulatory scrutiny may vary: e.g. fair lending laws (in US/EU) demand checking that models do not inadvertently use proxies for protected attributes (a form of confounding fairness).

title: Sampling Biases in Lending
one_screen: In lending analytics, *sampling bias* occurs when collected data systematically exclude certain outcomes. Common biases: **survivorship bias** (ignoring lost/terminated loans) and **selection bias** (e.g. analyzing only accepted applications). These distort estimates like default rates.
bodyText: **Sampling bias:** A sample differs from the true population by design. In credit, a notorious case is “only current customers”: if a bank studies default rates using only customers who renewed their credit cards, it misses those who defaulted or left, underestimating risk. CASRAI warns that bias doesn’t shrink with more data – it leads precisely wrong estimates. **Selection bias:** When the sample is chosen by outcome. For example, analyzing PD using only approved loans ignores applicants who were denied (who might be higher risk). This underestimates risk because we selected out lower-scoring individuals. Another example: surveying customers about repaying loans will naturally exclude those already delinquent or defaulted – giving an overly rosy repayment picture. **Survivorship bias:** A type of sampling bias where only “survivors” are seen. For instance, if a study of corporate bond defaults only includes companies still listed, it misses those that defaulted or delisted. In retail credit: if we only analyze auto loans that have not been repossessed, we ignore those lost deals, again biasing PD down. CASRAI’s classic example: looking only at airplanes that returned (survivors) misleads reinforcement strategy. Similarly, analyzing only ongoing loans ignores those that “didn’t survive” to be included. **Avoidance:** Always define a clear population: e.g. “all loans originated in 2018, tracking until 2021, including those closed by default, pay-off, or charge-off.” Use full origination data, not just current books. If data is truncated (e.g. only current borrowers), acknowledge bias and adjust (maybe via weight or external default statistics). Regulators (e.g. RBI IRB) expect PD models to account for these biases in historical data. ### Permanent rule Always include all relevant cases in your sample, especially failures. Missing defaulters or rejects biases any risk estimate. Double-check that your data frame contains both “survivors” and “non-survivors” from a cohort. ### Permanent trap Using only successfully repaid loans to model performance. This creates survivorship bias: only the “winners” are analyzed, making the portfolio look safer than it is. ### Never confuse **Survivorship bias** — only survivors of a process are seen (e.g. only extant accounts). --- **Selection bias** — systematic inclusion/exclusion during data collection (e.g. excluding denied applicants). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Data representativeness is a universal modeling principle. However, some jurisdictions explicitly emphasize these biases: e.g. the ECB’s IRB guidelines caution against using internal data that exclude defaulted obligors.

title: Linear Regression for Credit Scoring
one_screen: Linear regression models a continuous outcome (like credit line utilization or loss amount) as a weighted sum of predictors. Key assumptions include linearity, independent errors, and homoscedasticity. Coefficients indicate the average change in outcome per unit change in predictor, holding others constant.
bodyText: In regression, we fit a model `y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + ... + βₖxₖ + ε`. For credit analytics, `y` might be a continuous risk measure (e.g. loss given default, log of balance, etc.), and `x` variables could be borrower attributes. The fitting (ordinary least squares) finds β’s minimizing squared residuals. **Assumptions:** (1) Linear relationship: each predictor adds/subtracts constant effect on mean `y`; (2) Independent errors: each loan’s deviation from model is not autocorrelated; (3) Homoscedasticity: error variance constant across `x` values; (4) Errors ~ Normal (for inference). In practice, check residual plots to validate these. If heteroscedastic, use robust SE or transform y (e.g. log). **Interpretation:** A coefficient β indicates that a one-unit increase in that predictor multiplies the outcome by β on the original scale (if y is raw), or adds β to log(y) if log-linear model. E.g., if modelling log-default-loss, `exp(β₁)` approximates multiplicative effect. Always contextualize: e.g. if `x` is credit score, β negative means higher score → lower loss on average. **Example:** Suppose modeling log(outstanding balance) = α + β*(age) + γ*(income) + ε. If β=0.01, each additional year of age raises balance by ~1% (on average). This could be plausible if older borrowers tend to have larger mortgages. **Use in scoring:** Linear regression is less common for binary outcomes (default/no default) – that is logistic (QNT-10). However, linear models help in predicting continuous risks (like loss given default or exposure). They are also a building block for scorecards (though credit scorecards often use logistic or point systems). **Validation:** Check R² (fit quality) but more importantly check predictions vs holdout data. For credit risk, regulators expect residual errors to be uncorrelated with key factors (no omitted variables with pattern). ### Permanent rule Always verify regression assumptions. In credit context, it’s common to transform skewed variables (e.g. take log of balances) so that residuals are more normal/homoscedastic. ### Permanent trap Interpreting linear model as implying causality. E.g., saying “higher X causes higher risk” just from regression correlation is incorrect without domain insight (see QNT-06). Also, forgetting to check residuals: a high R² does not guarantee unbiased estimates if assumptions fail. ### Never confuse **Slope coefficient (β)** — change in the response per unit x, ceteris paribus. --- **Correlation coefficient (r)** — measures linear association between two variables, but is not a regression parameter. High `r` does not directly tell you the slope; regression gives β that predicts y from x. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Regression math is universal. However, regulators (like RBI guidelines) may require special considerations (e.g. using macro variables for IFRS9 forecasting models), but that’s about inputs, not the regression method itself.

title: Multicollinearity and VIF
one_screen: *Multicollinearity* occurs when predictors in a regression are highly correlated, inflating coefficient variances and making individual effects hard to separate. The **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)** quantifies multicollinearity: VIF=(1−R²_j)^(-1) for regressing predictor *j* on others. A VIF>5 (or 10) signals problematic collinearity.
bodyText: In credit models, multicollinearity often arises when using overlapping information: e.g. two credit bureau scores, or income and loan amount. Such redundancy doesn’t harm overall prediction accuracy much, but it makes coefficient estimates unstable. For instance, if income and loan size correlate strongly, including both may lead to neither coefficient being precisely estimated (large SE). To calculate VIF for predictor X_j: regress X_j against all other X’s and get R²_j. Then VIF_j = 1/(1−R²_j). Example: if a predictor has R²=0.9 when regressed on others, VIF=10. This indicates its variance estimate is 10 times what it would be if uncorrelated with others. High VIF means small changes in data can flip the sign or magnitude of β_j. This is dangerous when regulators or stakeholders expect stable interpretability. Remedies: drop or combine correlated variables (e.g. use principal components), or regularization (see QNT-12). But dropping variables may lose predictive info, so trade-off is needed. **VIF interpretation:** - VIF≈1: no correlation with other X’s. - VIF>5: moderate collinearity. - VIF>10: serious collinearity. Often one simplifies by ensuring predictors have pairwise correlations <0.8 or VIFs <5. ### Permanent rule Check VIFs during regression. If any predictor’s VIF is high (≥10), address it by removal or transformation. Credit-score industry best practice is to avoid multicollinearity so that variable effects are interpretable and stable. ### Permanent trap Leaving collinear variables in, thinking “it doesn’t matter since model fit is okay.” It *does* matter: if collinearity is ignored, the model can behave erratically on new data or give misleading coefficient signs, which is unacceptable for risk models. ### Never confuse **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)** — measures how much the variance of a coefficient is increased due to collinearity. --- **Standard Error (SE)** — the uncertainty of a coefficient. VIF tells why SE might be high: because variables overlap. VIF is not a direct measure of predictor importance (that’s given by coefficient/SE or other metrics). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Multicollinearity is a numerical issue, not jurisdiction-dependent. However, some IRB model validators may scrutinize models for collinearity to ensure stability.

title: Logistic Regression and Credit Scoring
one_screen: Logistic regression is the workhorse for credit scoring (binary default prediction). It models the log-odds of default as a linear function of predictors. Coefficients translate into *odds ratios*, telling how predictors change the odds of default.
bodyText: For binary outcome *Y* (default=1, non-default=0), logistic regression assumes: Here p = P(default|x). Solving gives p = exp(linear)/(1+exp(linear)). This keeps p between 0 and 1. In credit scoring, predictors x are often applicant attributes (income, delinquencies, etc.). **Interpretation:** β_j is the change in log-odds per unit increase in x_j. Exponentiating gives the *odds ratio* (OR): exp(β_j) is how many times the odds multiply when x_j increases by 1. For example, if β_income = -0.2, then OR=exp(-0.2)=0.82, meaning each extra $10k of income (if x_j scaled per 10k) multiplies odds of default by 0.82 (18% reduction). In scorecards, such coefficients are often translated to points. Logistic regression doesn’t assume normal residuals, but assumes linear logit and independent observations. It handles multicollinearity same as linear (high VIF is a problem). Sample size should be adequate: rule of thumb ~10 events per predictor. **Why it’s workhorse:** Because the output is a probability, intuitively meaningful. Regulators and credit officers can interpret “Probability of Default” directly. Also, logistic outputs are monotonic and unbounded in either direction (unlike linear which could predict <0 or >1). Many scorecards use logistic or simplified versions of it. **Industry bins & WOE:** Often continuous predictors are binned and converted to Weight-of-Evidence (WOE) to ensure monotonic relationships. WOE transforms category’s default rates into log-odds, aligning with logistic assumptions. Then a logistic on WOE-encoded features is linear in log-odds, making the model easier to interpret in PD terms. ### Permanent rule Always express logistic coefficients in odds ratios for interpretation: OR = exp(β). For example, OR<1 means higher x reduces default odds; OR>1 means increases. Double-check that no predicted p<0 or >1 (should never happen in logistic). ### Permanent trap Misreading coefficients: thinking β itself is the percentage point change in probability. It is not. Only the odds (exp(β)) have the multiplicative effect. E.g. β= -0.1 doesn’t mean 10% drop in PD; it means ~10% drop in odds (OR≈0.90). ### Never confuse **Odds** — ratio p/(1-p) of default vs non-default probability. --- **Probability** — p itself (0 to 1). Logistic uses odds in its link. People often mistakenly add β to p directly; the linearity is in log-odds, not in probability. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Logistic regression is standard in all jurisdictions for credit scoring. Some regulators (e.g. RBI) allow logistic scorecards for retail IRB models, given interpretability needs. All use the same math.

title: Weight of Evidence (WOE) and Information Value (IV)
one_screen: **Weight of Evidence (WOE):** A transformation of categorical/binned variables for use in logistic models. For each bin/category, WOE = ln(%goods / %bads). It encodes the risk difference of each bin relative to the overall data. **Information Value (IV):** A summary measure of a variable’s predictive power, computed as Σ(bad rate - good rate) * WOE. Credit scoring often bins continuous features into monotonic risk groups, computes WOE and then fits a logistic on those WOE values.
bodyText: Banks commonly use WOE because it yields linear relationships in log-odds space and deals well with missing values. Example: Suppose credit score binned: - Score 1-300: 10% defaults (bads), 90% good => WOE = ln(0.90/0.10)=2.2. - Score 301-600: 5% defaults, 95% good => WOE = ln(0.95/0.05)=2.94. Higher WOE means a bin has relatively more goods (lower default risk). The logistic regression will use these WOE values to model default odds linearly. **IV** is used to rank variable strength: higher IV implies stronger separation between goods/bads. Rough guide: IV<0.02 not useful; 0.1-0.3 medium; >0.5 extremely predictive. It sums the “divergence” of distribution. It’s not regulatory but common industry practice for feature selection. **Why binning:** Continuous variables may have non-linear PD relationships. Binning (e.g. by quantile) and computing WOE enforces piecewise-constant relationship, simplifying model. It also handles missing by treating missing as a separate bin. A caveat: bins should have enough data to avoid volatility. ### Permanent rule When using WOE, ensure monotonicity: bins should be sorted so that WOE moves consistently (e.g. increasing WOE with score). This avoids non-monotonic risk segments which can cause logistic coefficients to be unstable or non-intuitive. ### Permanent trap Creating too many bins or bins with small counts. This inflates IV artificially and causes overfitting. Also, forgetting to check monotonic trend: if WOE jumps up then down across bins, it suggests your model may overfit bin boundaries rather than true risk. ### Never confuse **WOE** — numeric encoding of bins: ln(%goods/%bads). --- **IV** — aggregate measure of how well a variable’s distribution separates goods/bads. High IV implies big differences in rates across bins. Unlike WOE, IV is a single number per variable. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** WOE and IV are industry conventions, not mandated by regulators. All jurisdictions use similar methods. However, if under IRB, RBI expects documented binning rationale. IFRS 9 does not specify this detail.

title: Regularisation: Ridge and Lasso
one_screen: *Regularisation* adds a penalty to regression coefficients to prevent overfitting, especially when many predictors or multicollinearity exist. **Ridge (L2)** adds sum of squared coefficients to loss, shrinking them towards zero. **Lasso (L1)** adds sum of absolute values, shrinking and possibly zeroing some coefficients. Which to use depends on goals: ridge keeps all features (shrunk), lasso selects a subset (drives some to zero).
bodyText: In credit modeling, regularisation can improve out-of-sample PD predictions. Ridge (L2) is preferred when many correlated predictors exist (it stabilizes coefficients). Lasso (L1) is useful when you suspect only a few variables matter; it effectively does variable selection by zeroing weaker ones. Often, a hybrid Elastic Net (combination of L1+L2) is used if there’s grouping of correlated features. For example, in a model with dozens of socioeconomic variables (many correlated), ridge would shrink all, reducing variance. If you have hundreds of transactional features (most irrelevant), lasso would pick a smaller subset for simplicity. **Interpretation:** With ridge, coefficients are biased smaller but all remain in model. With lasso, coefficients above threshold become zero (variable dropped). In credit, we must be cautious: lasso’s dropping may run into regulatory issues if dropping variables changes model logic. Usually, final modeler inspects which features lasso kept. **Implementation:** Choose λ (penalty weight) by cross-validation. Larger λ = stronger penalty (smaller coefficients). Compare performance on validation: if too high, model underfits. The permanent rule: regularise to combat overfitting, but always re-express final model in original terms. For some models, especially under IRB, explicit variable reduction might require re-approval. ### Permanent rule Ridge (L2) for many small signals or multicollinearity; Lasso (L1) when you want feature selection (fewer predictors). Always cross-validate to pick the penalty strength. ### Permanent trap Blindly using lasso and trusting it removed only noise. It may drop a variable important in reality but slightly less statistically strong. Likewise, too much regularisation (large λ) biases coefficients heavily, harming all predictions. Always check business sense of retained features. ### Never confuse **Ridge (L2)** — penalizes square of coefficients; shrinks but keeps variables. --- **Lasso (L1)** — penalizes absolute values; can set some coefficients to zero (feature selection). Both add a term λ∑β² or λ∑|β| respectively to loss. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Regularisation is a mathematical technique, not regulated differently. However, some regulatory models may ban black-box tech; explicitly mention if lasso removes key explanatory variables, the resulting model still needs justification of omitted factors.

title: Decision Tree
one_screen: A decision tree recursively splits data by feature thresholds to predict an outcome. It is intuitive and easy to visualise, but a single deep tree often overfits the training data, capturing noise rather than true patterns. Pruning, setting a max depth, or limiting leaf size controls complexity and improves generalisation.
bodyText: A decision tree is a flowchart-like predictive model. Internal nodes test feature values (e.g. “income > ₹50,000?”), branches follow outcomes (Yes/No), and leaves give a prediction (class label or regression value). For example, a credit model might first split borrowers by income, then by past defaults, assigning high default risk to those meeting certain conditions. By partitioning the dataset into homogeneous subsets, a tree fits flexible, non-linear relationships without requiring feature scaling or dummy coding. In credit scoring, trees can capture interactions (e.g. low income * poor history). However, if grown unconstrained, a tree can split until each leaf has few samples, fitting noise and idiosyncrasies. A fully grown tree has low bias but very high variance: it may classify every training case correctly but fail on new data. To mitigate over-complex trees, practitioners use **pruning** (removing branches that add little predictive power) or stop splitting when few samples remain. Cross-validation can determine optimal tree size. Trees are inherently “white-box” models: one can trace the path for a given prediction, e.g. “Income was low collateral insufficient decline loan.” This makes them interpretable, a desirable property in credit risk. ### Permanent rule Each split partitions data to increase purity (e.g. reduce variance or Gini impurity). Every split is a simple rule on one feature, building a decision path to a final prediction. ### Permanent trap Assuming a deeper or more complex tree always improves results. In fact, very deep trees usually overfit: training accuracy rises while test accuracy falls. ### Never confuse **Decision tree** — a single model with branches of feature-threshold tests leading to predictions, easy to interpret. --- **Random forest** — an ensemble of many trees (each on a random sample), where the final prediction is an aggregate (majority vote or average). A random forest is not one big tree, but many small trees combined to reduce variance. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The concept of a decision tree is mathematical and independent of regulation.

title: Random Forest
one_screen: A random forest constructs an ensemble of decision trees on bootstrapped samples of the data and averages (or votes on) their predictions. This “bagging” approach greatly reduces a single tree’s variance, making the model more stable and accurate, especially on noisy credit data.
bodyText: Random forests apply the bootstrap-aggregation (bagging) technique to decision trees. We draw \(m\) random samples (with replacement) from the training data, train a separate tree on each sample, then combine the results. In classification (e.g. default/no default) the forest takes a majority vote; in regression (e.g. loss given default) it averages outputs. Additionally, at each split, a random forest only considers a random subset of features (e.g. \(\sqrt{p}\) of \(p\) total) to decide the split. This feature subsampling de-correlates the trees, further reducing variance. The ensemble is thus robust: even if some trees overfit their sample, the majority smooths out idiosyncrasies. The model requires minimal preprocessing: features of different scales or missing values are handled inherently by trees. In a credit scoring example, we might build 100 trees on different bootstrap samples of loan records. Each tree might split on various borrower attributes. The forest’s predicted probability of default is the average of all trees’ PD outputs. This typically outperforms one tree, as shown in practice: adding more trees (up to a point) usually lowers test error. Importantly, random forests can provide a measure of *out-of-bag* error (error on samples not included in each bootstrap), which serves as an internal validation. ### Permanent rule A random forest uses *all* trees at inference, so the final prediction is an average (regression) or majority vote (classification) of many decorrelated trees. This ensemble effect dramatically lowers variance versus one tree. ### Permanent trap Assuming a random forest cannot overfit. In practice, if trees are too deep or features too many, forests can still overfit noise. Also, forests reduce variance but do little to correct bias: if no tree can capture an effect, the ensemble won’t either. ### Never confuse **Random forest** — an ensemble that builds many trees on random samples (bagging) and aggregates their outputs for robustness. --- **Gradient boosting** — an ensemble built sequentially, where each tree is trained to correct the residuals of the prior ensemble. Unlike a random forest’s parallel bagging, boosting trains trees one after another. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Random forests are a universal statistical technique with no jurisdiction-specific differences.

title: Gradient Boosting
one_screen: Gradient boosting builds a strong predictive model by sequentially adding trees that each fit the residual errors of the ensemble so far. The final model is a weighted sum of many simple trees, tuned by a learning rate. This approach often achieves high accuracy on tabular risk data, which explains why it is a dominant method in credit modeling.
bodyText: In gradient boosting, we start with a simple model (often predicting the mean outcome). Then we iteratively train new decision trees on the *residuals* (errors) of the current model. Each tree’s predictions are scaled by a learning rate (shrinkage) and added to the ensemble. Formally, the algorithm minimizes a loss function (e.g. squared error or logistic loss) via gradient descent: each new tree targets the negative gradient of loss with respect to the model’s predictions. Popular implementations like XGBoost or LightGBM use shallow trees (e.g. max depth 3–5) to keep each tree weak and prevent overfitting. For example, to predict loan default probability, we might start with a base prediction of 0.1. The first tree learns where this is underestimating defaults and pushes those cases higher. The next tree then corrects remaining errors, and so on. After 100 trees, the model might be much more accurate than logistic regression, especially capturing non-linear and interaction effects. Gradient boosted trees excel on credit data because they handle mixed variable types and missing values easily, and can learn complex patterns that linear models miss. ### Permanent rule Each new tree in boosting improves the model by focusing on what previous trees missed. The trees are combined additively: final prediction = initial + shrinkage×tree1 + shrinkage×tree2 + … (often in log-odds for classification). ### Permanent trap Ignoring the learning rate or early stopping. A very small learning rate requires many trees (long training), while a large rate or too many trees can easily overfit. Always validate the number of trees and shrinkage on hold-out data. ### Never confuse **Gradient boosting** — an ensemble that fits trees sequentially to residuals, adding them to the model in a stagewise fashion. --- **AdaBoost** — another boosting method that reweights misclassified samples instead of fitting residuals; it focuses on misclassified points and uses weighted voting, rather than explicit gradients. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Gradient boosting’s mathematics is universal; no regulator prescribes or forbids its use.

title: Feature Importance vs Explanation
one_screen: Feature importance scores rank variables by their overall influence on model predictions, but they do not explain individual decisions. In contrast, local explanation methods (like SHAP values) allocate credit to features for a specific prediction. Feature importance is a global summary metric; it does not show how a change in a feature value will move the prediction for a particular loan.
bodyText: Global feature importance (e.g. total gain or split frequency in a tree, or magnitude of coefficients in a linear model) measures each feature’s average effect on model performance. For instance, a credit score might have the highest importance in predicting default rates on average across all borrowers. However, this does not explain why any one borrower was classified as default or not. Importance reflects correlation with the target, not causation or individual impact. Moreover, importance can be misleading if features are correlated: one might appear unimportant simply because another correlated feature “soaked up” its effect. Local explanations, by contrast, break down a single prediction. For example, a SHAP (Shapley) value tells us how much a borrower’s income and history contribute to that borrower’s predicted default probability. Feature importance might list “Income: 0.4, Balance: 0.3, Age: 0.1”, meaning on average income was most influential. But it won’t reveal that in one case a high income actually lowered that borrower’s risk by 5%. Feature importance is useful for feature selection or understanding model trends; explanations are necessary for interpreting individual credit decisions (often a regulatory requirement). ### Permanent rule Feature importance scores are an aggregate, global measure. They tell *which features matter most overall*, but not *how* they influence a given prediction. ### Permanent trap Assuming a high importance feature always increases predictions or that it explains individual cases. For example, “LoanAmount” might be important globally, but the importance metric alone cannot say if a particular high loan amount raises or lowers risk for a specific applicant. ### Never confuse **Feature importance** — global ranking of features by average contribution to the model’s performance. It is an aggregate statistic, not an explanation of any single outcome. --- **SHAP (Shapley) values** — local explanation values that decompose a specific prediction into contributions from each feature. They explain individual decisions, unlike global importance. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The distinction between global importance and local explanation is mathematical and does not vary by jurisdiction. Regulators universally want model explanations for individual decisions, even if different names are used.

title: SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations)
one_screen: SHAP assigns each feature a “contribution” value for a specific prediction, based on cooperative game-theoretic Shapley values. These values guarantee local accuracy (they sum to the model output minus a baseline) and consistency (features that change a prediction more get higher attribution). SHAP provides interpretable, additive explanations for individual credit scores.
bodyText: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) treats each feature as a “player” in a game whose payout is the model’s prediction. The SHAP value of a feature for one observation is the average change in prediction when adding that feature, across all combinations of features. Practically, tree-based models (random forest, boosting) can use TreeExplainer to compute SHAP exactly in polynomial time. The result is that for a given borrower, we get a breakdown: e.g. “+0.05 default probability from low credit score, –0.02 from high income, …, totaling the predicted PD of 0.12.” Plotting SHAP values across many loans gives a global view, while individual SHAP explanations show why each decision was made. Crucially, SHAP values satisfy properties of fairness: efficiency (contributions sum to output), and consistency (if one model increases a feature’s effect, its SHAP value won’t decrease). This makes them theoretically attractive for interpretability. In credit risk, regulators expect that each driver of a decision can be explained. SHAP is one way to meet this interpretability requirement without sacrificing the accuracy of complex ensembles. It allows both global insight (feature importance as average absolute SHAP) and local explanations. ### Permanent rule SHAP values for one prediction sum to the difference between the model’s output and a baseline. This ensures the explanation is exact (local accuracy). Each feature’s SHAP indicates how much it pushed the score up or down. ### Permanent trap Treating SHAP as proving causality. SHAP distributes contributions *given the model*, not necessarily reflecting causal effects. Also, using a too-narrow background dataset can bias SHAP values. ### Never confuse **SHAP value** — a local explanation: the contribution of a feature to one specific prediction. It is computed under the model’s logic. --- **Feature importance** — a global metric summarizing a model. Unlike SHAP, it does not decompose individual predictions and may miss interactions. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** SHAP is a mathematical construct; regulatory emphasis on explainability is common (e.g. Fed SR11-7, PRA SS3/16) but does not alter SHAP’s definition.

title: Stationarity
one_screen: A time series is *stationary* if its statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelations) do not change over time. Stationarity is required for many modeling techniques (e.g. ARIMA), because these assume the series has no trend or changing volatility. If a credit-related series (like default rate) exhibits trends or evolving variance, it must be transformed (differenced, detrended) before such methods apply.
bodyText: In a stationary series, the average and variability remain roughly constant. There is no long-term upward or downward drift (no trend) and no changing seasonality. For example, a stationary default rate might oscillate around 2% with similar magnitude fluctuations each period. If instead default rates are rising in a credit cycle, the series is non-stationary. Non-stationarity can lead to spurious or unreliable forecasts: for instance, ARIMA models assume consistent autocorrelations over time. To test stationarity, analysts use plots (constant mean/variance visually) and tests like Augmented Dickey-Fuller. If non-stationary, one may *difference* the data (subtract each value from its predecessor) or remove a deterministic trend to achieve stationarity. A stationary transformed series is then suitable for ARMA/ARIMA modeling. ### Permanent rule Stationarity means “no trend, constant mean and variance over time.” In practice, if the mean or variance changes (e.g. rising loan volumes or volatility), remove these effects before modeling. ### Permanent trap Treating a visibly trending or seasonal series as stationary. Running ARIMA without differencing when data have trend will yield misleading parameters. Always test a series (plot it and use unit-root tests) before assuming stationarity. ### Never confuse **Stationarity** — a property of a time series (constant statistical properties over time). --- **White noise** — a special stationary series where each value is random with zero autocorrelation. All white noise series are stationary, but not all stationary series are white noise (white noise has no structure to exploit). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Stationarity is a mathematical property. Regulatory models (like CIRB) don’t change this: all quantitative models assume stationarity or explicitly handle non-stationarity.

title: Trend and Seasonality (Decomposition)
one_screen: A time series often contains a *trend* (long-term increase/decrease) and *seasonality* (regular periodic fluctuations). Decomposing the series separates these components plus a residual. For example, credit losses might rise over years (trend) but have higher losses in certain months (seasonal). Identifying and removing trend/seasonality yields a stationary residual suitable for modeling.
bodyText: The **trend** is the smooth, non-random movement over time (upward or downward). Seasonality is a pattern that repeats every fixed period (e.g. every 12 months or every quarter). Decomposition methods (additive or multiplicative) express the series as `Observed = Trend + Seasonality + Residual` (or multiplied if percentage effects). In practice, one might use moving averages or STL (seasonal-trend decomposition) to estimate these. For instance, a bank’s monthly default rate may show a small upward trend due to economic slowdown, plus spikes every year-end (seasonality). By isolating the trend, forecasters can model the remaining (stationary) part more easily. Seasonality can be additive (constant amount) or multiplicative (proportional). When modeling, seasonal series may require seasonal differencing (e.g. subtract value from same month last year) or inclusion of seasonal ARIMA terms. Credit data with seasonal effects (e.g. holiday spending) must handle these patterns explicitly. ### Permanent rule Trend is a long-term direction in the data; seasonality is a repeated cycle of fixed length. Always remove or model these before applying models that assume stationarity. ### Permanent trap Confusing a slowly changing trend for seasonality (or vice versa). For example, attributing a monotonically rising credit loss rate to seasonality can mislead forecasts. Always inspect plots at multiple time scales. ### Never confuse **Trend** — a general upward or downward movement over time. --- **Seasonality** — a periodic pattern repeating at fixed intervals (like higher purchases every Dec). Trend affects the baseline over time, seasonality oscillates around that baseline. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The concepts of trend and seasonality are mathematical. Forecasters in any jurisdiction must address them identically.

title: Autocorrelation and Partial Autocorrelation
one_screen: The autocorrelation function (ACF) measures how correlated a time series is with itself at various lags. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measures correlation at a lag after removing the effects of shorter lags. Analysts use ACF/PACF plots to identify ARIMA model orders: an AR(p) process has a PACF that cuts off after lag p, while an MA(q) process has an ACF that cuts off after lag q.
bodyText: Specifically, the ACF at lag \(k\) is the Pearson correlation between the series and itself shifted \(k\) periods. A slow decay in the ACF suggests strong autocorrelation (often indicating non-stationarity or an AR component). The PACF at lag \(k\) adjusts for all lags 1..\(k-1\), isolating the direct effect of lag \(k\). In practice, one plots ACF and PACF with confidence bands. For example, if credit default counts show correlation at 1 and 2 month lags but drop to near zero at higher lags, the ACF would have spikes at 1 and 2 then fall off. The PACF might spike at lag 1 and cut off, indicating an AR(1). Interpreting these plots guides model choice. A sharp cutoff (near zero correlation beyond lag \(p\)) in PACF suggests an AR(\(p\)); a cutoff in ACF suggests an MA(\(q\)). In seasonal data, repeated ACF spikes can indicate periodicity (e.g. monthly cycle). ### Permanent rule ACF shows how past values influence future values cumulatively, while PACF shows only the direct lagged influence. Use ACF/PACF to help choose ARIMA orders: e.g. AR(p) if PACF cuts off at p. ### Permanent trap Reading random noise or one-off spikes as significant. Autocorrelation estimates can be noisy, especially with small samples or a trend. Always check significance bands and consider transformations if needed. ### Never confuse **Autocorrelation (ACF)** — correlation of the series with itself at lag k, including indirect effects of shorter lags. --- **Partial autocorrelation (PACF)** — the autocorrelation at lag k after removing contributions from all intermediate lags (1 to k-1). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** ACF/PACF are statistical tools independent of regulatory context. Their interpretation in model selection is the same everywhere.

title: ARIMA and SARIMA
one_screen: An ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model combines autoregressive terms (AR), integration (I – differencing), and moving average terms (MA) to model a time series. The series is differenced \(d\) times to remove non-stationarity, then an ARMA(\(p,q\)) model fits the result. SARIMA extends this by adding seasonal AR, I, MA terms with seasonal period \(m\), allowing modeling of both trend and seasonal dependencies.
bodyText: ARIMA stands for AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average. In an ARIMA model, \(p\) is the number of AR terms (lags of the dependent variable), \(d\) is the number of differences to make the series stationary, and \(q\) is the number of MA terms (lags of the forecast error). For example, ARIMA(1,1,1) on default rates means first difference the series (to remove trend), then fit one AR and one MA component on the differenced series. SARIMA (Seasonal ARIMA) adds seasonal orders \((P,D,Q)_m\): \(P\) seasonal AR lags, \(D\) seasonal differences, and \(Q\) seasonal MA lags, with period \(m\) (e.g. 12 for monthly data). For instance, SARIMA(0,1,1)\(\times\)(0,1,1)\(_{12}\) is a common model for monthly data: it differences once to remove trend and once seasonally (lag 12), with one AR and one MA at lag 12. The forecasting equation is linear in the lagged differenced series and lagged errors. If defaults show both a trend and an annual cycle, SARIMA can capture both. Model orders are typically chosen using ACF/PACF plots and information criteria (AIC/BIC). ### Permanent rule ARIMA(p,d,q) = difference \(d\) times to stationarize, then fit ARMA(p,q). Seasonal ARIMA adds seasonal differences and terms for period \(m\). Always difference non-stationary series before modeling. ### Permanent trap Forgetting to difference a non-stationary series (taking \(d=0\) when a trend exists) or neglecting seasonality. This leads to poor model fit and biased forecasts. Always test for unit roots and seasonal cycles. ### Never confuse **ARIMA** — an ARIMA model always includes an integration (I) component; if \(d=0\), it reduces to ARMA. --- **ARMA** — a special case of ARIMA with \(d=0\). ARMA assumes the series is already stationary (no differencing). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The ARIMA framework is a mathematical model. Regulatory constraints (e.g. IRB validation) do not change its formulation, although practitioners may prefer simpler models if interpretability is required.

title: Forecast Backtesting (Rolling-Origin, MAPE/RMSE, Baseline)
one_screen: Forecast backtesting evaluates a model’s predictions on hold-out future data using time-aware cross-validation. Rolling-origin (a.k.a. walk-forward) splits move the training end forward in time and test on the next period. Performance is measured by metrics like Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Results must always be compared against a naive baseline (e.g. last-period carry-forward) to gauge real improvement.
bodyText: In rolling-origin evaluation, we simulate real forecasting: train on an initial window, predict the next \(h\) steps, record the error, then expand (or slide) the window forward and repeat. This avoids peeking into the future (random k-fold cross-validation would leak information). For example, use loans data from 2015–2018 to predict 2019 losses, then re-train on 2015–2019 to predict 2020 losses, etc. Errors from each fold are aggregated to assess model stability. Common metrics include RMSE (root mean square error) and MAPE (mean absolute percentage error). RMSE = \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum (forecast - actual)^2}\) penalises large errors more heavily. MAPE = \(\frac{100\%}{n}\sum |\frac{forecast - actual}{actual}|\) scales error by actual values; it is easy to interpret but blows up when actuals near zero. Always be aware of the failure modes: MAPE is undefined for zero actuals and may be skewed by small denominators. Crucially, compare the model’s scores to a simple benchmark. A typical naive baseline for time series is “no change” (e.g. forecast \(Y_{t+1} = Y_t\)) or “seasonal naive” (forecast equals last year’s value for seasonal data). If a model’s MAPE or RMSE is not substantially better than the baseline, it may not be useful. For instance, if credit volume declines by 1% each month, a model should beat the baseline forecast of “same as last month.” ### Permanent rule Always reserve future time for testing. Use a sequential backtesting (rolling-origin) that mimics real deployment. Compute forecast errors and compare to a naive model’s error. Metrics alone are meaningless without a baseline. ### Permanent trap Performing standard k-fold validation (random splits) on time series. This lets future information leak into training folds, giving overly optimistic error estimates. Always use time-ordered splits instead. ### Never confuse **MAPE** — Mean Absolute Percentage Error: measures relative error (%). Can exaggerate errors when actual values are small. --- **RMSE** — Root Mean Squared Error: measures absolute error magnitude. Penalises large deviations more. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Forecast evaluation is a general statistical procedure. Regulatory guidelines (e.g. IFRS 9 forecast validation) endorse testing forecasts against actuals and baselines, but the methods (rolling backtest, RMSE/MAPE) are the same everywhere.

title: Train / Validation / Test / Out-of-Time Samples
one_screen: Credit models must be evaluated on data that mimic real use. We split data into training (for fitting), validation (for tuning), and test (for performance). Crucially, one should hold out an **out-of-time** (future) sample that the model never sees, to measure true predictive power. In credit, using only random splits risks leakage across economic cycles, so time-based splitting is preferred.
bodyText: A **training** set is used to estimate model parameters. A **validation** set (or multiple cross-validation folds) is used to tune hyperparameters (e.g. depth, regularisation). A final **test** set (or sets) gives unbiased performance on data not used in fitting or tuning. An **out-of-time (OOT)** sample is a test set from a later period (e.g. loans originated in a later year) that simulates the model in production. For example, train on 2015–2017 loans, validate on 2018 loans, and test/OOT on 2019 loans. This ensures the model is evaluated on truly unseen, forward-looking data. Because credit risk often varies over time (economic up/downturns), it is misleading to randomly shuffle all data. Instead, split chronologically: use earlier periods for training/validation and later periods as test. This avoids look-ahead: the model never “knows” future conditions during training. Regulators expect performance on an OOT sample; it reveals if the model generalises across vintage shifts (e.g. a model trained in growth must still score well in recession). ### Permanent rule Reserve the latest data (out-of-time) as the primary test. Use only past data for development and validation to mimic deployment. ### Permanent trap Using future information in training. For example, randomly splitting data across years can mix up season/economy effects. Always ensure that validation and test sets occur later in time than training data. ### Never confuse **Validation set** — used during model development (e.g. hyperparameter tuning). --- **Test (evaluation) set** — held out until final model is chosen, used for final performance. Out-of-time is one type of test set (a test period in the future). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The principle of time-based splitting is universal. Banking regulators in all jurisdictions (e.g. Fed, RBI) emphasize out-of-time testing, as future prediction is the model’s true purpose.

title: Data Leakage
one_screen: Data leakage happens when a model’s training data inadvertently includes information that would not be available in practice at the time of prediction. This gives misleadingly good performance on training and validation, but fails in production. In credit, a common mistake is using future borrower information (like a snapshot of end-of-year balance) to predict a loan’s early default – this leaks the outcome into features.
bodyText: There are two main leakage types: *target leakage*, where predictors include the outcome itself (or its proxies), and *train-test contamination*, where observations in the test period influence training (e.g. shuffling time series). For example, if we include “*ever defaulted*” status (logged after six months) as an input to predict one-year default, the model essentially sees part of the answer. Another example: mixing borrowers from 2019 (test year) into 2018 training can let the model indirectly learn future trends. To avoid leakage, ensure each feature is computable from information available at model decision time. In credit scoring, use only origination attributes or lagged variables. Rigorously align time: treat all data as of a cutoff date. For instance, if predicting default within a year, use only features known at loan issuance. Data pipelines should separate historical features from label construction. Finally, always evaluate on truly unseen data (see QNT-23) – a sharp drop from training to test performance is a red flag for leakage or overfitting. ### Permanent rule Never include any variable that cannot be known at scoring time. Ask, “Would this feature be available in real-time?” If not, omit or shift it. ### Permanent trap Including any proxy of the target. For example, “balance after 1 year” to predict default in that year looks innocent but is label leakage. Also beware of merging data incorrectly (e.g. including post-default loan closure status). ### Never confuse **Data leakage** — model sees future or target-related information in training, giving overly optimistic accuracy. --- **Overfitting** — model is too complex for the signal in training data (but without artificial leaks). Both can cause test drop-offs, but leakage violates causality. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** All jurisdictions expect no data leakage in model development. Regulatory model validation (e.g. AIRB guidance) specifically checks that feature timing is correct.

title: Overfitting vs Underfitting
one_screen: **Overfitting** occurs when a model learns noise or spurious details in the training data, capturing patterns that do not generalise. **Underfitting** is when a model is too simple to capture the underlying signal, leaving systematic errors. The goal is a model of balanced complexity: low bias (good fit) without excessive variance (over-precision).
bodyText: Overfitting often appears with very flexible models on limited data. For instance, a deep decision tree or a high-degree polynomial might perfectly classify every sample by carving the feature space finely, but will perform poorly on new data. Symptoms of overfitting include much higher accuracy (or lower error) on training data than on validation/test. Underfitting happens with overly simple models: e.g. linear regression on a clearly nonlinear relationship yields poor fit both on train and test, with high bias. Bias-variance tradeoff underlies this: simple models have high bias and low variance (stable but inaccurate), complex models have low bias and high variance (accurate on train, erratic on new). In credit modeling, overfit models may pick up on quirks of one portfolio and fail on another vintage. Underfit models (like a too-simple PD formula) might miss obvious risk factors entirely. Cross-validation on time-based splits (QNT-22/QNT-23) helps detect both: if training error is low but test error is high, that’s likely overfitting. Regularisation (limiting complexity, pruning trees, L1/L2 penalties) and sufficient data are key to avoiding overfitting. Underfitting is remedied by adding relevant features or increasing model flexibility. ### Permanent rule Seek the simplest model that achieves acceptable performance. Every model has a bias-variance tradeoff: increasing complexity reduces bias but increases variance, and vice versa. ### Permanent trap Chasing a perfect training score (e.g. 100% accuracy) at the expense of generalization. Removing regularisation or adding unnecessary features in hopes of squeezing out a bit more fit often causes worse real-world performance. ### Never confuse **Overfitting** — model has captured random noise or idiosyncrasies in training data (high variance). --- **Underfitting** — model is too simple, missing important patterns in the data (high bias). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The bias-variance concept is universal. In regulatory terms, an overfit internal model fails validation; an underfit model might under-predict capital needs. All regulators emphasize balance via validation.

title: Documentation Standards for Models
one_screen: Thorough documentation is mandatory: it records the model’s purpose, data sources, methodology, assumptions, performance, and usage. Regulators (Fed, PRA, RBI, EBA) all require clear documentation so that the model can be validated and reproduced. Good documentation ensures continuity, accountability, and transparency in model risk management.
bodyText: Model documentation should include a description of the model’s objective (e.g. “estimate 1-year PD for mortgage portfolio”), data inputs (definition, source, period), transformations, algorithms, and parameter choices. It must detail development decisions (feature engineering, binning, regularisation), performance metrics on development/validation/OOT sets, and limitations. Assumptions (e.g. stability of economic conditions) should be explicit. The documentation also outlines how the model is used (deployment, decision thresholds) and maintenance plan. Regulators expect enough detail to reproduce results: for example, Fed guidance says an effective process “begins with a clear statement of purpose” and that model development involves explicit assumptions. The PRA similarly requires detailed documentation (even from vendors) “sufficient to validate the model’s use”. In practice, documentation may be a written report and annotated code. It should evolve with the model (version control) and be reviewed periodically. Incomplete documentation is a frequent model validation finding. Banks should follow templates (e.g. internal model policy or SS11/13 guidelines) ensuring all sections are covered. Thorough documentation is not just bureaucracy: it captures the business context and justification for each model choice, preventing the “black box” problem. ### Permanent rule Document *everything*: purpose, data, methodology, parameters, results, assumptions, validation, and intended use. This should be in a permanent model report and supported by traceable code. ### Permanent trap Assuming code comments or an informal narrative suffice. Documentation must be formal and comprehensive. A common mistake is to omit rationales (“why this feature?”) or validation results. Regulators will flag missing sections. ### Never confuse **Model documentation** — a detailed report created by developers (data descriptions, logic, results). --- **Validation report** — an independent assessment by a separate party. It is not a substitute for documentation but relies on it. Developers must still document the model fully. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Principles are consistent globally. The Fed’s SR11-7, the PRA’s model guidance, RBI’s risk model norms and IFRS9 guidance all emphasize documentation. For instance, the PRA’s recent policy explicitly aligns IRB documentation requirements with model risk principles.

title: Relational Model & Table Keys
one_screen: The relational model organizes data into structured tables (relations) with rows and columns, using keys to connect data across tables. Each table represents an entity (e.g. **Loan**, **Customer**), rows are records, and columns are fields. A **primary key** is a unique identifier for each row (cannot be NULL). A **foreign key** in one table references a primary key in another to link related data (e.g. an *Account* table has a CustomerID referencing the *Customer* table). This design avoids redundancy (no repeated customer details in every loan row) and enforces data integrity through relationships.
bodyText: The *Loan Book* in banking is not a single table: loans have borrowers, products, schedules, etc. Each aspect lives in its own table with keys linking them. For example, a *Facility* table may link to multiple *Account* rows (one-to-many), and accounts link to *Exposure* or *Transaction* tables. Keys ensure SQL queries join these tables reliably. ### Permanent rule Every table should define a **primary key** column(s) that uniquely identifies each row. ### Permanent trap Putting unrelated data in one wide table (no keys) or not enforcing uniqueness can lead to corruption (e.g. duplicate loan records). ### Never confuse **Primary Key** — uniquely identifies a row in its table (no duplicates, no NULLs). --- **Foreign Key** — references a primary key in another table, establishing a link.

title: SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY Basics
one_screen: In SQL, `SELECT` chooses columns (fields) to return, `WHERE` filters rows based on conditions, and `ORDER BY` sorts the output.
bodyText: For example, on an *Exposure* table, one might retrieve loan amounts and borrower IDs for high-risk loans: Here `SELECT LoanID, Principal, BorrowerID` picks columns, `WHERE RiskRating = 'High'` filters rows to high-risk ones, and `ORDER BY Principal DESC` sorts the resulting loans by size (largest first). The `WHERE` clause applies conditions (e.g. numerical comparisons, string matches) to each row; only rows meeting all conditions appear in the result. After filtering, `ORDER BY` arranges the rows by one or more columns. Without `ORDER BY`, SQL does not guarantee any specific row order. ### Permanent rule If a specific ordering is needed, always include an `ORDER BY` clause. By default, results are unordered. ### Permanent trap Omitting a `WHERE` filter can return huge result sets. Ensure conditions are correct; unintended broad filters (e.g. `WHERE 1=1`) can slow the query and return irrelevant data. ### Never confuse **WHERE** — filters rows before grouping or sorting (applies to individual rows). --- **ORDER BY** — sorts the final result rows (after filtering). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** The semantics of `SELECT`, `WHERE`, and `ORDER BY` are standard SQL across jurisdictions.

title: Aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING
one_screen: The `GROUP BY` clause groups rows by column values for aggregate calculations, and the `HAVING` clause filters those groups.
bodyText: For instance, to summarize a loan portfolio, one might compute total outstanding by product: This splits the data by each `ProductType` (group), then `SUM` is applied per group. Often combined with `COUNT`, `AVG`, etc. To filter on aggregate values (e.g. only products with large totals), use `HAVING`: This returns only products where the summed balance exceeds a threshold. Note `HAVING` comes after grouping, unlike `WHERE` which filters rows before grouping. ### Permanent rule All non-aggregated columns in the `SELECT` list must appear in `GROUP BY`. ### Permanent trap Omitting required `GROUP BY` columns (or aggregating every column) causes SQL errors. Also, forgetting `HAVING` conditions when needed means large groups won’t be filtered. ### Never confuse **WHERE** — filters individual rows before grouping. --- **HAVING** — filters entire groups after aggregation. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Aggregation with `GROUP BY`/`HAVING` is consistent across SQL dialects. [threshold]`." />

title: SQL Joins (inner, left, right, full)
one_screen: SQL `JOIN` combines rows from two tables based on matching column values. An *INNER JOIN* yields only rows with matches in both tables, while *LEFT/RIGHT/OUTER JOIN* include all rows from one side (and NULLs for the other).
bodyText: For example, joining a *Facility* table to its *Account* table: each facility (one side) may link to multiple accounts (many side). An inner join lists only facilities that have accounts, whereas a left join lists all facilities with matching accounts (NULL account fields if none). Beware of **fan-out**: joining a 1:M relationship will duplicate the "one" side row for each "many" side row, potentially inflating counts. Always ensure join keys are correct and understand cardinality. ### Permanent rule Always specify an `ON` condition (join key) to match rows. For example: `ON Facilities.FacID = Accounts.FacID`. ### Permanent trap Forgetting the join condition (or typo) leads to a Cartesian product (every A with every B). Also, joining on the wrong key can cause hidden duplicates (fan-out). ### Never confuse **INNER JOIN** — returns only rows where keys match in both tables. --- **CROSS JOIN** — returns Cartesian product (every row of A with every row of B), no key condition. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** JOIN semantics (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL) are standard SQL.

title: Set Operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
one_screen: SQL set operators combine result sets like mathematical sets. `UNION` stacks rows from two queries (duplicates removed by default). `UNION ALL` includes duplicates. `INTERSECT` returns only rows present in both queries. `EXCEPT` (or `MINUS`) returns rows in the first query that are not in the second.
bodyText: Example: to list all unique borrower IDs from two legacy loan tables: This yields each ID once. To find IDs present in both tables: ### Permanent rule All SELECTs combined by UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT must have the same number of columns and compatible types. ### Permanent trap Forgetting that `UNION` removes duplicates; use `UNION ALL` if you need to preserve them. Also ensure column order and types match. ### Never confuse **UNION** — appends rows from queries into one result (distinct by default). --- **JOIN** — combines columns from tables based on a key. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Set operations behave the same in standard SQL for all jurisdictions.

title: Subqueries vs. CTEs (Common Table Expressions)
one_screen: A *subquery* (nested query) is an inline SELECT within another query, whereas a *CTE* (WITH clause) defines a named temporary result set you can reference in the main query. CTEs improve readability for complex logic and can be referenced multiple times.
bodyText: For example, instead of nesting multiple subqueries, use a CTE: This defines `RecentLoans` once, then queries it. A subquery approach would nest the SELECT inside another SELECT. ### Permanent rule A CTE must be immediately followed by a SELECT (or INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) that references it. ### Permanent trap A CTE’s scope is limited to one statement; it cannot be reused outside. Also, avoid overly deep nesting – break logic into multiple CTEs if needed. ### Never confuse **Subquery** — an unnamed SELECT inside another query (inline, not reusable). --- **CTE (WITH)** — a named temporary table defined for one query (improves clarity and reuse). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** CTEs and subqueries are standard SQL features everywhere.

title: Window Functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, running totals)
one_screen: SQL window functions perform calculations across rows related to the current row without collapsing groups. For example, `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns a sequential number to rows in a partition, while `RANK()` assigns equal numbers to tied values. `LAG(col,1) OVER(...)` gets the previous row’s value, and `LEAD` gets the next row’s. You must include an `OVER(PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)` clause. Window functions are ideal for credit roll-forwards: e.g. computing a loan delinquency at each period and comparing to the prior period using `LAG` or cumulative sums.
bodyText: Example: to assign row numbers within each product line: Here `ROW_NUMBER` restarts count for each `ProductType` group. `RANK()` would give the same sequence number to ties. ### Permanent rule Always specify an `ORDER BY` inside the window if using `LAG`, `LEAD`, or ranking; otherwise the result order is arbitrary. ### Permanent trap Forgetting `PARTITION BY` leads to global ranking instead of per-group. Also, not knowing `RANK()` vs `ROW_NUMBER()` can miscount ties. ### Never confuse **ROW_NUMBER()** — assigns unique sequential numbers (1,2,3...). --- **RANK()** — assigns the same rank to ties (1,2,2,4...). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Window function syntax is SQL-standard (though exact function names may vary slightly by dialect).

title: CASE Statements for Conditional Bucketing
one_screen: The SQL `CASE WHEN` expression assigns values based on conditions. It’s often used to bucket or categorize data. For instance, creating delinquency buckets:
bodyText: Each `WHEN` tests a condition and returns the corresponding label. An `ELSE` provides a default (for any values not matched). The result of `CASE` is a single column value. ### Permanent rule Always include an `ELSE` clause in `CASE` unless you intentionally want NULL for unmatched cases. ### Permanent trap Omitting `ELSE` yields NULL for rows that meet none of the `WHEN` conditions. Also, `CASE` is evaluated in order – once a condition matches, later ones are skipped. ### Never confuse **CASE** — standard SQL conditional expression (multi-branch). --- **DECODE** (Oracle) — an older function only in Oracle SQL, similar to a simple `CASE`. Prefer `CASE` for portability. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** `CASE WHEN` is ANSI SQL standard everywhere. = 90 THEN 'High' WHEN score >= 50 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END`." />

title: NULL Handling and Three-Valued Logic
one_screen: In SQL, `NULL` represents missing or unknown data. Comparisons with `NULL` yield *UNKNOWN*, not true or false. SQL employs three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN). For example, `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN, so a `WHERE` filter excludes those rows. To test for missing data use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.
bodyText: For instance, to find accounts without an open date: Regular operators (`=`, `<`, etc.) cannot be used with NULL. Use `ISNULL()` or `COALESCE()` functions to substitute defaults when needed. ### Permanent rule Always use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL` to check for NULL values. ### Permanent trap Treating NULL as a value in conditions (e.g. `WHERE Balance != 0` won’t catch NULL balances). Also, when using `JOIN`, NULLs can cause unmatched rows. ### Never confuse **NULL** — absence/unknown value (three-valued logic). --- **0** — numeric zero, a definite number (not NULL). ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** SQL’s handling of NULLs is universal.

title: Date Handling and Reporting Periods
one_screen: SQL provides date/time functions to manipulate and extract parts of dates. Common functions include `YEAR(date)`, `MONTH(date)`, or `DATEPART` to group or filter by time units. For example, to group loan originations by year: ```sql SELECT YEAR(OriginationDate) AS Year, COUNT(*) FROM Loans GROUP BY YEAR(OriginationDate); ``` This uses `YEAR()` to extract the year component. One can similarly use `MONTH()`, or perform arithmetic (e.g. adding intervals). Reporting often requires custom periods (e.g. fiscal year or quarters) — these can be calculated with date functions or by joining a calendar table.
bodyText: Dates can also be compared or ranged: e.g. `WHERE SaleDate BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'` for a calendar year. ### Permanent rule Convert strings to actual `DATE` or `DATETIME` types (using `STR_TO_DATE` or client-side parsing) to leverage date functions. Do not treat dates as plain text. ### Permanent trap Ignoring the time component can yield unexpected results (e.g. missing same-day records). Always truncate times or use date boundaries. ### Never confuse **DATE** — stores year-month-day (no time). --- **DATETIME/TIMESTAMP** — includes time (hours-min-sec). Make sure to use the correct type for dates versus full timestamps. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.** Date arithmetic and functions follow SQL standards universally.

title: Query Performance Basics (Indexes, Table Scans, Execution Plans)
one_screen: Indexes speed up queries by allowing the database to quickly locate rows on indexed columns. A full table scan reads every row and is efficient only if a large fraction of rows qualify. For example, if querying a small subset (e.g. 1% of rows) on an indexed column, the database will use the index; if ~10% or more of rows match, a sequential scan may be faster.
bodyText: Use `EXPLAIN` (or equivalent) to view the execution plan of a query. This shows which indexes (if any) are used and the estimated cost. The plan also shows join methods (nested loop, hash join, etc.) and whether tables are scanned.
