bodyText: ### Core mechanism Positions + assumptions → integrated measures → limits/appetite → ALCO decision → execution → remeasurement → escalation. ### Ownership | Function | Produces | Approves / decides | Consumes | Challenges | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Treasury / ALM | NII/EVE, funding, liquidity, FTP analysis | delegated execution | ALCO decisions | — | | ALCO | integrated balance-sheet view | funding/hedging/pricing actions within mandate | risk and finance analysis | assumptions through committee debate | | Business lines | forecasts and product behaviour | customer decisions within limits | FTP and limits | economics/feasibility | | Finance | earnings/accounting/capital effects | finance policies | treasury forecasts | reconciliation | | Independent risk | risk measures/limit monitoring as designed | risk limits within delegation | ALM data | models, assumptions, breaches | | Board / board risk committee | appetite-level reporting | risk appetite and key policies | escalation | senior-management effectiveness | ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule No material ALM action should be approved on one favourable metric when it worsens another material constraint on the same balance sheet. ### Never confuse [First-line treasury control] and [Independent risk challenge] **First-line treasury control** — manages the bank’s structural positions within authority. --- **Independent risk challenge** — sets/challenges risk standards and assesses whether first-line measurement and actions remain within appetite; it does not become the dealing owner. ### Permanent trap Running ALCO as a dashboard meeting. A committee that reviews ratios without making or escalating balance-sheet decisions is observing risk, not governing it. ### Jurisdiction variants No delta in core governance logic. Legal committee mandates, board responsibilities and supervisory documentation differ.

title: One balance sheet, four regulatory implementations
one_screen: Mechanics stay common across borders; deltas sit in scope, calibration, reporting, supervisory process and dates. **As at August 2026, RBI’s 2025 IRRBB framework is issued but not yet effective.**
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | IN — RBI | UK — PRA | EU — CRR/EBA | US — agencies | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Liquidity | local LCR + SLR/MSF/FALLCR; NSFR | PRA LCR/NSFR + ILAAP | CRR LCR/NSFR + ILAAP/SREP | tailored LCR/NSFR + Regulation YY | | IRRBB | forthcoming; **not effective Aug 2026** | Pillar 2 | EBA GL + 2024 RTS + CSRBB | interagency guidance | ### Where it sits ### Permanent rule Never import another jurisdiction’s acronym, threshold or effective date merely because the mechanism is common. ### Permanent trap Relabelling a foreign policy with the local regulator. Scope, calibration, terminology and transition status can differ. ### Jurisdiction variants #### IN (RBI) LCR changes are in force from **1 April 2026**; the SLR HQLA carve-out remains **2% MSF + 16% FALLCR** as at August 2026. NSFR applies since **1 October 2021**. RBI’s 28 November 2025 Forthcoming Instructions say IRRBB’s effective date will be communicated separately: **not implemented as at August 2026**. #### UK (PRA) SS24/15 has applied since **20 January 2026**. July 2026 liquidity amendments are **proposals**, with consultation closing **11 September 2026** and proposed implementation **1 January 2027**. #### EU EBA/GL/2022/14 applies from **31 December 2023**. Delegated Regulations (EU) 2024/856 and 2024/857 apply from **14 May 2024**. LCR/NSFR remain within the CRR framework. #### US The 2019 category-tailoring framework remains the LCR scope architecture as at August 2026; NSFR applies since **1 July 2021**. Regulation YY supplies liquidity governance for covered firms.

title: Equities
one_screen: An equity is a residual claim on a company: debt and other senior claims are paid first, and shareholders own what remains. Its price therefore reflects both expected future cash generation and the uncertainty around that residual.
bodyText: Equity represents ownership rather than a contractual promise to repay principal. A common shareholder usually has voting rights, a residual claim on assets after creditors, and potential participation in dividends and capital appreciation. Unlike a bond coupon, a dividend is generally discretionary: the board may reduce or omit it, subject to applicable law and the company’s circumstances. The economic value of an equity can be viewed as the present value of cash flows ultimately available to shareholders. In practice, market prices move because expectations change about revenue, margins, investment, financing, competitive position, interest rates and risk. A company can report rising profits while its share price falls if the market had expected even stronger results or if the discount rate applied to future cash flows rises. Primary and secondary markets serve different functions. In a primary issuance, the company raises capital by selling newly issued shares. In the secondary market, investors trade existing shares with one another; the company normally does not receive the trade proceeds. Market capitalisation equals share price multiplied by shares outstanding, but it is not the same as enterprise value, which also reflects net debt and other claims. Equity risk is multi-dimensional. Market risk moves the whole price; idiosyncratic risk comes from the issuer; liquidity risk affects the ability to transact near observed prices; corporate actions such as dividends, splits, rights issues and buybacks change positions or economics. For a banking professional, the important operational point is that the security identifier, listing venue, currency, settlement cycle, corporate-action treatment and legal owner can all matter independently of the headline share price. ### Permanent rule Equity is a residual claim: higher upside comes with lower contractual seniority than debt. ### Permanent trap Treating a listed share as if it promises repayment at a fixed date. It does not have a contractual maturity like a plain bond. ### Never confuse **Market capitalisation** — share price multiplied by shares outstanding; an equity-value measure. --- **Enterprise value** — a broader value of the operating business that adjusts equity value for debt, cash and other claims. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Fixed Income
one_screen: A fixed-income instrument converts financing into contractual cash flows: interest, principal and sometimes embedded options. Its value is driven by the timing and certainty of those cash flows and the discount rates used to value them.
bodyText: A bond is a debt instrument. The issuer receives funding and promises specified payments to investors. A plain fixed-rate bond has a face value or principal, a coupon rate, payment dates and a maturity date when principal is due. Other debt instruments may pay floating rates, no interim coupon, amortising principal or cash flows linked to inflation, credit events or options. The basic valuation rule is simple: a bond’s price is the present value of its future contractual cash flows, discounted at rates appropriate to their timing and risk. Two bonds with identical cash flows can still trade at different yields if they differ in liquidity, tax treatment, collateral, legal ranking or market convention. Credit quality matters because promised cash flows are not guaranteed merely because they are contractual. Seniority determines where an instrument sits in the capital structure. Secured debt has claims over specified collateral; senior unsecured debt ranks ahead of subordinated debt; equity is residual. Maturity describes when principal is contractually due, while duration describes price sensitivity to interest-rate movements. These are related but not interchangeable. Fixed-income analysis separates several risks. Interest-rate risk changes the value of otherwise unchanged cash flows. Credit risk concerns whether the issuer pays in full and on time. Spread risk changes the market compensation demanded for credit and liquidity. Optionality changes the cash-flow pattern itself: a callable bond may be redeemed when refinancing is favourable to the issuer, limiting investor upside. For operations and risk, the instrument definition must include coupon convention, day-count basis, business-day rule, payment calendar, redemption terms, seniority, currency and settlement convention. A one-line label such as “5-year bond” is insufficient to reproduce its economics. ### Permanent rule Value the cash-flow contract, not the product label. ### Permanent trap Using maturity as a synonym for interest-rate risk. A long maturity can have low or high duration depending on coupons and optionality. ### Never confuse **Maturity** — the contractual date by which principal is due. --- **Duration** — a measure of a bond price’s sensitivity to changes in yield or interest rates. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Clean Price and Dirty Price
one_screen: A bond quote may exclude accrued interest even though settlement does not. Clean price is the quoted price without accrued interest; dirty price is the amount economically paid for the bond before fees: clean price plus accrued interest.
bodyText: Coupon interest accrues economically between payment dates. Suppose a bond pays a coupon every six months. The seller who has held the bond for part of the coupon period has earned part of the next coupon even though the issuer will pay the full coupon to whoever owns the bond on the payment date. Settlement therefore compensates the seller for accrued interest. The standard relationship is: Dirty price = Clean price + Accrued interest The clean price is useful for price comparison because it removes the predictable saw-tooth movement caused purely by coupon accrual. The dirty price, sometimes called the full price, is the value used to determine the cash consideration for settlement, subject to market-specific conventions and transaction charges. Accrued interest depends on the coupon amount and the fraction of the coupon period that has elapsed. That fraction is determined by a day-count convention such as Actual/Actual, 30/360 or Actual/365. Two instruments can therefore accrue differently even when they have the same coupon rate and calendar dates. Around a coupon payment date, the mechanics can look counter-intuitive. Immediately before coupon payment, accrued interest is high. After the coupon is detached and paid, accrued interest resets, while the clean price should not mechanically jump by the same amount merely because time passed. This is why analysts distinguish clean and dirty measures. The distinction also matters in reconciliations. A trader may discuss a clean-price move, the risk system may mark a full price, and the settlement instruction may reflect principal amount plus accrued interest. If systems disagree on the field definition, a correct trade can appear to have a valuation or cash break. ### Permanent rule Always identify whether a bond price field is clean or dirty before comparing valuations or settlement amounts. ### Permanent trap Explaining a dirty-price increase caused by one day of accrual as market P&L. ### Never confuse **Clean price** — bond price excluding accrued coupon interest. --- **Dirty price** — clean price plus accrued interest; also called full price. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Yield to Maturity and the Price–Yield Relationship
one_screen: Yield to maturity is the single discount rate that equates a bond’s market price with the present value of its promised remaining cash flows. For a plain fixed-rate bond, price and yield move in opposite directions because a higher discount rate lowers present value.
bodyText: Yield to maturity, or YTM, compresses a bond’s price and scheduled cash flows into one annualised rate. It is the discount rate that makes the present value of remaining coupons and principal equal to the observed full economic price under the relevant market convention. It is therefore an internal rate of return on promised cash flows, not a guarantee of realised return. The inverse price–yield relationship follows directly from present-value mathematics. If all promised cash flows are unchanged and the discount rate rises, each future payment is worth less today, so the bond price falls. If the discount rate falls, present values rise and the price increases. A bond trading below par usually has a YTM above its coupon rate; one trading above par usually has a YTM below its coupon rate, assuming a plain fixed-rate bullet bond. YTM has assumptions and limitations. It treats the promised cash-flow schedule as if it occurs, so defaultable bonds can have a quoted YTM that overstates economically expected return. It also embeds a reinvestment assumption for interim coupons if interpreted as a realised compound return. Callable, puttable and otherwise optional bonds may need yield-to-call, yield-to-worst or option-adjusted measures because the maturity cash-flow path is not fixed. A small yield movement does not cause the same percentage price change for every bond. Sensitivity depends mainly on duration and convexity, which are separate concepts. YTM tells where the bond sits on a price–yield curve; duration and convexity describe the local shape of that curve. Operationally, YTM calculations depend on clean/full-price handling, settlement date, coupon schedule, day count, compounding frequency and redemption value. Two systems can produce different yields from the same headline price if conventions differ. ### Permanent rule For a plain fixed-cash-flow bond, hold cash flows constant: yield up means price down, and yield down means price up. ### Permanent trap Calling YTM the investor’s guaranteed return. Default, reinvestment, sale before maturity and optionality can all change realised return. ### Never confuse **Coupon rate** — contractual interest rate applied to face value. --- **Yield to maturity** — discount rate implied by current price and promised remaining cash flows. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Duration and Convexity
one_screen: Duration is the first-order estimate of how a bond price changes when yield changes; convexity is the second-order correction for the curve in the price–yield relationship. Duration gives the slope, convexity improves the estimate when moves are larger.
bodyText: Duration is both a cash-flow timing concept and a practical risk measure. Macaulay duration is a present-value-weighted average time to receive cash flows. Modified duration converts that concept into approximate percentage price sensitivity to a small parallel change in yield. If modified duration is 5, a 1 percentage-point rise in yield implies roughly a 5% price fall before allowing for convexity. The approximation is: Percentage price change ≈ − Modified duration × yield change The minus sign reflects the inverse price–yield relationship. Duration is local: it is most accurate for small changes and for instruments whose cash flows do not change when rates move. Convexity captures curvature. A plain option-free bond normally has positive convexity, meaning the price gain from a given fall in yield is larger than the price loss from an equal rise in yield. Adding a convexity term improves the approximation: Percentage price change ≈ −D × Δy + ½ × Convexity × (Δy)^2 Embedded options can change the shape materially. A callable bond may exhibit reduced or negative effective convexity when rates fall because the issuer becomes more likely to call it, capping price appreciation. For instruments whose expected cash flows change with rates, effective duration and effective convexity are more useful than measures assuming fixed cash flows. Duration is not maturity. A 10-year high-coupon bond generally has lower duration than a 10-year zero-coupon bond because more value is received earlier. Duration is also not credit spread duration unless the shock being measured is explicitly a spread change. At portfolio level, duration supports hedging and risk aggregation, but parallel-shift duration misses changes in curve shape. Key-rate durations or bucketed sensitivities are needed when different maturities move by different amounts. ### Permanent rule Use duration for local slope and convexity for curvature; neither is a substitute for understanding the cash flows and options. ### Permanent trap Quoting a single duration number as if it captures every possible yield-curve movement. ### Never confuse **Maturity** — time until contractual principal repayment. --- **Duration** — price sensitivity to yield changes, derived from the timing and present value of cash flows. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Credit Spreads
one_screen: A credit spread is the extra yield demanded over a reference curve for bearing risks not present in the reference instrument. It is compensation for expected credit loss plus risk, liquidity and technical premia—not a direct default-probability reading.
bodyText: Credit instruments are often analysed relative to a lower-risk benchmark rather than by absolute yield alone. A simple spread may be the yield on a corporate bond minus the yield on a government bond of similar maturity. More sophisticated measures include interpolated spreads, asset-swap spreads and option-adjusted spreads. Each answers a slightly different question. A wider spread means the market demands more compensation relative to the reference. Spreads may widen because the issuer’s perceived default risk rises, recovery expectations fall, market liquidity deteriorates, investors reduce risk appetite, supply increases or the benchmark itself moves differently. Conversely, improving credit quality or strong demand may tighten spreads. Spread is not expected loss. In a stylised credit model, expected loss depends on probability of default, loss given default and exposure. A market credit spread includes more than that expected loss: investors may require compensation for uncertainty, downgrade risk, liquidity, capital usage and market imbalances. This is why reverse-engineering a probability of default from a raw spread without a model can be misleading. Spread risk also matters before any default occurs. If a bond’s spread widens, its market value usually falls even if the issuer continues paying. The price sensitivity to spread moves is often measured with spread duration or credit spread DV01 rather than pure interest-rate duration. Reference choice matters. A spread to a sovereign curve, swap curve or matched government security can differ. Comparing two spread series without checking the benchmark, maturity mapping, option treatment and price source can create false conclusions. For bank trading and risk data, spread fields should therefore be treated as calculated measures with lineage: underlying price, reference curve, interpolation rule, optionality treatment and timestamp all matter. ### Permanent rule A credit spread is a relative market price of risk, not a pure measure of default probability. ### Permanent trap Reading a 300 bp spread as a 3% annual probability of default without specifying recovery, horizon and pricing model. ### Never confuse **Credit spread** — yield or pricing difference relative to a chosen reference. --- **Expected credit loss** — modelled loss from default risk, commonly driven by PD, LGD and exposure. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: The Yield Curve
one_screen: A yield curve maps interest rates or yields across maturities for instruments sharing a defined credit and market basis. Level, slope and curvature are separate sources of risk: the curve can move without shifting in parallel.
bodyText: A yield curve is not one universal object. It is a term structure built from a defined set of instruments or market quotes: government securities, overnight-index swaps, interbank instruments or another consistent basis. The horizontal axis is maturity or tenor; the vertical axis is a yield, zero rate, forward rate or related measure depending on the curve. An upward-sloping curve has longer rates above shorter rates; an inverted curve has some longer rates below shorter rates; a flat curve has little difference. The shape reflects many forces: expected future short rates, inflation expectations, term premia, supply and demand, liquidity and policy expectations. The curve should therefore be treated as a market pricing object, not a deterministic forecast. Three broad movements are useful mental models. A level move shifts rates broadly together. A slope move changes the difference between short and long rates. A curvature move changes the middle relative to the ends. Real curves can exhibit combinations of all three. Pricing requires more than reading a par-yield chart. Many derivatives and bonds are valued using zero-coupon discount factors derived by bootstrapping liquid market instruments. Forward rates can then be implied between future dates. A par rate, zero rate and forward rate at the same headline maturity are not interchangeable. Risk measures must match this structure. A single duration assumes a parallel move and can hide offsetting exposures. Key-rate DV01 or bucketed sensitivities show how value responds to specific sections of the curve. Curve construction also has operational dependencies: instrument set, day counts, calendars, interpolation, compounding and extrapolation. The practical test is always: which curve, built from which instruments, for which purpose? “The five-year rate” is incomplete unless the rate family and convention are known. ### Permanent rule Always name the curve and the rate type before interpreting a point on it. ### Permanent trap Assuming every yield-curve shock is parallel and therefore fully captured by one duration number. ### Never confuse **Par yield** — coupon rate that makes a bond price at par for a given maturity under the curve. --- **Zero rate** — discount rate for a single cash flow at a specific maturity. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Repo and Reverse Repo
one_screen: A repo is economically secured borrowing: one party sells securities now and agrees to repurchase equivalent securities later at a higher price. The same transaction is a reverse repo from the cash lender’s perspective.
bodyText: A repurchase transaction combines a spot sale of securities with a forward repurchase. The party needing cash delivers securities and receives cash; at maturity it pays the repurchase price and receives equivalent securities back. The difference between sale and repurchase price expresses the repo interest. From the cash provider’s perspective, the transaction is a reverse repo. Collateral reduces but does not eliminate counterparty exposure. If the borrower defaults, the cash lender can rely on the collateral subject to legal enforceability and market value. A haircut creates a buffer: cash advanced is less than the market value of collateral. Margining can restore the agreed collateralisation when prices move. Haircuts, eligible collateral, valuation frequency and substitution rights therefore matter as much as the headline repo rate. Repo is also central to market liquidity. Dealers finance securities inventories, investors obtain leverage, and market participants borrow cash against high-quality assets. “Special” repo can arise when a particular security is in strong demand; the economic value of obtaining that security can push its repo rate below general collateral rates. Legal form matters. Market-standard cross-border repo is commonly documented under the Global Master Repurchase Agreement, or GMRA, developed by ICMA. A master agreement supports consistent transaction terms and close-out/netting mechanics across a relationship, but legal enforceability depends on the governing law, counterparty and jurisdiction. Repo must not be confused with an unsecured loan merely because the economic purpose is funding. Securities are transferred under the agreed legal structure. Operationally, both cash and securities legs must settle, collateral must be valued and lifecycle events such as coupons, substitutions and margin calls must be handled. ### Permanent rule Repo and reverse repo are two perspectives on the same secured financing transaction. ### Permanent trap Treating collateral as eliminating credit risk. Wrong-way risk, gap risk, liquidity and legal enforceability remain. ### Never confuse **Repo** — transaction viewed from the party selling securities and receiving cash initially. --- **Reverse repo** — the same transaction viewed from the party providing cash and receiving securities initially. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Securities Lending
one_screen: Securities lending temporarily transfers securities to a borrower against collateral, with an obligation to return equivalent securities. The lender earns a fee or investment spread; the borrower obtains the securities, often to support short selling, settlement or market making.
bodyText: In a securities-lending transaction, the lender transfers securities and the borrower undertakes to return equivalent securities later. The borrower provides collateral, commonly cash or other securities, and pays an economic fee. If cash collateral is used, the lender may invest it and rebate part of the return; if non-cash collateral is used, the fee is usually stated more directly. The borrower needs the security itself rather than simply cash. Common motives include covering a short sale, avoiding a settlement failure, supporting market-making inventory or facilitating arbitrage. A security that is difficult to borrow can command a high fee because its scarcity has economic value. Legal title and economic exposure must be separated. Under title-transfer forms, the borrower becomes legal owner of the delivered securities and can use them, but owes equivalent securities back. The lender generally retains the economic benefit of distributions through manufactured payments or contractual adjustments. Corporate actions therefore require careful processing: dividend, voting, rights and recall mechanics can affect the lender differently from outright ownership. Collateralisation reduces counterparty exposure but creates operational and market risks. Collateral must be valued, haircuts applied, margin calls processed and concentration limits monitored. If collateral is reinvested, the lender also takes investment and liquidity risk in the reinvestment portfolio. The Global Master Securities Lending Agreement, or GMSLA, published by ISLA, is a major market-standard agreement for securities lending. Different versions use different collateral structures, including title-transfer and security-interest approaches. Documentation determines default, close-out and collateral rights; the product label alone does not. The closest economic cousin is repo, but the transaction driver differs: repo usually starts with a need for cash financing; securities lending usually starts with a need for a specific security. ### Permanent rule Ask what the scarce asset is: in securities lending it is usually the security; in repo it is usually funding, unless the repo is special. ### Permanent trap Calling a securities loan an unsecured loan because the borrower can use the security. Collateral and master-agreement mechanics are central. ### Never confuse **Securities lending** — temporary transfer of securities against collateral with an obligation to return equivalent securities. --- **Repo** — sale and agreed repurchase of securities, commonly used for secured cash financing. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: FX Spot, Forward and Swap
one_screen: FX spot exchanges two currencies near the trade date; an FX forward locks an exchange for a future date; an FX swap combines a spot leg and an offsetting forward leg. The key is to track both currencies, both directions and every value date.
bodyText: Foreign exchange is quoted as one currency in terms of another. In a pair such as EUR/USD, the first currency is the base and the second the quote currency under the stated market convention. Buying one currency necessarily means selling the other. A spot transaction exchanges agreed amounts on the spot value date for the market spot rate. “Spot” does not always mean same-day settlement; the standard value date depends on the currency pair and market convention. A forward fixes today the exchange rate for a future value date. No principal necessarily changes hands at trade date; at maturity the parties deliver the two currencies unless the contract is non-deliverable. An FX swap is two linked exchanges in opposite directions on different dates. A typical transaction exchanges currencies on the near leg and reverses the exchange on the far leg at a pre-agreed forward rate. Economically, this creates secured-like funding in one currency against another without leaving a net open FX position if the amounts and dates are matched. The spot rate and forward rate should not be interpreted as a simple market forecast. Forward points mainly reflect relative interest-rate conditions, while balance-sheet costs, hedging demand and cross-currency basis can also matter. Operational errors often arise from direction. “Buy USD/INR” may be interpreted differently if a system stores the base currency, pay currency or dealer perspective. Every trade record should therefore identify bought amount, sold amount, currencies, exchange rate, near/far value dates and settlement instructions explicitly. Settlement itself can create principal risk when one currency is paid before the other is received. Payment-versus-payment arrangements are designed to reduce this risk. ### Permanent rule Never infer trade direction from a rate field alone; record which currency is bought, which is sold and on which date. ### Permanent trap Treating the forward rate as the market’s pure forecast of the future spot rate. ### Never confuse **FX forward** — single future exchange of two currencies at a rate fixed today. --- **FX swap** — near exchange plus an offsetting far exchange of the same two currencies. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN — Perishable, checked 28 August 2026.** RBI permits forex transactions only through authorised persons and for permitted purposes under FEMA. For FCY-INR derivatives, permitted purpose depends on user/product rules; RBI’s public FAQ states hedging exchange-rate risk as the permitted purpose for FCY-INR forex derivatives, while FCY-FCY derivatives are not similarly purpose-restricted. **UK — No product-mechanics delta.**EU — No product-mechanics delta.**US — No product-mechanics delta.**

title: Covered Interest Parity and Forward Points
one_screen: Covered interest parity links spot FX, forward FX and interest rates in two currencies under no-arbitrage. Forward points are therefore primarily a funding relationship, not a directional prediction—and persistent basis can appear when balance sheet and hedging constraints make arbitrage costly.
bodyText: Covered interest parity, or CIP, compares two ways to obtain a hedged return across currencies. An investor can invest domestically, or convert into a foreign currency, invest there and lock the future reconversion with an FX forward. In an ideal frictionless market, the hedged returns should match; otherwise an arbitrage would exist. Using S as spot and F as forward under a consistent quote convention, the simplified one-period relation can be expressed as: F / S ≈ (1 + domestic rate × time) / (1 + foreign rate × time) The exact formula depends on quotation and compounding conventions. Forward points are commonly F − S, often scaled into market “points”. If domestic and foreign rates differ, the forward generally departs from spot even when nobody has a directional view on the future currency level. This is why “currency at a forward premium” must be handled carefully. Premium and discount depend on which currency is the base and which is the quote. A sign that looks intuitive under one quotation reverses under the reciprocal quote. In real markets, CIP can deviate. Since the global financial crisis, cross-currency basis has persisted because dealer balance sheets, capital, liquidity, credit and hedging demand make the textbook arbitrage costly. The basis is economically the extra adjustment required to reconcile FX-swap-implied funding with direct cash-market funding. For risk and valuation, forward points need the correct spot date, forward date, two discount curves and quotation convention. A one-day date error around holidays can change the interest accrual and therefore the expected points. The core test is not “where will spot go?” but “what relative funding conditions and basis are embedded between these two dates?” ### Permanent rule Forward points are first a relative funding price; do not read them as a standalone currency forecast. ### Permanent trap Using CIP as if it must hold exactly after transaction costs, credit, capital and balance-sheet constraints. ### Never confuse **Forward points** — difference between forward and spot FX rates under the market quote convention. --- **Cross-currency basis** — deviation indicating that FX-implied funding differs from direct cash-market funding after the standard parity relationship. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Non-Deliverable Forwards
one_screen: An NDF locks an exchange-rate outcome without exchanging the restricted underlying currency at maturity. The parties cash-settle the difference between the contracted forward rate and an agreed fixing, usually in a freely deliverable settlement currency.
bodyText: A non-deliverable forward, or NDF, is economically similar to an FX forward but differs in settlement. The notional amount of the restricted or non-deliverable currency is used to calculate the payoff; it is not delivered. On the fixing date, an agreed reference rate is observed. The contract then settles a net cash amount, commonly in US dollars, on the settlement date. A simplified payoff depends on the difference between the contracted NDF rate and the fixing rate, adjusted for the quotation convention and notional. Because quote direction changes the formula, the safe operational method is to define the two currencies, settlement currency, notional currency, forward rate, fixing source, fixing date and payment date explicitly. NDFs developed particularly where capital controls, convertibility restrictions or market access constraints made offshore deliverable forwards difficult. They allow hedging and price discovery without requiring offshore delivery of the underlying currency. As currencies liberalise, deliverable and NDF markets can coexist, converge or shift in relative importance. The NDF rate is not simply the expected fixing. It reflects interest-rate differentials, market positioning, liquidity, credit and regulatory segmentation. The offshore NDF market and onshore deliverable market can therefore price the same currency differently, especially under stress. NDF lifecycle risk is concentrated around fixing and settlement. A wrong fixing source, observation time, holiday calendar or disrupted-rate fallback can cause a material cash difference. Confirmation terms are therefore essential. The Indian rupee is a major NDF currency in offshore markets, but access to INR non-deliverable derivative contracts is governed by RBI rules for authorised dealers and user categories. The universal product mechanic remains cash settlement against a fixing. ### Permanent rule An NDF uses the underlying currency to calculate value but does not require its principal delivery at maturity. ### Permanent trap Building an NDF payoff without locking down quote direction and fixing source. ### Never confuse **Deliverable forward** — both currency principals are exchanged at maturity. --- **NDF** — a net cash difference is settled using an agreed reference fixing. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN — Perishable, checked 28 August 2026.** RBI’s master directions govern when authorised dealers may offer non-deliverable derivative contracts involving INR. The permitted user, purpose and location of the authorised dealer matter; do not infer permission from the existence of an offshore INR NDF market. **UK — No product-mechanics delta.**EU — No product-mechanics delta.**US — No product-mechanics delta.**

title: Derivatives: Linear and Non-Linear Payoffs
one_screen: A derivative takes its value from an underlying market variable. Linear derivatives change value roughly one-for-one with that variable; non-linear derivatives change sensitivity as the underlying moves, which is why options require more than a single directional risk measure.
bodyText: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on another price, rate, index, credit event or market variable. Derivatives can transfer risk without requiring the full underlying asset to change hands at trade date. Common families include forwards, futures, swaps and options. The first useful classification is payoff shape. A linear derivative has a payoff that is approximately a straight-line function of the underlying variable over the relevant range. A long forward on an asset gains when the underlying rises above the contracted forward price and loses when it falls below it. An interest-rate swap is more complex in cash-flow construction, but its value is still driven largely by linear rate sensitivities around current market conditions. Options are non-linear. A purchased call has limited downside to the premium but increasing upside above the strike. Its sensitivity to the underlying, delta, changes as the underlying price moves; gamma measures that change. Non-linearity means a hedge that is correct now may not remain correct after a market move. Derivative notional is not the same as market value or maximum loss. Notional is a reference amount used to calculate payments. A swap with a very large notional can have a small current market value, while future exposure can still be material. For options, the premium, strike, notional, expiry and volatility jointly shape risk. Derivatives also introduce counterparty, collateral, liquidity, legal and operational risks. Exchange trading or central clearing can change those risks without changing the basic economic payoff. The practical starting point for any unfamiliar derivative is therefore to draw its contractual cash flows and payoff. Product names are less reliable than answering: what is referenced, what is exchanged, when, under what condition, and how does the payoff change when the market variable moves? ### Permanent rule Draw the payoff before naming the risk. ### Permanent trap Using notional as if it were current fair value or a direct measure of maximum loss. ### Never confuse **Linear derivative** — sensitivity is approximately constant with respect to the underlying over small moves. --- **Non-linear derivative** — sensitivity itself changes as the underlying or other inputs move. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Forwards and Futures
one_screen: Forwards and futures both lock future economic exposure, but the market infrastructure differs. A forward is typically bilateral and customisable; a future is standardised, exchange-traded and margined through a clearing framework.
bodyText: A forward obliges two parties to transact an underlying asset or cash equivalent at a future date for a price agreed today. The contract can be tailored for notional, date, underlying and settlement terms. Because it is bilateral, the parties face each other subject to their legal agreement, collateral arrangement and any applicable clearing requirement. A futures contract expresses similar directional economics but is standardised by an exchange. Contract size, delivery months, eligible deliverables or cash-settlement method and trading rules are predefined. The clearing house becomes central to performance through the market’s clearing structure. Positions are marked to market and variation margin moves gains and losses through cash over the life of the contract. That daily settlement creates an important difference. A forward usually realises most value at maturity or close-out, while a future transfers P&L through daily margin. If interest rates are correlated with the underlying, the timing of those cash flows can make futures and otherwise comparable forwards have slightly different prices. Futures require initial margin or equivalent performance resources and are subject to exchange price limits, position limits or other market rules where applicable. Standardisation improves fungibility and liquidity but removes some customisation. Forwards can match a bespoke exposure exactly but may be less liquid and more operationally bespoke. Neither contract is “safer” in all senses. Central clearing materially changes counterparty and liquidity risk, but it also creates margin liquidity requirements and dependence on clearing infrastructure. Bilateral forwards can be collateralised and may also be centrally cleared in some markets. The BA test is to separate economic exposure from processing model: contract economics, trading venue, clearing status, margining, settlement method and legal documentation are distinct data attributes. ### Permanent rule Separate payoff equivalence from infrastructure differences. ### Permanent trap Assuming an exchange-traded future and a bilateral forward with the same maturity must have identical operational cash flows. ### Never confuse **Forward** — future transaction under bilaterally agreed terms. --- **Future** — standardised future transaction traded on an exchange and processed through its clearing framework. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Options: Moneyness, Intrinsic Value and Time Value
one_screen: An option buys asymmetry: the holder has a right, not an obligation, to transact at the strike. Option premium is commonly decomposed into intrinsic value plus time value, while moneyness describes where spot sits relative to strike.
bodyText: A call option gives its holder the right to buy the underlying at the strike price; a put gives the right to sell. The holder pays a premium for that right. The writer receives the premium and assumes the contingent obligation if the option is exercised under its terms. At expiry, a plain call’s intrinsic value is max(S − K, 0), while a plain put’s is max(K − S, 0), where S is the underlying price and K the strike. Before expiry, the option can be worth more than current intrinsic value because there is still time for favourable market moves. That additional component is time value. Moneyness is a relative description. A call is in the money when the underlying is above the strike and a put is in the money when the underlying is below the strike. “At the money” is used when spot or the relevant forward is close to strike, depending on market convention. In-the-money does not mean profitable overall: a call can have positive intrinsic value but still fail to recover the premium originally paid. Time value generally increases with remaining time and expected volatility, all else equal, because more possible future paths can create favourable exercise outcomes. It normally decays toward zero as expiry approaches. Interest rates, dividends, carry and settlement style also affect option value. American-style options can generally be exercised before expiry; European-style options only at expiry. The labels describe exercise style, not geography. A complete option definition must include call/put, buyer/seller, underlying, strike, expiry, notional, style, settlement, premium and any barrier or other feature. Without these, “long option” is not a complete economic position. ### Permanent rule In-the-money describes exercise value relative to strike; it does not tell you the trade’s total profit after premium. ### Permanent trap Assuming an option with zero intrinsic value before expiry is worthless. It may still have substantial time value. ### Never confuse **Moneyness** — relationship between underlying price and strike under the relevant option convention. --- **Profitability** — economic P&L after premium and all relevant cash flows. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: The Option Greeks
one_screen: The Greeks are local sensitivities, not separate risks: delta measures underlying-price sensitivity, gamma the change in delta, vega volatility sensitivity and theta time decay. They describe how an option’s value responds when one input moves while others are held approximately constant.
bodyText: Option value depends on multiple variables simultaneously, so a single P&L number does not explain the risk. The Greeks approximate how value changes when specific pricing inputs move. Delta is the change in option value for a small change in the underlying. A call generally has positive delta and a put negative delta from the holder’s perspective. Delta is often used to construct a local hedge in the underlying. Gamma is the rate at which delta changes as the underlying moves. Long plain options generally have positive gamma: large moves in either direction can improve the delta-adjusted payoff relative to a static hedge, though the option holder pays for that convexity through premium and time decay. Vega measures sensitivity to implied volatility. Long plain options generally benefit when implied volatility rises, all else equal. Despite the name, vega is not a Greek letter. Theta measures the passage of time, commonly expressed as expected value decay per day with other inputs held constant. Long plain options often have negative theta because the opportunity for favourable future movement shrinks as expiry approaches. Rho measures sensitivity to interest rates and can matter more for long-dated options. Cross-Greeks and higher-order sensitivities become important for complex books, but delta, gamma, vega and theta provide the core mental model. The Greeks are model-dependent and local. A delta measured now can change after a price move, volatility change or passage of time. They also depend on conventions such as spot versus forward delta and volatility quoting practice. A trader may describe a position as “delta neutral” while still carrying substantial gamma and vega. Neutralising first-order direction is therefore not equivalent to eliminating option risk. ### Permanent rule Greeks are local derivatives of value; always ask the unit, sign convention, model and valuation point. ### Permanent trap Calling a delta-neutral book risk-free. Gamma, vega, theta, basis and model risks remain. ### Never confuse **Delta** — first-order option-value sensitivity to the underlying. --- **Gamma** — sensitivity of delta to changes in the underlying. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Optionality
one_screen: Optionality means one party controls a future choice whose value changes with market conditions. It can be explicit, as in an option contract, or embedded inside another product, as in a callable bond or prepayable loan.
bodyText: Optionality is broader than a listed option. Any contract that gives one party a meaningful right to change timing, quantity or price contingent on future conditions contains optionality. A callable bond gives the issuer a right to redeem early. A puttable bond gives the investor a right to sell back. A mortgage borrower may have a prepayment option. A swap may contain cancellation rights, caps, floors or extension features. The owner of an option benefits from discretion: exercise when favourable, decline when unfavourable. The other party is short that discretion. This asymmetry changes valuation because future cash flows are no longer fixed. Expected exercise depends on market levels, volatility, time, transaction costs and behavioural or contractual constraints. Embedded optionality can reverse otherwise simple risk. A fixed-rate bond without options usually rises when rates fall. A callable bond may stop rising as quickly once refinancing becomes attractive to the issuer. The investor is effectively short a call on the bond, so positive duration alone no longer tells the whole story. Optionality also appears operationally. A cancellation right may require notice by a specific cut-off. A barrier option may activate or terminate when a price is observed under defined market-source rules. A wrong event date, fixing source or exercise status can therefore produce a valuation and settlement break even when the model is correct. For analysis, identify four elements: who owns the choice, what action can be taken, when it can be taken, and what market state makes exercise valuable. Then ask how that choice changes expected cash flows and sensitivities. The durable insight is that products with the same headline maturity, coupon or notional can carry radically different risks if optionality differs. The option owner’s flexibility is an economic asset; somebody else is paying for it. ### Permanent rule If future cash flows can change because one party has discretion, model the option before trusting linear risk measures. ### Permanent trap Treating a callable or prepayable instrument as a plain fixed-cash-flow bond merely because its coupon is fixed. ### Never confuse **Explicit option** — standalone contract whose main purpose is the exercise right. --- **Embedded option** — exercise right contained inside another instrument or financing contract. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Interest Rate Swaps
one_screen: A plain interest-rate swap exchanges fixed and floating interest cash flows on a notional principal. The notional usually is not exchanged; the swap converts the economic rate exposure of an asset or liability without refinancing the underlying principal.
bodyText: In a plain fixed-for-floating interest-rate swap, one party pays a fixed rate and receives a floating rate; the other does the opposite. Both legs are calculated on a common notional amount under defined day counts, payment frequencies, business-day rules and reference-rate conventions. The notional is normally a calculation base, not principal that changes hands. If a company has floating-rate debt and pays fixed in a swap while receiving a matching floating reference rate, the combination can approximate fixed-rate funding, subject to basis, credit, timing and documentation differences. At inception, the fixed rate on an at-market swap is chosen so the present values of the two legs are approximately equal, making initial fair value near zero before transaction costs and credit/funding adjustments. Afterwards, market rates move and the swap acquires positive value to one party and negative value to the other. A swap is not one “interest rate”. The fixed leg has a coupon schedule; the floating leg references a rate definition and reset method; discounting uses an appropriate collateral/funding framework; separate curves may be used for projecting floating coupons and discounting cash flows. This multi-curve setup became standard after the global financial crisis and benchmark reform. Risk can be expressed through DV01/PV01 by tenor bucket. A pay-fixed swap generally loses value when the relevant swap rates fall and gains when they rise, from the pay-fixed party’s perspective, all else equal. However, exact exposure depends on curve shape, reset dates and collateral terms. Operationally, the trade must preserve notional, currency, effective date, maturity, fixed rate, floating-rate option, reset frequency, payment frequency, day count, calendars, compounding method and clearing status. “Five-year swap” is not sufficient to reconstruct economics. ### Permanent rule An IRS exchanges interest cash flows; do not assume the notional principal itself is funded or transferred. ### Permanent trap Treating the floating leg, projection curve and discount curve as the same concept. ### Never confuse **Fixed leg** — contractual interest payments based on a predetermined fixed rate. --- **Floating leg** — payments determined from a specified floating-rate option and calculation method. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: IBOR Reform and Risk-Free Rates
one_screen: LIBOR is over. Modern rate markets use alternative overnight risk-free or near-risk-free benchmarks and explicit fallback mechanics. The durable lesson is that replacing a term unsecured bank rate with an overnight rate changes conventions, not just the ticker.
bodyText: Interbank offered rates such as LIBOR were historically embedded in loans, bonds, swaps and valuation systems. Benchmark reform replaced them because panel-based unsecured term borrowing became less robust as the underlying market shrank. Alternative reference rates are generally grounded more directly in overnight transactions or robust market data. The transition was not a simple label substitution. LIBOR contained bank credit and term components. Overnight risk-free rates such as SONIA for sterling and SOFR for US dollars have different economic bases. A contract moving from a forward-looking term IBOR to an overnight rate may need compounding in arrears, observation shifts, lookbacks, payment delays or a published term-RFR convention. Spread adjustments may be needed to preserve economic value during fallback. Fallback language is therefore a core contract feature. It defines what happens if the benchmark is unavailable, non-representative or permanently ceases. Derivatives markets used ISDA fallback frameworks; cash products may have different statutory or contractual solutions. Basis can remain between instruments that transition under different rules. **Perishable knowledge — checked 28 August 2026:** all 35 LIBOR settings have permanently ceased. The final synthetic US dollar LIBOR settings ceased after publication on 30 September 2024. References to “current LIBOR fixing” in a 2026 production system should therefore trigger a legacy-data or contract-state question, not a request for today’s rate. India’s benchmark landscape differs by product; MIBOR and other domestic benchmarks should not be casually called “Indian LIBOR”. Benchmark family, administrator, tenor, calculation method and fallback must be stored explicitly. For BAs and risk teams, the main migration lesson is data lineage: every affected trade needs the original benchmark, fallback hierarchy, spread adjustment, effective trigger, calculation method and downstream valuation/reporting treatment. ### Permanent rule Benchmark migration changes economics and calculation conventions; never perform a ticker-only replacement. ### Permanent trap Assuming LIBOR still has live settings because legacy contracts or database fields still contain the word LIBOR. ### Never confuse **IBOR** — interbank offered-rate family historically intended to reflect term unsecured bank funding. --- **RFR** — risk-free or near-risk-free reference rate, commonly based on overnight markets. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN — No universal one-for-one LIBOR replacement exists across all INR products; use the benchmark specified by the instrument and applicable Indian market rules.**UK — Perishable, checked 28 August 2026.** SONIA is the principal sterling RFR. The FCA states that all LIBOR settings have permanently ceased; the final synthetic LIBOR settings ended by 30 September 2024. **EU — EURIBOR remains a separate benchmark and should not be described as LIBOR. Euro derivatives also use €STR-based conventions. **US — US dollar LIBOR has ceased; SOFR is the principal US dollar RFR used in the transition framework.**

title: OIS and Discounting
one_screen: An overnight index swap exchanges a fixed rate against an overnight-rate-based floating leg. In collateralised derivatives, overnight-rate curves became central to discounting because the collateral remuneration rate is part of the economics of funding future cash flows.
bodyText: An overnight index swap, or OIS, is an interest-rate swap whose floating leg is linked to an overnight reference rate compounded or averaged over the accrual period according to the contract. Examples include SONIA, SOFR and €STR-linked swaps. The fixed OIS rate is the market rate that equates the present value of fixed and overnight-based floating legs at inception. OIS rates matter beyond the product itself. For a collateralised derivative, the appropriate discount rate is closely connected to the rate earned or paid on posted cash collateral under the collateral agreement. Post-crisis markets therefore moved away from using a single unsecured IBOR curve for both projected cash flows and discounting. Multi-curve valuation separates the curve used to project a floating benchmark from the curve used to discount collateralised cash flows. This distinction can feel abstract but has a direct P&L effect. Suppose a swap pays a term benchmark but is collateralised daily in cash remunerated at an overnight rate. Future floating coupons may be projected from one curve while discounted using an overnight-based curve. Changing the collateral currency or remuneration convention can change discounting and therefore fair value. An OIS rate is not the same as the overnight fixing itself. The fixing is one observed overnight rate; an OIS rate is a market price for a future sequence of overnight outcomes over the swap period. Operationally, compounding details matter: observation dates, lookbacks, lockouts, holidays, publication times and negative-rate handling can all affect the floating amount. The exact ISDA floating-rate option and version should therefore be treated as contractual data. The mental model is two questions: which curve generates the future cash flow, and which curve discounts that cash flow back to today? They may be related, but they are not automatically identical. ### Permanent rule Projection and discounting are separate valuation functions. ### Permanent trap Calling an OIS curve merely the “risk-free forecast curve” and ignoring the collateral agreement that makes its use economically relevant. ### Never confuse **Overnight fixing** — observed overnight reference rate for a specific date. --- **OIS rate** — fixed rate on a swap against compounded/averaged overnight rates over a future period. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Credit Default Swaps
one_screen: A CDS transfers defined credit-event risk on a reference entity or obligation. The protection buyer pays premium; the protection seller makes a credit-event settlement if the contractually defined event occurs.
bodyText: A credit default swap, or CDS, is a derivative on credit risk rather than a funded bond purchase. The protection buyer pays periodic premium, often quoted as a spread on notional. The protection seller receives that premium and owes a settlement amount if a contractually defined credit event occurs during the protection period. The reference entity is the legal borrower whose credit is referenced. Reference obligations and deliverable obligations can matter for determining events or settlement under the applicable definitions. A credit event is not simply “the bond price fell”. It must satisfy contractual definitions such as bankruptcy, failure to pay or restructuring where applicable. After a credit event, settlement can be physical or cash depending on contract and market process. In cash settlement, an auction-determined recovery price is commonly used so that loss is approximately notional × (1 − recovery price), subject to the contract. This resembles LGD economically but is a market settlement value, not an accounting recovery estimate. CDS spread reflects the market price of credit protection. It is influenced by default expectations, recovery, liquidity, risk premia, funding and technical demand. It should not be converted directly into probability of default without a pricing model. Buying CDS protection can hedge a bond’s default/spread exposure, but hedge effectiveness depends on matching reference entity, seniority, maturity, currency, restructuring terms and basis. The cash bond and CDS can trade at different implied spreads; this difference is called the CDS-bond basis. Counterparty risk remains because the protection seller must perform precisely when the reference credit may be deteriorating. Collateral, clearing and legal documentation therefore matter alongside reference-credit risk. ### Permanent rule A CDS pays on a defined contractual credit event, not on any deterioration in credit quality. ### Permanent trap Treating CDS notional as a funded loan exposure or treating a spread widening as if a credit event has already occurred. ### Never confuse **Reference entity** — borrower or legal entity whose credit risk the CDS references. --- **Counterparty** — the party on the other side of the CDS contract that must perform under the derivative. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Credit Indices
one_screen: A credit index packages CDS exposure to a standard basket of reference entities into one tradable contract. It gives broad credit-spread exposure, while single-name defaults are handled through defined index mechanics rather than turning the product into a static bond fund.
bodyText: A credit default swap index references a standardised basket of corporate or sovereign credits. Major index families include CDX and iTraxx. Instead of negotiating separate CDS trades on every constituent, a market participant can buy or sell protection on the index and obtain diversified credit-spread exposure in one contract. The index has a series and version. Periodically, a new series is launched with a refreshed constituent set according to index rules. The old series continues to trade “off the run”. This creates an important data requirement: “five-year index” is incomplete without family, series, version and maturity. Index premium is commonly quoted as a spread, though some higher-risk indices can trade with upfront amounts plus a standard coupon. When a constituent experiences a credit event, the index notional and cash flows are adjusted under the relevant rules. The remaining index continues to exist rather than being recreated from scratch for every default. Credit indices serve several purposes: macro hedging of a credit portfolio, directional views on market credit spreads, relative-value trades and liquidity management. They are usually more liquid than a large set of equivalent single-name CDS positions, but basis risk arises because an institution’s actual portfolio will not exactly match index constituents, weights, maturities or seniorities. An index is not the same as a tranche. The unfunded index provides proportional exposure to the underlying names. A tranche concentrates losses into a defined attachment/detachment layer and introduces strong non-linearity and correlation sensitivity. For risk data, map the index contract to its legal identifier, series, constituent set and effective dates. A position can appear unchanged at the front-office label level while its risk mapping changes when a new index series becomes the market benchmark. ### Permanent rule Index family plus series/version is part of the instrument identity. ### Permanent trap Treating a CDS index as interchangeable with a cash bond index or with a tranched credit product. ### Never confuse **CDS index** — standard basket of CDS reference credits traded as one derivative. --- **Credit tranche** — layered loss exposure with attachment and detachment points and non-linear default sensitivity. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Exchange-Traded and OTC Markets
one_screen: Exchange trading standardises the contract and market process; OTC trading allows bilateral or platform-based negotiation of bespoke terms. Trading venue, clearing venue and legal counterparty are separate questions.
bodyText: Exchange-traded markets list standardised instruments under exchange rules. Contract size, expiry, tick size, trading hours and settlement method are predefined. Orders interact through the venue’s market structure, and listed derivatives are ordinarily processed through a central clearing framework. Over-the-counter, or OTC, means the transaction is not executed as a listed exchange contract. Terms can be customised and trading may occur bilaterally, through dealers or on electronic platforms. OTC does not automatically mean “uncleared”: many OTC derivatives are centrally cleared, either because regulation requires it or because parties choose clearing. This leads to three separate dimensions. Execution asks where and how the trade is agreed. Clearing asks whether a CCP interposes itself after execution. Settlement asks how the resulting cash or securities obligations are finally discharged. A trade can be executed on an electronic venue, centrally cleared and then cash-settled; those are three different lifecycle facts. Standardisation generally supports liquidity, transparency and fungibility. Bespoke OTC terms can better match a real exposure but increase confirmation, valuation and operational complexity. OTC legal relationships also depend heavily on master agreements, collateral documents and counterparty-specific terms. Price discovery differs by market. An exchange may publish a visible order book, while dealer OTC markets can use request-for-quote, streaming prices or voice negotiation. “OTC” therefore should not be used as a synonym for opaque or manual. For technology and controls, instrument source, execution venue, trading capacity, clearing status, clearing broker, CCP, confirmation route and settlement method should be separate fields. Combining them into one “market type” flag creates ambiguity that later appears in reporting, margin and reconciliation logic. ### Permanent rule Execution venue does not determine clearing status by itself. ### Permanent trap Using “OTC” to mean bilateral, uncleared, manual and uncollateralised all at once. ### Never confuse **Execution** — the process by which parties agree the trade. --- **Clearing** — the post-trade process that establishes and manages obligations, potentially through a CCP. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Central Counterparties and Novation
one_screen: A CCP interposes itself between market participants so each faces the CCP rather than the original trading counterparty for cleared obligations. Novation changes the legal counterparty; it does not make risk disappear.
bodyText: A central counterparty, or CCP, becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer for transactions accepted for clearing. In a common legal mechanism, the original bilateral contract is replaced or transformed so that each participant has an obligation to the CCP rather than directly to the original counterparty. This concentration changes the shape of counterparty risk. Bilateral exposure across many trading partners can be multilateral-netted within the clearing framework. The CCP collects margin, maintains a default-management process and holds financial resources designed to absorb losses under defined scenarios. Participants may contribute to a default fund in addition to posting initial and variation margin. Variation margin transfers current mark-to-market gains and losses. Initial margin is intended to cover potential future exposure during the period needed to close or hedge a defaulted position. A CCP may also apply concentration, liquidity or add-on charges. Clearing therefore reduces some bilateral risks but creates dependence on the CCP and its members. Liquidity demands can rise sharply when volatility increases and margin calls grow. A participant can be economically hedged but still fail if it cannot meet cash margin on time. Novation must also be distinguished from trade affirmation. Matching confirms that both sides agree trade economics; novation changes the legal counterparty relationship. Not every clearing model uses identical legal wording, so system design should not hard-code one legal mechanism globally. The PFMI set international standards for systemically important CCPs and other financial market infrastructures. For a BA, the key data chain is original trade → clearing eligibility → clearing submission → acceptance → cleared position → margin and settlement. A rejected clearing submission may leave the original bilateral risk alive, depending on the legal arrangement. ### Permanent rule CCP clearing redistributes and manages counterparty risk; it does not abolish credit or liquidity risk. ### Permanent trap Assuming a matched trade is already novated to the CCP before clearing acceptance. ### Never confuse **Novation** — replacement of an original contractual relationship with new obligations involving another counterparty. --- **Netting** — combining multiple obligations into reduced net obligations under enforceable rules. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Clearing, Settlement and Settlement Cycles
one_screen: Clearing determines what each party owes; settlement discharges those obligations by moving cash and securities. T+1 means standard settlement is one business day after trade date—it does not mean every market, instrument or failed trade settles then.
bodyText: Trade execution creates obligations, but ownership and cash are not fully exchanged until settlement. Clearing sits between these points: trades are validated, matched, netted where applicable and translated into settlement obligations. Settlement then moves securities through a depository or settlement system and cash through the relevant payment mechanism. A settlement cycle is expressed relative to trade date, T. Under T+1, a trade agreed on Monday normally has Tuesday as its intended settlement date, subject to market holidays and instrument-specific rules. Faster settlement reduces the period during which market and counterparty exposures can accumulate, but it also compresses the time available for allocation, affirmation, funding, securities borrowing and FX. Delivery versus payment, or DvP, links delivery of securities to payment so that one leg does not complete without the corresponding other leg under the infrastructure’s model. In FX, payment versus payment, or PvP, addresses principal risk across currencies. These mechanisms reduce settlement risk but do not guarantee that a participant will have the required cash or securities on time. Settlement fails remain possible. A fail can arise from missing securities, insufficient cash, incorrect standing settlement instructions, unmatched economic details or operational cut-offs. The intended settlement date and actual settlement date are therefore separate data fields. **Perishable knowledge — checked 28 August 2026:** major jurisdictions are not synchronised. India and the US already use T+1 broadly for cash equities; India also operates optional T+0 for eligible equity-cash trades. The UK and EU are preparing for T+1 on 11 October 2027. Cross-border operating models must therefore handle mismatched cycles until convergence. The durable control is to model settlement by instrument and market, not by a global “T+1” assumption. ### Permanent rule Trade date, intended settlement date and actual settlement date are distinct lifecycle facts. ### Permanent trap Hard-coding one settlement cycle for all securities because a jurisdiction’s headline equity market is T+1. ### Never confuse **Clearing** — determination and management of obligations before final discharge. --- **Settlement** — final transfer of cash, securities or other assets that discharges those obligations. ### Jurisdiction variants **IN — Perishable, checked 28 August 2026.** SEBI states that the existing equity-cash settlement cycle is T+1 and has also introduced an optional T+0 cycle for eligible trades, with scope expanded after the 2024 beta. **UK — Perishable, checked 28 August 2026.** The UK government has committed to mandate T+1 from 11 October 2027; until then the general statutory standard remains T+2 for the relevant securities. **EU — Perishable, checked 28 August 2026.** The European Commission has proposed 11 October 2027 for the EU move to T+1. **US — Perishable, checked 28 August 2026.** The standard cycle for most broker-dealer securities transactions moved to T+1 on 28 May 2024.

title: The Trade Lifecycle
one_screen: A trade is not complete when it is executed. It must be captured, enriched, validated, confirmed, cleared where relevant, settled, valued, margined, reported and maintained through every lifecycle event until maturity or close-out.
bodyText: The trade lifecycle is the controlled transformation of an agreed transaction into legally, operationally and financially completed obligations. Different products use different infrastructure, but the core stages recur. Execution creates the commercial agreement. Trade capture records economics in the institution’s systems. Enrichment adds reference data such as legal entity, book, account, settlement instructions and clearing attributes. Validation checks that mandatory fields and eligibility rules are satisfied. Confirmation or affirmation establishes that counterparties agree the terms. Clearing may follow for eligible derivatives or securities markets. Once accepted, the trade can become a cleared position with CCP margin obligations. Settlement moves cash, securities or other deliverables. For longer-lived derivatives, the lifecycle then continues through resets, fixings, coupons, option exercises, margin calls, collateral substitutions and valuations. Regulatory reporting can occur at multiple points and is not the same as internal booking. A trade can be correctly settled but incorrectly reported if identifiers, timestamps or counterparty classifications are wrong. Conversely, a reporting acknowledgement does not prove economic settlement. Events change the trade after booking. A partial termination reduces notional. A novation changes a counterparty. An amendment changes terms. A compression exercise may replace many trades with fewer economically equivalent ones. Corporate actions can alter securities positions. Every event requires lineage from the original trade state to the new state. The most useful BA model is state plus event. Instead of treating a trade as one database row, treat it as an object whose state changes through authorised events. Each downstream system should know whether it consumes original economics, current economics, event history or settlement outputs. Breaks occur when two systems are correct about different states. The control question is therefore: what event has each system processed, using what effective timestamp and source? ### Permanent rule A trade lifecycle is a sequence of state changes, not a single booking event. ### Permanent trap Calling a trade “done” once front office has booked it. ### Never confuse **Trade state** — the current contractual and operational condition of a transaction. --- **Lifecycle event** — an authorised occurrence that changes, settles or terminates part of that state. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Front Office, Middle Office and Back Office
one_screen: Front, middle and back office are responsibility patterns, not universal organisation charts. Front office takes and manages commercial risk; middle-office functions control and explain it; back office completes confirmations, payments, settlements and records.
bodyText: The three-office model is a useful map of responsibilities, but real banks divide work differently. A function’s name should never be treated as proof of its control role. Front office originates, prices, executes and manages positions. Traders, sales staff and structurers may own revenue and market-risk decisions within limits. Their systems prioritise fast pricing, inventory, client activity and position management. Middle-office responsibilities commonly include independent trade validation, P&L explanation, risk monitoring, limit control, product control, valuations, collateral oversight or change support. Some firms place product control in finance, market risk in an independent risk function and collateral in operations. The durable principle is independence from the risk-taker where a control must challenge the risk-taker. Back office focuses on completion and books-and-records processes: confirmations, settlements, payments, reconciliations, asset servicing, static-data maintenance and exception management. Automation has blurred traditional boundaries, but accountability remains essential. A single trade can therefore move through several control lenses. Front office says, “Is the price and risk right?” Product control asks, “Is the P&L complete and independently explainable?” Risk asks, “Is exposure within appetite and limits?” Operations asks, “Can the contractual cash and asset movements be completed?” Finance asks, “Is it reflected correctly in books and disclosures?” Segregation of duties matters because the person who can create or change a risk position should not also be the sole person validating its valuation, limit use and settlement. System entitlements, maker-checker controls and independent price verification operationalise this principle. For BAs, map responsibilities through RACI and data ownership rather than organisational labels. “Middle office owns it” is not a requirement. Identify who creates, approves, enriches, challenges, settles and reconciles each field or event. ### Permanent rule Design controls around independence and accountability, not around department names. ### Permanent trap Assuming every bank uses the same FO/MO/BO boundary. ### Never confuse **Risk owner** — function authorised to take or manage commercial exposure. --- **Control owner** — function accountable for independently validating or constraining that exposure or its processing. ### Jurisdiction variants **No delta.**

title: Static Data and Reference Data
one_screen: Reference data tells systems what an entity, instrument, calendar or code means; transactional data tells them what happened. A wrong static field can contaminate thousands of correct trades, which is why golden sources, effective dating and lineage matter.
bodyText: Trading systems depend on data that changes less frequently than trades but controls how trades behave. Instrument reference data can include identifiers, issuer, currency, coupon, maturity, day-count basis, option terms and exchange. Counterparty data can include legal entity identifiers, regulatory classifications, agreements and settlement eligibility. Market reference data includes calendars, currencies, indices and benchmark definitions. Standing settlement instructions specify where cash or securities should move. “Static” does not mean immutable. A counterparty can merge, a rating can change, an instrument can undergo a corporate action, a benchmark can cease and settlement instructions can be updated. Reference data therefore needs effective dates and version history. The central design problem is identity. A ticker is not globally unique. A legal entity name can vary across systems. A listed company, its parent, a bond issuer and a trading counterparty may be related but legally distinct. Stable identifiers such as ISINs, LEIs and internal mastered IDs help, but mappings and validity periods still matter. Golden source means the authoritative source for a defined field, not one database that must own everything. Market data may come from a vendor, legal-entity data from client onboarding, product definitions from a securities master and accounting mappings from finance. Each field should have an owner and lineage. Reference-data errors have multiplicative effects.
